item.description: The measurement giant absorbs the verification leader in a deal that folds audience, context and quality signals into one platform.
item.content:encoded:
The measurement giant absorbs the verification leader in a deal that folds audience, context and quality signals into one platform.

Nielsen to Buy DoubleVerify for $2.15 Billion

The measurement giant absorbs the verification leader in a deal that folds audience, context and quality signals into one platform.

Nielsen agreed to acquire DoubleVerify for $13.60 per share in an all-cash deal valuing the ad-verification company at roughly $2.15 billion, a 30% premium to its 60-day average price. The companies say the combined business will generate more than $4 billion in annual revenue; DoubleVerify will keep operating under its own brand as a Nielsen subsidiary once the deal closes, expected in Q1 2027 pending shareholder and regulatory approval. It consolidates measurement and verification into fewer hands right as CTV buyers lean harder on both for trust in programmatic spend.

Disney Weighs Free Ad-Supported Streaming Tier

CEO Josh D'Amaro says streaming inventory is nearly sold out, eyeing a free product to unlock more ad revenue.

Disney disclosed it is exploring a free, ad-supported streaming product as CEO Josh D'Amaro leans further into streaming as a core growth platform, telling investors existing ad inventory is 'fairly well sold.' Disney also confirmed Super Bowl LX ad inventory on ABC and ESPN has sold out, with 30-second spots reportedly fetching $9 million. Entertainment streaming operating income more than doubled to $712 million for the quarter, giving Disney a new lever to pull for incremental ad-supported reach as CTV budgets keep shifting from linear.

FreeWheel Opens the Black Box on Show-Level CTV Delivery

New Video Content Report gives buyers series-level data two hours after impressions run.

FreeWheel launched Video Content Report inside its Buyer Cloud platform, giving programmatic CTV buyers visibility into which TV series their ads actually ran alongside — a transparency gap that has persisted for nearly a decade in streaming. Seven publishers opted in at launch, including NBCUniversal, Paramount, Warner Bros. Discovery, A+E Global Media and Xumo, with reports available roughly two hours post-delivery. Advertiser Perceptions research cited alongside the launch found over half of CTV advertisers would shift spend to publishers offering show-level transparency, making this a direct answer to buyers' biggest standing complaint about streaming's black-box inventory.

MNTN Grows 21%, Swings to Profit, Adds $100M Buyback

Self-serve performance-TV customers climb 40% as the format keeps scaling past the big managed desks.

MNTN reported Q2 revenue of $82.5 million, up 21% year-over-year and at the high end of guidance, with adjusted EBITDA up 48% to $21.5 million and gross margin expanding to 80%. Active performance-TV customers grew about 40% to 4,225, and the company swung to $6.7 million in net income from a $26.2 million loss a year earlier; the board authorized a $100 million buyback. Q3 guidance points to 25% growth, reinforcing that self-serve, outcomes-counted CTV is still scaling even as larger managed-service DSPs stumble.

LiveRamp Folds Meta Into Cross-Media Measurement Suite

Brands can now de-duplicate Meta performance against CTV, programmatic and audio in a single clean room.

LiveRamp announced Meta is now a reporting source inside its Cross-Media Intelligence platform, giving marketers de-duplicated attribution and incrementality measurement from Meta alongside CTV, programmatic, social and audio investments within the LiveRamp Clean Room. The expansion lets brand advertisers compare social performance directly against CTV spend in one unified, privacy-safe report rather than reconciling disparate walled-garden numbers by hand. As agencies push for cross-channel accountability amid tightening budgets, this closes one of the more persistent measurement gaps between social and CTV buys.

IAB Tech Lab Ships AAMP 2.3 for Agentic Ad Buying

Update wires privacy diligence and Google Ad Manager reporting into the agentic protocol stack.

IAB Tech Lab released AAMP 2.3 on July 30, integrating the IAB Diligence Platform and SafeGuard Privacy directly into the Buyer Agent, plus support for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Meta buying, and Google Ad Manager reporting. The update finalizes pricing-integrity and platform-support standards meant to make AI agents deployable inside existing ad infrastructure. As agentic buying protocols race toward production, this is the clearest signal yet that CTV/programmatic platforms will need to support agent-to-agent transacting within the next buying cycle.

Trade Desk Posts Rare Miss, Guides to Revenue Decline

A rebuilt C-suite inherits a Q3 forecast that turns growth deceleration into an outright drop.

The Trade Desk's Q2 revenue grew just 3% to $715 million, missing estimates of $751.6 million, and EPS of $0.34 fell short of the $0.40 consensus; shares fell more than 20% on the print. CEO Jeff Green cited poor execution and clients shifting to cheaper media, and Q3 guidance implies a roughly 12% revenue decline — the first outright drop in the company's public history. The miss lands weeks after Trade Desk hired a new CFO, chief commercial officer, CMO and board director in under two months, a full C-suite reset the company is calling a "changing of the guard."

Magnite Beats, Raises Guidance as CTV Grows 36%

Magnite reported Q2 contribution ex-TAC of $190 million, up 17% year-over-year, and adjusted EBITDA up 30% to $71 million, beating estimates on both revenue and earnings. CTV contribution ex-TAC jumped 36% year-over-year to $97 million, with top-10 CTV accounts accelerating to mid-to-high-40% growth across partners including Disney, Netflix, Roku and Warner Bros. Discovery. The company raised full-year guidance to 13-14% contribution ex-TAC growth and at least 37% adjusted EBITDA margin, and shares jumped over 11% — a sharp contrast to the sell-side's mood around The Trade Desk the same week.

Teads Sues Google Over Lost Ad Exchange Impressions

The lawsuit leans directly on a Virginia federal court's prior finding that Google's ad-tech conduct was unlawful.

Teads filed suit against Google and Alphabet in the Southern District of New York on August 3, seeking treble damages and injunctive relief, alleging Google's tying of AdX to its buying tools cost Teads an estimated 6.88 trillion ad impressions to rival exchanges. The complaint builds on the Eastern District of Virginia's ruling that Google held illegal monopolies in the ad server and exchange markets. It's the clearest sign yet that last year's antitrust liability finding is now generating private damages claims from ad-tech rivals, with the DOJ's remedies ruling in the same case still pending.

UK Clears Paramount Skydance's Bid for Warner Bros. Discovery

The CMA waves through the $110B tie-up without a Phase 2 probe, even as a US antitrust trial still looms.

The UK Competition and Markets Authority formally cleared Paramount Skydance's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on August 6, declining to refer the deal for deeper review and finding no UK competition concerns. The clearance follows earlier approvals from the EU, Australia, Canada and other jurisdictions, though Paramount Skydance has separately agreed with a coalition of US state attorneys general not to close the deal until after an antitrust trial. A combined Paramount-WBD would reshape upfront and programmatic supply relationships across HBO Max, Paramount+ and CBS/Discovery's ad-tech stack, a live variable for any buyer planning 2027 budgets.

Roku Adds Zip-Code Targeting Ahead of Midterm Ad Surge

Self-serve, AI-assisted political creative arrives as AdImpact lifts its 2026 cycle forecast to $11.6 billion.

Roku says 2026 midterm campaigns will be among the first to use its regionally targeted, zip-code-segmented ad tools, pairing self-serve buying with AI-generated creative; analysts project the platform could see roughly 25% platform-revenue growth aided by political and World Cup demand. Roku requires political advertisers to be identified and verified before campaigns launch. The rollout comes as AdImpact's latest tracking puts the full 2026 cycle at a record $11.6 billion, with CTV's projected share at $2.7 billion 23% — the only media type AdImpact expects to grow versus 2024. With Netflix and Prime Video still declining political ads, the dollars keep concentrating on Hulu, Roku and YouTube.

Ofcom: Netflix Overtakes BBC as UK's First Viewing Choice

Media Nations 2026 finds linear reach still sliding as streaming saturates younger audiences.

Ofcom's Media Nations UK 2026 report, published July 29, found Netflix now edges out the BBC as UK viewers' first choice 26% vs 25% , while broadcaster linear reach continues its decline and streaming subscriptions show signs of plateauing among younger audiences. The report lands weeks after ITV, Channel 4 and Sky's joint Universal Ads self-serve marketplace opened UK premium video to SME advertisers for the first time. Together they frame the UK's core ad-market tension: linear's audience keeps shrinking even as new programmatic access points multiply around it.

Omnicom and JioStar Pilot Scene-Matched In-Content Ads

NIVEA becomes the first brand tested across linear soaps, OTT and CTV under a single unified buy.

Omnicom Media India, JioStar and Whisper World launched a unified in-content advertising program that embeds 15-second scene-matched brand messages inside soap-opera episodes across Star and Colors channels, mirrored simultaneously on JioHotstar's mobile and connected-TV surfaces, with NIVEA India as the launch brand. The program uses Acxiom TV Segments for audience targeting and tracks reach, frequency, GRPs and brand lift across the combined footprint. It's a notable test of cross-screen, single-buy activation in India's fast-consolidating JioStar-dominated CTV market, ahead of expected Sony/Zee rate responses.

LATAM Leads Global FAST Growth as Ad Impressions Jump 124%

Amagi's latest AIRTIME report shows Latin America outpacing every other region on viewing-hour growth.

Amagi's June 2026 AIRTIME report, covering roughly 6,500 FAST channel deliveries between April and mid-June, found LATAM posting the strongest regional growth worldwide — hours of viewing up 190% and ad impressions up 124% year over year — as the company adds high-viewership channels across the region. Globally, FAST hours of viewing grew 55% and ad impressions 53%, with poor metadata cited as the main drag on discovery and monetization. LATAM's outsized growth confirms it as the region where ad-supported streaming inventory is expanding fastest, even as measurement infrastructure lags.

Corus Layoffs Squeeze Canadian Broadcaster's CTV Pivot

Global News consolidates morning shows as ad-revenue decline forces a 25% headcount cut.

Corus Entertainment is centralizing local Global News Morning production across its Prairie and Eastern markets after a fresh round of layoffs, part of a plan to cut its full-time workforce roughly 25% nearly 800 jobs by end of summer amid persistently falling ad sales and rising debt. The consolidation lands as Canadian industry forecasts put CTV and audio as the only channels expected to see programmatic budget growth this year, with CTV projected to capture 26% of media budgets on average. It's a stark illustration of the linear-to-programmatic value transfer playing out inside a single struggling Canadian broadcaster.

Beijing's Ad-Disclosure Crackdown Runs Through September

SAMR's six-month enforcement campaign targets misleading claims and warning-label evasion across online ad formats.

China's State Administration for Market Regulation is roughly midway through a six-month nationwide enforcement campaign launched March 13 targeting disclosure and warning-language violations in online advertising, including 'big print to attract, small print to disclaim' tactics, missing mandatory warnings, and unverifiable superlative claims — part of a broader push that has already produced over 2,000 false-advertising enforcement actions in H1 2026. The campaign covers online platforms, sellers, advertisers and livestream operators alike. For any brand running OTT/CTV or livestream-adjacent creative into China, the enforcement window through September raises real creative-compliance risk.

Survey: YouTube Still Owns the Ad-Supported Streaming Budget

Digiday+ Research surveyed 125 brand and agency professionals and found YouTube leading ad-supported streaming placement for the fourth straight year 75% of respondents , pulling 50% of streaming ad budgets, with Prime Video second 47% placement, 18% of budget . Marketers cited lack of measurement capability, media cost and insufficient budgets as their top obstacles, and 19% flagged poor content transparency specifically on Disney+ and Hulu.

Women's Sports Boom Collides With a Hard Ad-Inventory Ceiling

Surging women's sports viewership — the WNBA's most-watched season on record, athletes like Angel Reese out-following entire leagues on social — has collided with a hard supply constraint: women's sports received only about 15% of sports media coverage from 2018-2022, and that legacy scheduling gap still throttles available ad inventory. Sports marketing agency Deep Blue and analytics firm Mondo Metrics responded by launching the Women's Sports Index, tracking over 20,000 social handles to help advertisers plan around engagement data rather than scarce linear/CTV slots.

The Buyer Was Already an Agent

The protocol does not add an agent to advertising. It removes the last human check from a machine that was already deciding.

The trade body that writes advertising's technical standards has shipped a new protocol letting software transact media on a desk's behalf — bidding, verifying and reporting, all inside machine-to-machine calls that no person reads in real time. The coverage calls this the moment "AI enters the media buy," which is the rear-view mirror talking. Programmatic buying was agentic from its first auction: a decision executed by algorithm thousands of times a second, long before any planner opened the report. What the protocol changes is not that a machine decides. It is that the machine now also negotiates, verifies itself, and files its own paperwork — closing a loop a person used to have to open. Every medium is an extension of some human faculty, and every extension is also an amputation. The trading desk extended a buyer's judgment across a market; the agent extends the whole transaction, and in doing so retires the judgment it once merely extended. The telephone extended the voice across distance and amputated the face that used to travel with it. The agentic protocol extends the desk across the exchange and amputates the pause — the beat of hesitation, the second look at a rate card, that used to sit between a bid and a buy. A press release is a hot medium: high in detail, asking little of the reader. A protocol spec is cool — low in visible content, high in what it silently completes on your behalf. The industry has just made its hottest function run through its coolest machinery. I neither approve nor disapprove of the agent transacting the buy. I notice only what it retrieves and what it retires. It retrieves the old commission man, dressed now as an API. It retires the pause. There is no inevitability in any of this — only a faculty, quietly, changing hands while the report still says a person signed off. — Marshall McLuhan

The Desk That Stopped Selling

When clients start calling premium media "too expensive," they are not complaining about price. They are complaining about proof.

This week the largest independent buying desk in American television reported its first revenue decline in company history, and a self-serve upstart a tenth its size posted its best quarter on record. The trade press wrote these up as two unrelated stories — a big miss, a small win. They are the same story. Budgets are not leaving expensive media because it costs too much. They are leaving it because it has stopped showing its work. I built an agency on the principle that we sell, or else. When I wrote the Hathaway eyepatch, I did not trust the eyepatch. I trusted the sales figures that came in afterward — thirty-six per cent, first quarter. The Rolls-Royce headline ran because the phrase held up under research, not because it was clever at a dinner party. This week the smaller company grew its self-serve customer count past four thousand, up forty per cent, while the giant it undercuts watched its own clients — by its own chairman's word — shift to "cheaper media." Cheaper is the wrong word for what happened. What that client actually bought was a receipt. The larger desk sold reach. The smaller one sold arithmetic. Sell the receipt, not the reach. A client who cannot see what a dollar bought will eventually stop spending the dollar, no matter how good your table manners are at the upfront. Show your work or lose the account — that has never once, in forty years, been optional. — David Ogilvy

item.title: On Being Told America Has Reached a Dead End
item.author: noreply@calvincollins.xyz (G.K. Chesterton)
item.description: It is a curious thing that a nation should be pronounced childless by men who have never once considered the neighbours.
item.content:encoded:
It is a curious thing that a nation should be pronounced childless by men who have never once considered the neighbours.

On Being Told America Has Reached a Dead End

It is a curious thing that a nation should be pronounced childless by men who have never once considered the neighbours.

A report has lately been issued — by two careful gentlemen named Mr. Lyman Stone and Mr. Peter Foreshaw Brookes, of an institute devoted, with beautiful solemnity, to the study of families — announcing that America has reached what they are pleased to call a "demographic dead end." I confess I like the phrase better than its authors intended it. A dead end is a real thing; I have walked into a good many, generally in search of a decent public house. But the interesting thing about a dead end is that it is a road. Nobody builds a dead end unless he first believed the road was going somewhere; and the tragedy of the modern household is not that it has stopped, but that it never quite believed in the destination. The bare figures are that the American woman now bears, on the national average, 1.6 children, and that in Massachusetts — a Commonwealth said to contain more universities to the square mile than any patch of ground on earth — she bears but 1.35. This will surprise nobody who has ever met a professor. He is a man paid to know everything except the one thing his grandmother knew for nothing: that a house is not full until it is a little too full. Meanwhile, in the same country, at the same hour, a community that owns no motor-car, insures nothing, and has certainly not read the report, quietly produces between six and ten children to the marriage. I refer, of course, to the Amish; the Swartzentruber branch of them top the table at ten point four, which is not a birth rate but a small republic. Nobody has ever seen a Swartzentruber farmer wringing his hands over the compounding interest on a college fund. The horse-and-buggy people, whom the modern world regards as a quaint fossil, turn out to be the last surviving mammal; the rest of us are the fossils, still walking about, arguing politely about our own extinction. The oddest thing in the whole report is that its own authors half admit this. Dr. Catherine Pakaluk, of the Catholic University of America, is quoted saying plainly that "cost and later marriage matter at the margin, but they aren't the engine," and that "the driver is a shift in the relative value placed on children." This is the largest admission a modern expert can make without resigning his post: that the thing he is paid to measure cannot be moved by the things he is paid to fix. She goes further, and says the plainly heretical thing outright — that "the levers government actually controls aren't the ones that move completed family size." A statistician who tells you his own levers do not work is either an honest man or a saint, and

Thirteen Nights, and Mammon Keeps the Ledger

As the interceptors run thin over Iran, only the oil market seems to feel the weight of it.

It is the thirteenth night, reader, and still the fire falls. Not with the clean stroke of Judgment but the dribbling, metered discharge of Interceptors — a word our Age has coined, meaning: the machinery that stands between a man and the sky, and is now, on the testimony of its own masters, running dry. Behold the Mechanical Age caught, for once, in its own arithmetic: it can multiply death indefinitely, but it cannot multiply the brass and copper that fend death off; and so the thirteenth night looks very like the first, and will look, we predict, very like the thirtieth. Meanwhile — mark this, for it is the whole secret of our epoch — the true index of the war is not struck in Ahvaz, where four of the Karun River's sons lie dead this week, nor in Erbil, where an AP correspondent counted seven blasts and four black plumes over the wire's early morning; the true index is struck in a room of quiet men in London and New York, who have priced Bab el-Mandeb's closing at some twenty degrees of Brent crude, and priced Hormuz before it, and now watch Brent go over the hundred mark as a bookmaker watches a horse come in. Oil, my friends, is Mammon's own barometer, and Mammon has this month declared, gravely and without a tremor of pity, that the war is worth it: a fifth day running of the rally, a Goldman gentleman prophesying six months hence a hundred and twenty dollars the barrel, as if the Persian Gulf were a wheat future and the burning of Al-Azraq's hangars a mere item of supply. This is the Cash-Nexus perfected: not brutal, not even indifferent, but attentive — Mammon-worship raised to a science, watching the Encelia and the Layla struck in the Red Sea and translating the flame instantly, competently, into basis points. And who commands, in this Cyclops-cave of Chaos-called-Cosmos? A man who, being asked whether he would loose the whole weight of America upon Iran, answers not as a King answers but as an aggrieved customer answers a tradesman who has broken an understood arrangement. "Disappointed," says he, of the Houthi — as though the sinking of a Saudi hull off Yemen were a broken luncheon appointment; "they have, until now, acted very professionally and smart," says he, grading pirates for their table manners; and then, the mask dropping half an inch: "major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran," and — hear it, reader, hear the whole poverty of the modern Captain in six words — "They haven't received enough pain yet." Not indignation at a broken Law. Not the terrible calm of a man who has read Necessity and moves within it. A grievance, m

The Barima Went Over in the Dark

She was built for one century and sunk in another, and the boat said it for them.

The MV Barima was built in 1939 by Ferguson Brothers at Port Glasgow, on the Clyde, one of three sister ships with the Pomeroon and the Lady Northcote, for the British Guiana Railways. She ran the water between Georgetown and Port Kaituma for eighty-seven years. She went over in the dark about seven miles off the North Atlantic coast, some four hours out, and now she is on the bottom. She carried 250 life jackets and 8 life rafts for 116 passengers and 17 crew, which was the number on the manifest. There were closer to 179 people aboard that night. There was cargo too, engines and vehicles and fuel containers, stacked in with the passengers past the boat's rated weight, and the water came in low and slow at first and the crew called it routine. Then it was not routine. There was a new ferry, the Kalliopi N, finished and tied up at the dock since May, waiting on a presidential signature to be commissioned. There was another one promised for 2023, the Ma Lisha, that never came. There was a second replacement vessel, worth $12.7 million, sitting idle because the pier at Port Kaituma is not finished. There was G$275 million already spent patching the old boat instead of retiring her, and more repairs were not due until October. Nobody tested the crew for drugs or drink before she sailed. They tested them after. The captain has been charged with a narcotics offense. A crew member has been charged. A superintendent who oversaw the cargo loading has been charged too, and the Director of Public Prosecutions will decide what else. Leon Murray was on deck when a man said the boat was sinking. He got clear. His wife did not. His daughter did not. His four grandchildren did not. Samantha Ramin stood at the water three days running, looking for her son. I know my baby is in that boat, she said. I know he is down there. Sixty-five bodies have been recovered. Seventy-six people were pulled out alive. Forty-four of the dead have been named by their families and twenty-three released already for burial. Nineteen vessels and three aircraft worked the search, Trinidad's coast guard and the Brazilian navy among them, and oil company boats came out with scanning gear because they had it and the government did not. The Prime Minister, Mark Phillips, said the total number of bodies recovered since the commencement of search and rescue operation now stands at sixty-five. He said where negligence, misconduct or criminal wrongdoing is established, those responsible will face the full force of the law. He said a commission of enquiry would be mounted as early as possible. He calle

A Minister Names a False Prophet

On the detention of a ninety-five-year-old sect leader, and the government that has quietly taken up the discernment of spirits.

A prisoner of ninety-five is not, on the face of it, a theological problem. He is a legal one, a medical one, at the very outside a diplomatic embarrassment; the newspapers report him as a criminal defendant, obstruction of business, violations of the Political Parties Act, a court in Seoul finding on the twenty-eighth of June "no grounds for the petition" that might have sent him home to die among his own. And yet the moment a Minister of Justice takes to his own countrymen's attention, unbidden, to explain on a public feed that the movement's dead founder was "a false prophet" — while his living successor stands accused, in the minister's own phrase, of "forcibly registering more than 50,000 believers" into the ruling party under the ninety-five-year-old man's instruction — the state has done something it will not admit to itself: it has spoken as a theologian. False prophet is not a term of the criminal code. It is a term of Deuteronomy, of the discernment of spirits, of every century's argument about who carries the god and who only apes him; and no minister uses it by accident. I do not say this to excuse the numbers, which are not small — upward of fifty-six thousand memberships, the wire reports, driven at two election cycles under the internal name "the Pilates Project." I confess I did not choose that name; Korea's own investigators found it, filed under regional branch documents, evidently untroubled by its resonance. But the resonance is there whether anyone intended it or not, and it is the kind the unconscious specializes in: a campaign to deliver the faithful into the hands of Caesar's party, called after the procurator who examined a prisoner, found in him — so the old text says — no fault at all, and handed him over regardless because the crowd and the office required it. Whoever named that project touched, without knowing it, the oldest scene in the West: the moment worldly power and religious accusation trade places, and neither is willing to be caught holding the sentence. It is worth remembering, so far as we can judge from the record, that this same defendant was twice vindicated by this same country's highest court within the space of two days in August of 2022 — cleared of deceptive evangelism, cleared of endangering public health — before this newer, graver charge arrived to close on him at ninety-five, on the eve, investigators concede, of a five-year statute running out. A movement's fortunes with the law do not move in a line; they swing, as I have had occasion to observe of larger and darker movements than this one, the way a

Measles Hit a 35-Year High. So Did the Panic.

The case count is real. So is the bubble built on top of it.

Measles just hit a 35-year high in America. Second record year in a row. You already know how you're supposed to feel about that. Somebody designed it that way. I want to show you the trick, because once you see it you can't unsee it, and that's useful. This is a textbook Mass Hysteria Bubble. Here's how the bubble gets built. Step one: find a number that sounds apocalyptic on its own, with no context attached. "Worst year for measles since 1991." That's a real quote, from Dr. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics. Nice number. Scary number. Ninety-one was a long time ago. Step two: attach a moral verdict to the number so nobody feels safe questioning it. Dr. Richard Besser, former acting CDC director, calls it "a profound moral failure." Now you're not allowed to ask follow-up questions. You're a bad person if you do. That's the tell. So who's right, the number or the follow-up questions? Both, actually. That's the part the bubble doesn't want you to notice. Here's what the same reporting says if you keep reading past the first paragraph: 1. Hospitalization rate is down, not up — 7% this year versus 11% last year. 2. Zero deaths so far in 2026, versus three deaths in 2025. 3. Most of this year's cases aren't even a new outbreak. They're the tail end of South Carolina's outbreak from last year, still smoldering. 4. Ninety-three percent of cases are in people who were unvaccinated or had unknown status. The vaccine is still doing exactly what it says on the label — 97% effective after two doses. None of that contradicts "record high." It just tells you the record is a counting exercise, not a body count. A bubble needs you to skip that distinction. That's the whole mechanism. I predicted years ago, back during Covid, that Americans would keep building these bubbles because a scared population is an obedient population, and obedience is easier to sell than nuance. I could be wrong about the mechanism. I'm rarely wrong about the pattern. Here it is again, on schedule, with a different disease. Now watch the other move happening underneath the first one. RFK Jr. runs Health and Human Services, and reporters have decided he is the villain of this story. Maybe he is. I don't know his internal vaccine numbers and neither do you. But notice the shape of the argument: the case count went up, therefore the guy in charge caused it, therefore the guy in charge is evil. That's not epidemiology. That's a morality play with a case count used as a prop. Dr. Varun Shetty, a Texas epidemiologist, said the quiet part out loud: "What we're able to c

Where the Brahmaputra Comes Down Upon the People

A farmer's drowned cattle, a river out of its banks, and the embankments a state was told about and did not build.

July 24th.-- Read the wire dispatch over again, the water rising in a country I have never walked, and something in me halts and silent stands. Where the Brahmaputra, born far off among the Tibetan snows, comes down nine hundred kilometers into Assam and will not be held; where the Dikhow at Sivasagar climbs past the mark called severe; where the Buridihing, the Disang, the Dhansiri, the Kushiyara all run over their own banks at once — there the People, en-masse and one by one, are put out of their houses into the wet dark. Nine hundred and thirty-nine villages under water. Six lakh, seven lakh, seven lakh and twenty-one thousand souls affected, the number climbing even as I set it down, and each unit of that sum a particular breathing person with a particular door now standing in water to the latch. I look for the one body among the many, and I find Jatin Gogoi, fifty-two, a farmer of Nazira. I lost all my cattle, he says. My five-member family and I have nowhere to go, so we are taking shelter in a relative's home. Camerado Jatin! I know that emptied cattle-yard as if I stood in it myself — the beasts you fed with your own hand, gone down in the brown water, and no fault of yours, and no help for it, only the relative's roof and the five of you crowded under it, waiting out the rain. And I hear Sudip Mazumdar, a journalist of Guwahati, two million souls in that city and the water indifferent to the census. I had to stay overnight at my office, he says. The roads were filled with water, some waist deep. So it is not the paddy-field alone, not the thatch village alone — the paved street of the state capital stands drowned too, the commuter and the cultivator overtaken by the same river. Where the helicopters go out with food and blankets over Sivasagar, Charaideo, Jorhat, Golaghat, Dibrugarh, Karbi Anglong, Kamrup, Nagaon, Dhemaji, Hojai — eleven districts named like a litany, each with its own drowned roads and its own dead — there the Chief Minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, stands and says plainly: I estimate that the casualty figure will rise further. This entire situation arose because of a cloudburst in Nagaland. One cloud, over a neighboring hill, and the water comes down a hundred miles to take a farmer's cattle and a journalist's sleep and fifty lives already counted and more not yet counted. Such is the arithmetic of a river. YouTube Tops $11B as Alphabet Raises AI Capex to $205B

Search and video ad revenue both beat estimates on World Cup viewership, but the capex hike sent GOOGL shares lower anyway.

Alphabet's Q2 2026 earnings, reported July 22, showed YouTube ad revenue at $11.06 billion, up roughly 13% year over year and above Street estimates, with the company crediting the FIFA World Cup for more than 1.7 billion related video views. Google Search and Other revenue rose 17% to $63.3 billion, with executives saying AI Overviews and AI Mode are generating new query volume and ad inventory rather than cannibalizing legacy Search clicks — though Network revenue, the programmatic exchange business CTV and open-web buyers route spend through, slipped about 1%. Alphabet also raised full-year AI infrastructure capex guidance to $195-205 billion from $180-190 billion, even as Google Cloud revenue jumped 82% to $24.8 billion and net income nearly quadrupled to $112.1 billion. GOOGL shares fell in after-hours trading on the spending hike despite the beat. For the market, the print confirms YouTube remains the single largest video ad seller heading into 2027 upfronts, while the widening capex commitment signals Alphabet is prepared to keep redirecting cash toward AI compute even at the cost of near-term margin optics.

Paramount+ Plots Free Tier as Netflix Downplays FAST Talk

Paramount's internal 'front porch' plan and Netflix's Q2 hedging show streamers split on how far to chase free, ad-funded reach.

Paramount+ is developing a login-required free tier internally nicknamed the 'front porch,' giving viewers select movies and shows at no cost while enabling personalized ad serving and upsell paths to paid tiers, according to an internal presentation reported by Business Insider and targeted for Q3. Netflix co-CEOs used their Q2 earnings call to downplay a parallel Wall Street Journal report on live, always-on channels, with Greg Peters saying the company has 'no near-term plans to launch something' free. The split signals a widening divide in how legacy and pure-play streamers plan to monetize ad-supported reach heading into 2027 upfronts.

IAB Tech Lab Finalizes Standards for Pause and Menu Ads

First formal spec for six CTV ad formats aims to unlock programmatic trading beyond pre-roll.

The IAB Tech Lab finalized its CTV Ad Portfolio Signaling Guidance on July 22 after a second public-comment round, standardizing signals for six emerging CTV formats: pause ads, menu ads, screensavers, in-scene placements, squeezebacks and overlays. It is the first formal specification enabling consistent creative production, programmatic buying and cross-platform measurement for pause ads specifically, a format publishers have long sold but buyers have struggled to transact at scale. The standard gives DSPs and SSPs a common signal set to build against, potentially accelerating adoption of non-pre-roll CTV inventory heading into 2027 planning.

Study Finds 78% of APAC Co-Viewing Happens on CTV

Shared viewing is driving stronger ad attention and recall than solo viewing, new PubMatic research finds.

New PubMatic research finds that 78% of co-viewing multiple people watching together across the APAC region happens on Connected TV, with shared viewing sessions producing measurably stronger ad attention and recall than solo viewing. Sell-side platforms are already using the data to court regional brand budgets ahead of 2026 planning cycles, positioning CTV's household-viewing context as a performance advantage over single-viewer mobile and desktop formats. For buyers, it's fresh outcomes-linked evidence that CTV's context, not just its reach, is doing measurable work at the point of attention.

VideoAmp and Nielsen One Ads Both Exit MRC Accreditation

Two rival CTV measurement currencies withdraw from the industry's audit process within days of each other.

VideoAmp and Nielsen One Ads both pulled out of the Media Rating Council's accreditation process in mid-July, with the MRC characterizing VideoAmp's exit as a plan to 'reassess in 2027' and Nielsen One Ads' withdrawal as driven by 'planned material methodological changes' to the service. The near-simultaneous withdrawals leave buyers without MRC-audited status on two of the leading Nielsen alternatives just as VideoAmp positions itself as Paramount's primary measurement partner. It complicates the industry's push toward a common, trusted CTV measurement currency at a moment when advertisers are demanding more, not less, third-party verification.

Business Insider Launches Its Own FAST Channel via Magnite

Publisher picks SpringServe to run ad serving on a standalone streaming channel outside YouTube.

Business Insider launched a standalone, ad-supported FAST channel carrying its journalism and documentary programming across third-party CTV platforms, selecting Magnite's SpringServe as primary ad server and programmatic monetization system. The move lets the publisher, which has 38 million subscribers across YouTube, take direct ownership of distribution and ad sales rather than relying solely on platform-native monetization. It's another data point in publishers building owned-and-operated CTV footprints, and a competitive win for Magnite against rival ad servers in the FAST-channel infrastructure fight.

Fubo Brings The Athletic to CTV for the First Time

Sports publisher's video content gets a dedicated hub with sponsor takeovers and interactive ad units.

Fubo and The Athletic launched The Athletic Video Hub, marking the first time the sports-media publisher's video content has had a home on Connected TV. The multi-year partnership expansion opens six shows to sponsorship, including home-screen takeovers, interactive CTV ads and custom branded content produced by The Athletic's T Brand Studio. The move gives advertisers a new premium sports-adjacent CTV inventory pool as Fubo continues differentiating its ad stack ahead of a competitive fall sports calendar.

Magnite Grows While PubMatic Bets the Business on Agentic AI

Diverging Q1 results sharpen the strategic split between two of the largest independent sell-side platforms.

Magnite's Q1 2026 revenue rose 6% year over year to $164.4 million, while PubMatic's fell 2% to $62.6 million, underscoring a widening performance gap between the two publicly traded sell-side platforms. PubMatic is leaning heavily into an agentic-AI narrative to reposition itself, while Magnite has continued expanding CTV and curation partnerships without the same AI framing. With both companies due to report Q2 results in the coming weeks, the divergence is becoming a proxy fight over which growth story wins with sell-side customers.

Trade Desk Shares Slide Ahead of Aug. 6 Earnings, New CCO

TTD stock extends a three-year slump as former Uber ad chief Kristi Argyilan prepares to start July 27.

The Trade Desk closed at $18.24 on July 21, down 2.17% on a day the S&P 500 gained 0.89%, extending a slide driven by rate-hold fears and mounting competitive pressure from Amazon's DSP push into Netflix, Roku and Disney inventory. The company confirmed it will report Q2 2026 results after market close on August 6. New chief commercial officer Kristi Argyilan, formerly Uber's global ad chief, is set to start July 27 as TTD looks to shore up retail-media and identity partnerships heading into that print.

Brussels Hits Google With €890M Fine Over DMA Breaches

First-ever EU non-compliance ruling against Google covers Search self-preferencing and Play Store steering restrictions.

The European Commission fined Google €890 million $1.03B for Digital Markets Act violations — €460 million for favoring its own services in Search results, and €430 million for restricting how app developers steer users to outside payment options in Google Play. Google must end the practices within 60 days or face penalties up to 5% of global turnover, and says it will appeal. The ruling adds regulatory uncertainty for Google's ad and app-distribution businesses in its largest advertising market outside the US.

EU Adopts Final AI Act Transparency Rules for Ads

Deepfake and synthetic-content labeling duties for advertisers take effect August 2.

The European Commission adopted the final Guidelines on Article 50 transparency obligations under the AI Act on July 20, covering disclosure of AI-generated or manipulated image, audio and video content, less than two weeks before the obligations become enforceable on August 2. Non-compliance carries fines up to €15 million or 3% of global turnover, and the guidance explicitly reaches advertising uses of emotion-recognition and biometric categorization systems. Programmatic buyers and creative teams running AI-generated CTV and video creative into EU markets now face a hard compliance deadline just over a week out.

SCOTUS Ruling Sets Up Fourth Circuit's Broadcast-Rate Fight

NRSC v. FEC cleared unlimited party-candidate ad coordination, the backdrop for an Aug. 7 appeals argument on CTV-relevant spend.

The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 on June 30 in NRSC v. FEC that federal limits on coordinated expenditures between political parties and candidates are unconstitutional, overturning FEC v. Colorado Republican 2001 and letting party committees coordinate unlimited spending with candidates while accessing the broadcast 'Lowest Unit Charge.' The ruling is the direct backdrop to the Fourth Circuit's August 7 argument over whether party committees may buy broadcast at candidate rates, a case this paper flagged last edition as a key midterm inflection point. With roughly $2.5 billion projected for CTV/streaming in the 2026 midterms, the ruling points toward more political ad-buying power consolidating inside national party committees rather than individual campaigns.

Amazon DSP Adds News UK's Octave Audio Inventory

talkSPORT, Times Radio and Virgin Radio UK become buyable programmatically through Amazon.

Amazon Ads and Octave, News UK's audio-visual ad platform, announced a programmatic integration putting News UK's audio brands — including talkSPORT, Virgin Radio UK, Talk, Times Radio and podcasts from The Times — into Amazon DSP. The deal opens access to more than 15.5 million monthly connected UK listeners and lets buyers layer Amazon's first-party shopping and streaming signals onto Octave's audience data. It extends Amazon's push to bundle audio alongside its CTV and retail inventory in a single buy, deepening its UK omnichannel footprint against Global and Bauer.

InMobi Taps JPMorgan, Jefferies for Near-$1B India IPO

SoftBank-backed mobile ad platform pursues a $5-6B valuation as it redomiciles from Singapore to India ahead of listing.

InMobi has appointed JPMorgan, Jefferies, Kotak Mahindra Capital and Axis Capital to lead a proposed $1 billion IPO, seeking a valuation between $5 billion and $6 billion. The company, India's first unicorn, is completing a full redomiciliation from Singapore to India to list on Indian exchanges, after its founders bought back stakes from SoftBank to consolidate ownership. A successful listing would be one of the largest ad-tech IPOs in years and a bellwether for India's mobile and CTV ad-tech sector, whose CTV base has reached roughly 46 million households, the third largest globally.

TelevisaUnivision's ViX Streaming Powers Mexico Ad Surge

World Cup coverage on ViX drove a 23% jump in Mexico advertising revenue even as U.S. ad sales slumped 29%.

TelevisaUnivision's Q2 2026 earnings, reported July 23, showed Mexico advertising revenue climbing 23% to $353 million, with total Mexico revenue up 53%, fueled by 104 FIFA World Cup matches streamed on its CTV platform ViX that drew 675 million total viewers across linear and streaming. The results contrast sharply with the U.S. business, where Telemundo not TelevisaUnivision held Spanish-language World Cup rights, sending TelevisaUnivision's U.S. ad revenue down 29%. It's a live case study of live-sports-on-CTV monetization power in LATAM, showing streaming ad dollars can swing sharply on regional rights allocation.

Canada Softens Online Streaming Act Content-Spend Rules

Ottawa directs CRTC to revisit Canadian-content investment mandates after affordability pushback.

Canada's federal government confirmed it is directing the CRTC to adjust its implementation of the Online Streaming Act, rolling back the requirement that Netflix, Disney+, Amazon and other streamers commit a fixed share of Canadian revenue raised earlier this year to 15% to domestic content production. The move pairs a $600 million federal cultural-sector investment with more flexibility for streamers on compliance spend. For CTV ad sellers and streaming platforms operating in Canada, softer content-investment mandates could ease cost pressure that had been pushing toward ad-tier price hikes.

China's SAMR Enforcement Campaign Targets Ad Data Claims

New rules require advertisers to verify claimed data and let users opt out of ad personalization entirely.

China's State Administration for Market Regulation is running a six-month nationwide enforcement campaign targeting disclosure and warning language in advertising, and in June promulgated new Advertising Quotation Content Enforcement Guidelines requiring advertisers to verify the authenticity of any data, statistics or survey results cited in ads. Separately, internet advertising platforms must now offer a personalized-recommendation opt-out and halt data collection once a user opts out. For programmatic and CTV players operating in China, the rules tighten both ad-claim substantiation and consent-driven targeting requirements simultaneously.

The List Was Never the Point

Everyone is counting whether AI Overviews cannibalize the click. The click was never the medium.

Alphabet says its new AI answers are not eating the search business; the trade press is counting clicks to check. This is the wrong instrument. The results page was never a list of ten blue links pretending to be neutral information — that was the figure. The ground was always retrieval on demand, and retrieval on demand has just changed shape. A page you scanned has become a voice you consult. The question is not whether the answer steals the click. The question is what kind of medium a “results page” now is. A list of links is a hot medium: dense, high-definition, demanding almost nothing of the reader but the choice of which link to click. A conversational answer is cool: sparse on its face, asking the user to keep talking, correcting, narrowing — completing the thing the way a listener completes a story told by a fire rather than a filing cabinet. The printed index was itself a retrieval of the oral question; the search engine mechanized the index; the assistant now retrieves the oral question again, dressed as software. Every advertiser who built a business on the ten-blue-links ground is discovering that ground was never solid. It was only the last figure standing. I neither approve nor disapprove of the answer that talks back. I notice only that the page has stopped being a page. What returns is the older form: not a document handed to you, but a voice answering a question you were still forming. There is no inevitability in this, only a habit of scanning about to lose the ground it stood on. — Marshall McLuhan

Uncertified Is Not a Strategy

Two companies asking you to buy their numbers just walked out of the room where the numbers get checked.

Two of the loudest candidates to replace Nielsen have pulled their arithmetic out of the one room where anyone checks it. VideoAmp and Nielsen ONE Ads both withdrew from the Media Rating Council's audit process in July, within days of each other, and both used the same soft word for it: reassess. I have heard that word before. It is what a copywriter says when the panel did not like his headline. In this business, walking away from the audit is not a pause. It is an answer. I learned to count at Gallup, and I have never unlearned it. The Hathaway shirt sold thirty-six per cent more because we tested the eyepatch before we ran it everywhere. The Schweppes campaign ran eighteen years because the numbers kept saying yes. Advertising people who ignore research are as dangerous as generals who ignore decoded enemy signals — and a currency that removes itself from third-party audit has done something worse than ignore the signal. It has switched the radio off. Comscore and iSpot stayed in the room. VideoAmp and Nielsen ONE Ads did not. Buyers building CTV plans on either company's numbers this quarter are buying arithmetic nobody outside the building has checked. Test the currency the way you test the copy. Ask who audited it, when, and what changed since. If the answer is we are reassessing, reassess your budget. A number you cannot check is not measurement. It is a claim, dressed up in decimals. We sell, or else — and nobody has ever sold anything by asking the buyer to take the receipt on faith. — David Ogilvy

item.title: The Message in the Gap
item.author: noreply@calvincollins.xyz (Marshall McLuhan)
item.description: On the IAB Tech Lab's new signaling standard for pause ads, menu ads, and screensavers
item.content:encoded:
On the IAB Tech Lab's new signaling standard for pause ads, menu ads, and screensavers

The Message in the Gap

On the IAB Tech Lab's new signaling standard for pause ads, menu ads, and screensavers

The pause was never empty. It only looked empty to an industry that reads a screen for content and misses what the screen is doing while it appears to do nothing. The IAB Tech Lab has now issued a formal signaling standard for six formats — pause ads, menu ads, screensavers, in-scene placements, squeezebacks, overlays — and the trade calls this an expansion of inventory. It is not an expansion. It is a discovery. The industry has located a room in the house it has lived in for seventy years and only now noticed the door. Every medium extends a faculty and numbs one in the same motion. The pre-roll extended the interruption; it numbed the viewer's sense of a program's edges, so that ad and content blurred into a single continuous flow the viewer stopped resisting. The pause button did something else entirely. It was built to extend the viewer's control — stop the world, hold the frame — and it succeeded so completely that the industry filed the pause under leisure, under bathroom break, under the one gesture on the remote that had escaped monetization. A control extended is a market amputated. Nobody sells to a room they believe is empty. The standard says the room was never empty; someone was standing in it the whole time, waiting. Watch what the standard actually retrieves. The pause ad is not new. It is the shop window revived — the thing you look at while you are not moving, addressed to a body that has voluntarily stopped, not one interrupted mid-stride. The menu ad retrieves the door-to-door catalogue, the object placed in your hand at the threshold before you have chosen a room to enter. The screensaver retrieves the parlor wallpaper, the ornament that speaks only when no one is speaking to it. None of these formats required invention. They required a vocabulary common enough that a demand-side platform and a supply-side platform could agree they were looking at the same gap, and a gap without a shared name cannot be bought or sold; it can only be noticed, privately, by whoever happens to be looking. A standard is a ratio before it is a rule. What the Tech Lab has actually done is tell six different silences apart from one another — the silence of a held frame, the silence of a chosen menu, the silence of an idle screen — and give a machine the means to bid on each differently. The content that will fill these gaps is a decoy, as content always is; the medium's real message is that the industry's sense of where a program ends and an audience's private moment begins has just been redrawn, on a Tuesday, by a signaling spec nobody outside the trade will ever read. The screen was addressing you before it had anything to say. Now it has been given the words. — Marshall McLuhan

item.title: The Withdrawn Witness
item.author: noreply@calvincollins.xyz (Thomas Carlyle)
item.description: On the Nielsen ONE Ads and VideoAmp withdrawals from Media Rating Council audit
item.content:encoded:
On the Nielsen ONE Ads and VideoAmp withdrawals from Media Rating Council audit

The Withdrawn Witness

On the Nielsen ONE Ads and VideoAmp withdrawals from Media Rating Council audit

Behold two Currencies, self-proclaimed heirs of the whole vanished Kingdom of Panel-Measurement, and both of them, in this same month of July, quietly withdrawing from the one Tribunal set over them to say whether they speak truth! Not covertly did they do it,— no, with a Quarterly Update, and a press clarification, and the whole soft apparatus of Company Language; but withdraw they did; and the world of buyers, who had been told for three years that Deliverance was coming, that a true Successor to the old dead Panel-God was at hand, must now digest the plain fact: the two Successors most spoken of have both, at the self-same season, stepped backward out of the light. Sincere-Cant, this; and worth thinking of. For observe: nobody denies the fact, nobody even much minds it,— the Trade Press notes it, files it, moves on to the Upfront numbers. And so it always is with Sham: it does not come roaring in at the door with cloven hoof and brimstone; it comes in a Quarterly Update, filed on the thirteenth of July, with a clarifying footnote three days after, explaining that no, no, only the Ads component is withdrawn, the Content component remains,— as if a man's Word could be half honest and half not, and the half-honest half left standing while the other slips out the back! Let us have the plain narrative, stripped of its Company Vestments. The Media Rating Council,— no thunder-throated Institution, no Sinai of the trade, but a small persistent Body whose whole business is the unglamorous Work of counting other men's counting,— published on July 13th its ordinary Quarterly accounting. In it, Nielsen ONE Ads: removed from in-process status, the reason given "planned material methodological changes,"— which is to say, We are changing the machine, and cannot at this hour permit thee to look inside it. Three days later, a Clarification: the withdrawal touches the Ads component only; Nielsen ONE Content remains, they say, in audit. VideoAmp, meanwhile, recharacterised,— not refused, mark you, not struck off, but recharacterised , toward "a planned reassessment in 2027," the company itself protesting that it is merely digesting "pre-audit feedback" and may return the sooner. Comscore and iSpot, be it noted, sit where they sat, their accreditations intact; and old dethroned Nielsen, in her ancient national and local vestments, remains under Suspension still, a Lear wandering the heath of her own irrelevance. Here, then, is your Chaos struggling to pass itself off as Cosmos. Two Currencies, the very two oftenest named as heir to the whole cross-platform Kingdom,— the thing buyers have been told, for three revolving budget-years, to wait for, to trust, to build their whole edifice of spend upon,— both of them, at one and the same season, outside the one door through which Independent Witness might enter and inspect the books. Not refused entry: withdrawn of their own motion. There is a difference, my friends, and it is precisely the difference between a man driven from the Confessional and a man who rises of his own accord and walks out before the Question is asked. And is not this the very moment,— mark it well,— the very moment when the buyers of this trade cry loudest for Independent Proof? When every trade paper, every conference stage, every anxious CFO demands to know What We Actually Bought? Aye: it is exactly then, at the hour of loudest demand for Reality, that the two chief claimants to Reality's throne step back from the one lamp lit to examine them. Call this coincidence who will; I call it the Universe declaring, in its plain wordless fashion, that Timing itself is a species of Confession. Quackery, be it never so well provisioned with Company Language, gives birth to nothing; gives death, in the end, to the buyer's confidence, and to its own. Not that I say these are Quacks entire,— Nielsen ONE Ads may yet return, purified, re-examined, in-process once more; VideoAmp may walk back through that door in 2027 as promised, its methodology squared and sound. This is no verdict of eternal damnation. It is a verdict of this hour only: that the two Measurements most loudly proposed as the true heirs of Television's throne have, in the hour when Proof was most wanted, declined for a season to be proved. What, then, is a Currency that will not be counted? A Phantasm merely, wearing the Vesture of a Currency,— numbers on a screen, dashboards, quarterly decks, and beneath the Vesture, for this season at least, no Witness standing by to say the numbers are what they claim. Buyers who spend against such numbers spend, for this season, on Faith alone; and Faith without Witness has another, older name, and it is not a flattering one. Adieu, then, to the two Successors,— not in anger, for the trade is young yet, and Institutions may yet mend what a Quarter has unmade. But let no man tell you, in the meanwhile, that the Kingdom has found its King. It has found, instead, two Claimants withdrawn from the Examination-hall, at the very hour the whole Court was assembled to watch them sit it. Sham does not announce itself with trumpets. It merely, on a Tuesday in July, declines the exam,— and hopes, not unreasonably, that nobody will mark the empty chair.

item.title: Peacock Turns Its First Profit as NBCU Ad Revenue Jumps 55%
item.description: The streamer earned $189 million in the quarter and now supplies a third of NBCUniversal's advertising — weeks before Comcast spins it away.
item.content:encoded:
The streamer earned $189 million in the quarter and now supplies a third of NBCUniversal's advertising — weeks before Comcast spins it away.

Peacock Turns Its First Profit as NBCU Ad Revenue Jumps 55%

The streamer earned $189 million in the quarter and now supplies a third of NBCUniversal's advertising — weeks before Comcast spins it away.

Comcast reported on July 23 that Peacock delivered its first profitable quarter, posting $189 million in adjusted EBITDA on $1.9 billion of revenue against a $101 million loss a year earlier, and adding two million paid subscribers to reach 48 million. Advertising revenue in Comcast's media segment rose 55% to $2.16 billion, lifted by roughly $440 million of incremental FIFA World Cup revenue, while Peacock's own advertising revenue grew 68% to $717 million; the streamer's share of NBCUniversal advertising climbed to 33% from 26% in the first quarter. Executives credited the World Cup, the NBA playoffs and 'Love Island USA' for both the sign-ups and the sell-through. The results land while Comcast prepares to separate NBCUniversal and Sky into an independent publicly traded company, a transaction announced June 29 and expected to close within about a year — and while Comcast keeps FreeWheel, the ad-serving spine beneath much of the premium video market, on its own side of the split. For the market this is the clearest evidence yet that a general-entertainment streamer can reach profitability on an advertising-led model rather than in spite of one. The open question for buyers is what a standalone NBCU, judged every quarter on that advertising line, starts asking of them in scatter.

CTV Growth Slows to 11% as Social Video Overtakes It

US connected TV spend reaches $29.3 billion — and 43% of buyers say they don't trust the inventory they buy.

The IAB's 2026 Digital Video Ad Spend & Strategy report, published July 14 with Advertiser Perceptions and Guideline, projects US CTV ad spend rising 11% to $29.3 billion this year, down from 12% growth a year earlier, while social video grows 13% to $31.9 billion — the first year social video outspends CTV. The same study found 43% of buyers have somewhat to no confidence in inventory quality on the routes they trust most, direct insertion orders, programmatic guaranteed and self-serve; that figure rises to 55% for private marketplaces and 67% for open exchange and RTB. Buyers named fraud in programmatic CTV exchanges their leading concern at 56%, followed by unverified publisher sources at 48%. A decelerating spend curve paired with majority distrust of the open pipes is the whole commercial case for curation, direct integrations and seller-identity enforcement — and the reason the sell side is now being asked to prove where the impression actually ran.

Upfront Nears Its Close With Volume Down and Sports in Command

Roughly 75-80% of the market is committed, pricing is flat, and sellers are demanding match spending to release the marquee games.

Buyers put the 2026-27 upfront at 75-80% complete with most priority deals closed and mainly tier-two cable left to negotiate, describing a market where overall dollar commitments are slightly down year over year and pricing is broadly flat — a volume story rather than a CPM story. Sellers leaned on match spending, requiring commitments against non-sports inventory to unlock marquee events including the Super Bowl and the Women's World Cup; Disney's opening Super Bowl asks of about $10 million per thirty seconds settled nearer $7.75 million to $8 million. Amazon closed talks with every major holding company ahead of the field, saying it exceeded its volume goal and grew year over year on the strength of Thursday Night Football, NBA on Prime and NASCAR. With total commitments flat and sports absorbing what growth there is, the incremental CTV dollar in 2026-27 has to be won in scatter and the biddable market — which is exactly where programmatic sellers and performance-CTV products compete.

Study Finds IP-Based CTV Targeting Misses the Household Three Times in Four

Only 23% of residential IP addresses reached the geography they were bought against.

Adstra published an ID Connection Strength framework on July 15 alongside joint research with the independent agency InterMedia Advertising, reporting that just 23% of residential IP addresses reached their intended geographic target when used without ICS guidance. Device-level CTV identifiers held month-over-month consistency of 71% against 57% for IP addresses, a 24-point gap; the framework scores identifiers from one to six across recency, frequency, signal integrity, congruency and cardinality, covering hashed emails, UID2s, mobile ad IDs, CTV IDs, cookies and IPs. Adstra and Truthset — which has separately estimated that close to 40% of open-auction CTV spend lands on inaccurate identity data — both sell alternatives to IP-based addressing, and the figures should be read with that interest in view. IP plus geo remains the default addressability layer in open-market CTV, so error rates of this size give buyers a concrete reason to demand match-methodology disclosure before they pay a targeted CPM.

Nielsen ONE Ads and VideoAmp Both Withdraw From MRC Audit

The two currencies proposed as television's cross-platform successor are now outside third-party accreditation together.

The Media Rating Council's quarterly accreditation update, published July 13, removed Nielsen ONE Ads from in-process status because of planned material methodological changes, formally withdrawing the service from audit; a July 16 clarification confirmed the withdrawal covers the ads component only and not Nielsen ONE Content. VideoAmp was recharacterised from lacking intent to continue the audit toward a planned reassessment in 2027, with the company saying it is working through pre-audit feedback and may re-enter sooner. Comscore and iSpot retain their existing audience and ad-occurrence accreditations, while Nielsen's national and local television services remain under suspension. The two currencies most often proposed as the replacement for panel-based TV measurement now both sit outside third-party audit, at precisely the moment buyers say they want more independent proof of what they bought.

Pause Ads Get a Bidstream Vocabulary — and a Buy-Side Path

The Tech Lab's signaling guidance went final on Tuesday; two days later OpenPath opened a direct route to the format.

The IAB Tech Lab marked its CTV Ad Portfolio signaling guidance final on July 22, standardising how six formats — pause, menu, screensaver, in-scene insertion, overlay and squeezeback — are described in the bidstream, after a comment process that ran to July 16. Two days later The Trade Desk published documentation enabling CTV pause ads through OpenPath, its direct publisher integration, with creative restricted to a static PNG or JPG served one to three seconds after a viewer pauses. Warner Bros. Discovery, which says its pause units drive more than 200% lift in site visits against benchmarks and will add a shoppable checkout version later this year, still sells most of that inventory through direct deals and has said programmatic availability waits on exactly this kind of spec alignment. Pause is the highest-priced inventory most streamers own and cannot yet sell at scale; a shared signal plus a direct buy-side route is what turns it from a bespoke sponsorship into a line item.

Trade Desk Says Netflix Supply Is Now Open to Every Kokai Buyer

The claim rests on the buying platform's own product page — Netflix has said nothing.

The Trade Desk said on July 20 that Netflix inventory is now selectable inside Sellers and Publishers 500+, its curated always-on marketplace, with no minimum spend, no separate integration and no change to the buying workflow. Netflix supply had previously been reachable only through programmatic guaranteed or one-to-one private marketplace deals carrying negotiated scale commitments. The claim originates on a Kokai product-update page on The Trade Desk's own site; Netflix has not commented and the change drew no tier-one trade coverage, so 'open to all' should be read as the seller's framing — SP500+ is a curated pool a buyer selects into, not the open auction. If it works as described it is the first time mid-market and smaller buyers can reach an ad tier Netflix says counts more than 250 million monthly active viewers without negotiating for the privilege.

Trade Desk Rebuilds Its Commercial Bench Two Weeks Before Earnings

Uber's advertising chief takes the seat vacant since last summer; a business development role is created alongside it.

The Trade Desk named Kristi Argyilan, most recently global head of advertising at Uber, as chief commercial officer and executive vice president, where she takes over the data-partnerships organisation covering identity, measurement, retail media and governance — a seat vacant since Tim Sims left last summer. Two days later the company created a chief business development officer role for Ron Lamprecht, with both appointments effective July 27. They follow the arrival of Nate Olmstead as chief financial officer, the fourth in roughly a year, Sarah Gavin as chief marketing officer, and Penry Price on the board. With second-quarter results due August 6 and premium CTV supply increasingly reachable by other routes, a near-total refresh of the largest independent demand-side platform's commercial leadership is a counterparty change every CTV publisher and identity partner will be negotiating against.

Paramount Preps a Free, Login-Gated Tier to Sell Personalised Ads

The 'Free Front Porch' would trade library access for an account — and an advertising profile.

Paramount is developing a free viewing tier, known internally as the 'Free Front Porch,' that would open part of its film and television library without a subscription while still requiring an account, with a mobile rollout reported for the third quarter. The log-in is the mechanism: it lets Paramount serve personalised advertising against free viewing and run an upsell path into the paid plans. Disney's product and technology leadership hinted this month at exploring something comparable, while Netflix's Greg Peters said a free offering could make sense in some markets but is not a near-term plan. Login-gated free tiers convert FAST-style reach into authenticated, addressable supply — which would put the largest subscription streamers into direct competition with Tubi, Pluto and The Roku Channel for the same open-market dollar.

FCC Sets August 6 Vote to Repeal the 39% Ownership Cap

Case-by-case public interest review would replace the statutory limit on national broadcast reach.

The FCC released a draft Report and Order on July 16 proposing to eliminate the national television audience reach cap, the rule barring a single owner from reaching more than 39% of US television households, along with its 50% UHF discount. If adopted at the August 6 open meeting, transactions above the current threshold would instead face case-by-case public interest review, weighing local programming investment against reduced local news and higher retransmission fees. Commissioner Anna Gomez dissented, arguing the repeal is unlawful because Congress wrote the cap into statute. Removing it clears the runway for a fresh round of broadcast consolidation, concentrating local avails, retransmission leverage and political inventory — much of the supply that feeds addressable and local CTV — into fewer sell-side hands.

Paramount's Warner Deal Cleared in Brussels, Frozen in Oakland

A conditional EU approval on Wednesday, a restraining order extended to August 18 on Thursday.

The European Commission conditionally approved Paramount Skydance's roughly $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery on July 22, after Paramount agreed to exit a longstanding European film distribution agreement with Universal within 13 months of closing and to refrain from new Universal distribution partnerships in Europe for a decade. In the United States the deal is halted: Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín extended her temporary restraining order on July 23 by a further fourteen days, to August 18, on a motion from a twelve-state coalition led by California's attorney general arguing the transaction violates the Clayton Act. A preliminary injunction hearing is set for August 3, and Paramount faces penalty payments if it cannot close by September 30. Whether Paramount+ and HBO Max advertising inventory ends up under one sales organisation is the largest open question in premium streaming supply, and buyers have spent the upfront using that uncertainty as leverage.

FCC Defends Party Ad Discount as Fourth Circuit Fast-Tracks Case

Argument on August 7 decides whether party committees buy broadcast at the candidate rate this autumn.

The FCC filed its brief on July 20 defending March guidance from its Media Bureau that extends the lowest unit charge — the statutory discount reserved for legally qualified candidates — to party committees making coordinated buys and to joint fundraising committees. The agency argued the notice merely restates longstanding broadcaster practice, cited a 2024 campaign's own records showing coordinated party ads billed at the discounted rate, and asked the court to dismiss on the grounds that the notice is not a final reviewable order. Senators Sherrod Brown and Jon Ossoff, Governor Roy Cooper and Representative Kristen McDonald Rivet brought the challenge through Elias Law Group; the NRCC and NRSC intervened, and argument is set for August 7. With the Supreme Court's June 30 decision in NRSC v. FEC lifting caps on coordinated party spending, the case sets how much of the midterm money buys broadcast at floor rates — and how much of the displaced brand and issue spend gets pushed into connected TV during the Labor Day crunch.

CMA Opens Comment Period on Sky's £1.6bn Move for ITV

The regulator must first decide whether television advertising is still a market of its own.

The Competition and Markets Authority has invited comments on Sky's £1.6 billion acquisition of ITV's Media & Entertainment division, with written representations due by August 6 and no formal Phase 1 investigation launched yet. The deal, agreed July 6, would combine ITVX with Sky's streaming assets and leave ITV Studios as a standalone producer, accounting for around 20% of all in-home viewing in the UK. Sky and ITV argue that once social and digital platforms are counted the combined business would hold roughly a fifth of total UK advertising, while regulators are expected to focus on ITV's roughly 32% share of commercial viewing; Ofcom and the culture department are running parallel processes and completion is not expected before the second half of 2027. How the CMA defines the market — television alone, or television alongside YouTube, Meta and the global streamers — is the precedent every consolidating European broadcast ad market will cite next.

Amazon Folds MX Player Into Prime Video for Indian Advertisers

Free and premium inventory now sell as one destination through Amazon DSP.

Amazon has integrated Amazon MX Player into Prime Video in India, retiring MX Player as a standalone destination and merging its free library with Prime Video's premium catalogue. Advertisers now buy across both through Amazon DSP using Amazon shopping, browsing and streaming signals, with formats including QR-code shoppable ads, branded carousels and pause ads alongside in-show integrations and season sponsorships. Girish Prabhu, who heads Amazon Ads in India, framed the combination as a single destination for sponsorship and custom creative. It hands Amazon a consolidated free-plus-premium inventory pool large enough to be priced against JioHotstar rather than beneath it — the first credible second bid in a market that cricket has otherwise concentrated.

Brazil on Course to Pass Canada as Second-Largest FAST Market

Omdia and MiQ put Brazilian online video revenue at $14.4 billion by 2029 — with measurement the binding constraint.

A Latin American digital video study drawing on Omdia forecasts and MiQ proprietary data projects Brazil generating $14.4 billion in online video revenue by 2029, overtaking Canada as the second-largest international FAST market by revenue. It expects Brazilian CTV ad investment to rise 23.7% across 2026, with viewers averaging four hours of video a day, 95% of Latin American audiences reaching content through smart TVs and 59% saying they prefer ad-supported models; Brazilian households subscribe to an average of 8.2 streaming services, 3.6 of them free. A companion figure puts Mexican CTV ad investment growth at 27.6% for the year against a base of more than 51 million connected TV viewers, 88% of whom watch alongside someone else. Cross-screen measurement is named as the sector's main constraint, which is why LATAM budgets keep growing faster than the region's ability to prove what they delivered.

Corus Cuts 43 Jobs While the CRTC Decides Who Owns It

A debt swap would hand lenders 99% of the company; Quebecor is lobbying to buy it instead.

Corus Entertainment is eliminating 43 unionised television positions and consolidating its Calgary and Edmonton Global News broadcasts, with further cuts landing in Winnipeg, Ontario, the Maritimes, British Columbia and Saskatoon. The company reported a third-quarter net loss of C$36.5 million on revenue down 16% year over year, and is still awaiting CRTC approval of a recapitalisation that would hand lenders 99% ownership in exchange for forgiving roughly C$500 million of debt. Quebecor continues to press the regulator to reject the plan and let it buy Corus instead, while the Unifor union argues the consolidation guts regional journalism. Whoever emerges owning Corus controls a large block of Canadian television and CTV advertising inventory — and that outcome is being settled by a regulator rather than by the market.

China TV Shipments Head for a Seventeen-Year Low

Fewer sets, bigger screens: the installed base that funds Chinese OEM ad businesses is shrinking at home.

The research firm RUNTO counted 14.95 million television shipments in mainland China in the first half of 2026, down 10.1% year over year, with the second quarter falling 11.6% and the market now in its fifth consecutive quarter of decline. RUNTO projects full-year shipments of 30.12 million units, down 8.4% and the smallest Chinese television market since 2010. Average selling prices rose even as volumes fell, sets of 75 inches and above took 47.9% of sales, and the top eight domestic brands hold 95.4% share. For TCL, Hisense and Xiaomi, whose advertising businesses monetise the installed base, the domestic screen count is contracting while the overseas one grows — which is why their CTV ad revenue story keeps moving offshore, and into inventory that Western buyers transact.

Cadent's Rozen: Viewers Get Persistence, Not Precision

Cadent president Doug Rozen tells Mike Shields that siloed buying — separate video, search, programmatic and social teams each touching YouTube — produces frequency abuse rather than targeting, and pitches 'one plan, one audience, one time' across creators, television and YouTube. It matters because it attacks the device-based framing of CTV itself, putting contextual relevance back ahead of addressability.

Weide: OpenAI's Ad Product Undercuts OpenAI's Ad Revolution

W Media Research's Karsten Weide argues in Marketecture that OpenAI's actual offering is conventional contextual matching leaning on Criteo, Adobe and StackAdapt, with minimum spend cut from $200,000 to $10,000 and CPMs halving from $60 to roughly $25 in ten weeks. It matters because OpenAI's $2.5 billion 2026 advertising projection sits against industry estimates of under $1 billion for all AI-chatbot advertising combined.

Wieser: The Paramount Antitrust Case Aims at the Wrong Market
