Madison and Wall's Brian Wieser calls the state attorneys general's case against Paramount a misallocation of enforcement, arguing viewers treat video services interchangeably and that concentration in theatrical film and cable networks is a legacy concern — streaming grew from $7 billion in 2015 to $60 billion in 2025 while pay television contracted. It matters because the same interchangeability logic is what buyers now use to price linear against CTV.

The Interface Was the Last Thing You Could Refuse

When the assistant acts on your behalf, the consumer stops being the audience and becomes the content.

Everyone is counting assistants. Which model answers, which one Brussels has just pried onto the Android home screen, which one the agency will license by autumn. That is the figure, and it is the least interesting thing in the room. The ground is the quiet disappearance of the interface itself — the menu, the search box, the cart, the thing you could look at and decline. We are told the assistant is a better servant. It is not a servant. It is an environment, and environments are invisible to the people inside them. Every medium extends one faculty and amputates another. The printed page extended the eye and amputated the ear. The remote control extended the hand and amputated the schedule. The agent extends the will and amputates the act of choosing — which is to say it removes the very faculty by which you knew yourself to be a person shopping rather than a market being cleared. The buyer who instructs a machine to buy his media has not gained leverage. He has become inventory of a new kind: a standing instruction, discoverable and priceable by other machines. Ask the trade why it has suddenly grown so anxious about a common vocabulary for a video impression and it will tell you plainly. The agents cannot negotiate in dialect. Watch what becomes of the advertisement in such a world. It cannot interrupt, because there is no longer a sequence to interrupt. It cannot be looked at, because nothing is being looked at. It becomes a rumour circulating among machines, and the human is told about it afterward, in a summary, by something that loves him. — Marshall McLuhan

The Machine Can Write a Thousand Ads. It Cannot Read the Report.

Speed was never the bottleneck in this business. Knowing the product was.

The trade is congratulating itself on velocity again. One agency announces that nine in ten of its people are now proficient with the new machines. A platform boasts that it can refresh a commercial in an hour rather than a fortnight. A streamer promises artificial intelligence in the planning and the buying. In all of this cheerful noise I have yet to hear a single man say whether the advertisements sold anything. Speed is not a virtue in advertising. It is merely a way of arriving at the wrong idea sooner. I once spent three weeks reading about a motorcar before I wrote a word of copy. The headline I finally used was not written at all — it was found, buried in an engineer's technical report: at sixty miles an hour the loudest noise in the Rolls-Royce came from the electric clock. No machine on earth could have produced that line, because no machine had read the report. Remember that five times as many people read the headline as read the body copy. A device that generates ten thousand headlines nobody has researched has not multiplied your productivity. It has multiplied your waste, and done it at a very impressive speed. Use the machines where they belong. Give them the split runs, the recall scores, the coupon returns — the drudgery of testing, which I did by hand and would gladly have handed to a computer. But keep them away from the copy until somebody in your building has spent three weeks with the product and can tell you one true thing about it that the customer does not know. Find the fact first. Then let the machine set it in forty languages. — David Ogilvy

item.title: The Cooling Break
item.author: noreply@calvincollins.xyz (Ernest Hemingway)
item.description: On the 2026 World Cup
item.content:encoded:
On the 2026 World Cup

The Cooling Break

On the 2026 World Cup

In the summer of that year the World Cup came to North America and they played it in the heat. There were sixteen stadiums across the three countries. Three of them, in Dallas and Houston and Atlanta, had roofs and cooled air, and the other thirteen were open to the sun. The grass had been grown for ten months on farms in North Carolina and hauled to the stadiums in refrigerated trucks and laid down over the football fields, and Rabiot said it played hard and rigid, and Vinicius said it dried out fast and the game went slow on it. Spain flew seven thousand eight hundred miles in the group stage and won the group anyway. France flew three hundred and thirty-four. It was the biggest country a World Cup had ever been played in, and the teams crossed it in airplanes between the matches, and at the end of June the great heat came up over the east and lay on Philadelphia and Boston and Kansas City and New York and did not lift at night. The weather service said the nights would not offer any relief. That was the country the football was played in. Twice in every match now the referee stops the play so the men can drink. It is in the rules this year for the first time. The play stops for three minutes in the twenty-second minute and again in the sixty-seventh, in all the hundred and four matches, whatever the weather. The coaches do not care for it. Tuchel, who has England, said he liked football more when it was two halves. Deschamps, who has France, said it is almost four quarters now. At the stops the men drink and pull ice vests on over their shirts and put chilled collars on their necks, and then the whistle goes and they play again. The matches go off at noon and in the middle of the afternoon because afternoon in America is evening in Europe, and the television is in Europe. The players' union said the afternoons in Kansas City and Miami and Monterrey were extremely high risk. The kickoff times stayed where they were. In Miami the first match went off at six in the evening on the fifteenth of June, Saudi Arabia against Uruguay. It was ninety degrees at the kick and in the stands you sweated standing still. The fire rescue took ten calls for heat that evening and carried two people to the hospital. Over the first four matches at Hard Rock Stadium the county logged thirty-seven heat calls and five transports. The night Brazil played Scotland it was eighty-one degrees, and there were no calls. When Colombia played Portugal there at the end of June, nothing to nothing, it was close to ninety at half past seven in the evening, and the Colombians sat through the water breaks in ice vests and the Portuguese wore the chilled collars. In Foxborough on the thirteenth of June a young Scottish winger named Ben Gannon-Doak came off after seventy-five minutes against Haiti with both calves cramped. "Both my calf muscles decided to leave the stadium before me," he said. Scotland won that night, 1–0, and went out in the group anyway. Uruguay went out too, two points, the highest-ranked team to go home before the knockouts, and it was their own goalkeeper's mistake against Spain that finished them. No player has gone down on the field from the heat. When the doctors are asked about that they reach back to Houston in 2017 for the last one who did. There are two and a half weeks still to run, and the hottest days have only now arrived. Twice the lightning has stopped it. In Philadelphia on the twenty-second of June they sent France and Iraq to the dressing rooms at the half, at ten minutes to six, and the crowd stood in the concourses for two hours and eleven minutes while the storm worked through. The rule says lightning inside eight miles stops the match for thirty minutes, and every new strike starts the thirty minutes over, and there is no rule for when it ends. France came back out and won 3–0. In Mexico City the storm came down two hours before Mexico played Ecuador at the Azteca, thunder and hard rain, and the kickoff went back an hour, and eighty thousand people danced in ponchos while they waited. Mexico won 2–0, Quiñones and Jiménez, their first knockout win in forty years, and no one has ever beaten Mexico at the Azteca in a World Cup. England comes there Sunday. The Azteca sits at seven thousand two hundred feet and there is less air in it, and Tuchel said you cannot physically adapt to it, so England will fly in two days before the match to keep clear of the days when the altitude does its worst work. Kane scored twice in the last fifteen minutes in Atlanta to get them there. The twenty-ninth of June was the day of the penalties. In Foxborough, Paraguay and Germany stood 1–1 after the extra time. Enciso had scored before the half and Havertz had headed the equalizer, and in the extra time Tah put the ball in the net and the video took the goal away. Then the kicks. The Paraguayan goalkeeper is named Orlando Gill. He saved from Havertz and he saved from Woltemade, and Tah, whose goal had been taken away, put the last kick over the bar. Germany had never lost a penalty shootout at a World Cup. They have lost one now. The same evening in Monterrey, in the hottest stadium of the sixteen, Morocco and the Netherlands stood 1–1, Gakpo in the seventy-second minute and Diop in the first minute of added time, and in the shootout Bounou saved the fourth Dutch kick and Saibari struck the winner. Morocco plays Canada in Houston on the Fourth of July, indoors, in the cooled air. Forty-two men from one Moroccan supporters' club asked the United States for visas to follow their team. Two got them. All three hosts are still in it. Canada had never won a knockout match and won one in Los Angeles, 1–0 over South Africa, Eustáquio in stoppage time. The United States beat Bosnia 2–0 at Santa Clara with ten men. Balogun scored the first and the video sent him off in the sixty-fourth minute, and Tillman put a free kick in to finish it. There is no appeal from the video. Balogun will watch the Belgium match in Seattl

item.title: Comcast to Spin Off NBCUniversal and Sky Into Standalone Company
item.description: Tax-free split hands the streamers and studios their independence — while FreeWheel, the ad-serving spine of premium video, stays behind with Comcast.
item.content:encoded:
Tax-free split hands the streamers and studios their independence — while FreeWheel, the ad-serving spine of premium video, stays behind with Comcast.

Comcast to Spin Off NBCUniversal and Sky Into Standalone Company

Tax-free split hands the streamers and studios their independence — while FreeWheel, the ad-serving spine of premium video, stays behind with Comcast.

Comcast said on June 29 it will separate NBCUniversal and Sky into an independent, publicly traded company through a tax-free spinoff, leaving Comcast focused on broadband, cable and wireless. The new media company will hold Universal Pictures, the NBC and Telemundo networks, streaming service Peacock, Bravo, the theme parks and UK broadcaster Sky, with co-CEO Mike Cavanagh becoming its chief executive; the split is expected to close in about a year. Crucially for the ad market, Comcast retains its core technology business — including FreeWheel, the ad-serving infrastructure that monetizes premium video for hundreds of media companies — and has not said what commercial agreement, if any, will govern FreeWheel's relationship with a separated NBCUniversal. The move reshapes one of the largest owners of premium CTV and streaming inventory, and a standalone NBCU under pressure to monetize Peacock is likely to lean harder into advanced-TV ad products and outcomes deals. For programmatic buyers, the open question is whether the plumbing and the inventory it serves are about to answer to two different owners.

Samsung Opens Smart TV Home Screen to Programmatic Buyers

The Trade Desk and DV360 gain access via Magnite's SpringServe, with a global rollout beginning in Q3.

Samsung Ads said its smart TV home-screen inventory is now buyable programmatically through DSPs including The Trade Desk and Google's DV360, powered by Magnite's SpringServe, with a global rollout across the US, EMEA and LATAM starting in Q3 2026. Samsung reaches more than 77 million active Smart TV households and calls it the largest programmatically accessible home-screen pool of its kind. The move pushes the highest-value real estate on the television — the first screen a viewer sees — into automated buying, intensifying the fight among Samsung, Roku, Amazon and LG for CTV's most premium surface.

Amazon Pushes Fire TV Home Screen as Prime Video Viewing Climbs

A redesigned interface and a World Cup hub frame Amazon's bid for home-screen ad dollars.

Amazon began shipping a redesigned Fire TV interface built around content discovery and a 2026 FIFA World Cup hub across its Fire TV Sticks, the Fire TV Cube and Ember smart TVs globally, positioning home-screen placements as a captive-audience ad surface. The company said Prime Video ad-supported customers now watch 17% more hours each month than a year ago, and touted more than 90% incremental reach when home-screen units are paired with Prime Video commercials. With most Fire TV placements now buyable through Amazon's DSP, the refresh sharpens Amazon's head-to-head fight with Samsung and Roku for the TV operating system buyers most want programmatic access to.

Disney Ties Compass Clean Room to Affinity Card-Spend Data

Debit- and credit-card transaction signals feed planning and outcome measurement across Disney's streaming inventory.

Disney unveiled a commerce-media capability with Affinity Solutions that layers historic purchase data from debit and credit card transactions onto Disney's audience graph, offering attribution and purchase insight across categories including retail and QSR through Disney's Compass clean room. Disney manages activation and distribution of the Affinity data across its properties, alongside existing Compass connections to LiveRamp, Snowflake and VideoAmp. The deal deepens the industry push to make premium CTV inventory measurable against real sales rather than proxy metrics, matching retail-data moves from Roku, Amazon and Walmart — and hands buyers another reason to grade streaming spend on outcomes.

Omnicom Measures Ad Frequency Across Rival Streamers in One Clean Room

A publisher-passed Creative ID lets a single instance track reach and frequency across Disney, NBCU and Paramount.

Omnicom unveiled capabilities in its cross-platform clean room that measure reach, frequency and performance across multiple streaming publishers and linear broadcasters in a single instance, built on the Acxiom identity infrastructure it gained through the IPG acquisition and powered in part by The Trade Desk. It is live with Disney, NBCUniversal, Paramount and a range of VOD and FAST partners, and relies on a publisher-embedded Creative ID passed back into the clean room — a first for major CTV publishers. Frequency capping across walled-off streamers is one of CTV's most persistent buyer complaints, so a holdco-scale fix the biggest publishers actually feed data into is a real step toward cross-platform accountability.

Gracenote and PubMatic Bring Content-Level, Live-Sports Deals to CTV

Episode-level data matched at auction through the IAB Tech Lab's Agentic Real-Time Framework.

Gracenote, Nielsen's content-intelligence business, and PubMatic announced a partnership matching bid opportunities against Gracenote episode-level data in real time, letting advertiser-selected inventory be tied to curated deal IDs and live-sports schedules. The integration runs on the IAB Tech Lab's Agentic Real-Time Framework inside PubMatic's AgenticOS, adding a fraction of a millisecond to each transaction. It targets a well-documented barrier — the 86% of media planners who cite thin show- or content-level data as a reason budgets stay in linear rather than CTV.

Yahoo DSP Adds Comscore, VideoAmp and iSpot Ahead of Upfronts

Video currencies jockeyed for position at Cannes as fall commitments loomed.

Video ad currencies and outcomes measurement dominated Cannes Lions 2026, with providers racing to lock in business as upfront negotiations heated up. Yahoo's DSP added CTV measurement integrations with Comscore, VideoAmp and iSpot, to be completed by fall when upfront spend takes effect, while Nielsen touted currency upgrades combining panels with larger datasets. The scramble underscores that CTV still lacks a single standardized currency — and every DSP-level integration chips away at incumbent dominance while giving buyers more ways to grade streaming spend.

Publicis and The Trade Desk Settle Months-Long Fee Dispute

The holdco reinstates TTD to its recommended DSP list; shares jumped roughly 6% on the news.

Publicis and The Trade Desk resolved a dispute that began in March, when Publicis pulled TTD from its recommended DSP list over how it applied ad-tech fees and told clients to pause spend. Neither side detailed the terms of the truce. With the settlement, and against the backdrop of the Fox–Roku deal, TTD shares rose about 6% on June 26. Because Publicis directs enormous advertiser budgets, its recommendation status is central to TTD's CTV revenue pipeline — and the episode shows how aggressively holdcos will now police ad-tech fee transparency.

PubMatic Launches Programmatic CTV Marketplace for Creators

MeatEater is the first partner in an auction that opens indie creator inventory to agentic demand.

PubMatic unveiled its Creator Marketplace, billed as the first programmatic CTV auction connecting independent creator media companies' premium inventory with programmatic and emerging agentic demand. MeatEater is the launch partner, with FreeWheel as ad server and Holmes Media handling supply-side scaling. The move extends programmatic pipes to creator-led CTV audiences long confined to direct sponsorships and walled gardens, opening a new supply lane just as agentic buying scales.

Texas ACR Suits Against Smart-TV Makers Advance, Testing CTV Data Model

Paxton's cases against Samsung, LG, Sony, Hisense and TCL target viewing-data collection at its source.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton's lawsuits against Samsung, LG, Sony, Hisense and TCL — alleging unlawful collection and monetization of viewing data via automated content recognition without adequate consent — continue to advance, with temporary restraining orders already obtained against Hisense and Samsung. The AG seeks injunctive relief, restitution and civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation, and the ACR focus is expected to remain a state-enforcement priority through 2026. Because ACR-derived viewing data underpins much of CTV's targeting and measurement value, the litigation puts the smart-TV ad model itself on trial.

EU AI Act Content-Labelling Code Sets July 22 Signing Deadline

A voluntary transparency code precedes deepfake and AI-content labelling duties that bind on August 2.

The European AI Office published the final Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content, with a July 22 deadline to be listed among initial signatories and Article 50 transparency obligations becoming applicable August 2. The code calls for clear labelling of deepfakes and AI-generated content on matters of public interest, recommending digitally signed metadata and imperceptible watermarking. As generative-AI creative floods CTV and political streaming ads, the labelling regime creates near-term compliance duties for any advertiser or platform serving AI-produced spots into the EU.

Supreme Court Strikes Party Spending Caps as Midterm Money Surges

A 6-3 ruling in NRSC v. FEC lets party committees spend unlimited sums in coordination with candidates — including on ads.

On June 30 the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in National Republican Senatorial Committee v. FEC that federal limits on coordinated party expenditures violate the First Amendment, striking caps that had ranged from about $65,000 for House races to as much as $4 million for Senate candidates. Effective immediately, national and state party committees may spend unlimited amounts in full coordination with a federal candidate on any campaign expense, advertising explicitly included. AdImpact already projects the 2026 cycle at $11.6 billion with connected TV the only major channel growing, at $2.7 billion — and removing a spending ceiling right before the election clears the way for more of that money to pour into streaming and broadcast inventory.

Sky Agrees Terms to Buy ITV's Broadcast and Streaming Arm for £1.6bn

Comcast-owned Sky would absorb ITVX; ITV Studios spins out as a standalone producer.

Sky, owned by Comcast, has agreed terms to acquire ITV's Media & Entertainment division — including the ITVX streaming service — in a deal reported at roughly £1.6 billion, with ITV Studios carved out as a standalone production business and a formal announcement expected within weeks. The transaction would still need clearance from the CMA, Ofcom and the UK culture secretary. A combined Sky-plus-ITV ad-sales operation could control well over half the UK TV ad market, concentrating British premium-video and addressable CTV supply under one owner just as the separate Sky–Channel 4–ITV joint marketplace comes online.

TAM: JioHotstar Leads IPL 2026 CTV Ads at 35%, Google Second

Connected TV drew a distinct, tech- and e-commerce-heavy advertiser base separate from linear.

TAM Sports' IPL 2026 report found Star India/JioHotstar topped connected-TV ad volumes at 35% over the tournament's opening 22 matches, with Google second at 20% and Havells, Renault and Reliance Consumer Products rounding out the top five. E-commerce, media and social categories dominated CTV at 35% of volumes, while linear TV stayed FMCG-led, and the report noted CTV drew more advertisers running exclusively on the medium than linear did. The split confirms Indian CTV is building its own demand pool rather than mirroring broadcast — a signal for how the market's ad currency and pricing will develop.

Brazil and Mexico Outpace US on CTV Adoption, Amagi Report Finds

LATAM's anchor markets top the mature US on connected-TV reach as FAST scales into a World Cup year.

Amagi's latest FAST report finds Brazil and Mexico posting higher CTV adoption than the US, with survey work across Brazil, Argentina and Mexico showing 91% of TV viewers streaming weekly and 79% receptive to ads in exchange for free or lower-cost content. Growth is driven by smart-TV uptake, global and local streamers, and expanding FAST services, alongside a steep rise in regional ad impressions. The findings reinforce LATAM as a top-tier CTV growth region and a receptive ad environment, drawing more global sellers and DSPs into the market.

Bell Media Extends Live CTV Sports Inventory West via TELUS Deal

Addressable live inventory on TSN and CTV now reaches TELUS TV+ across Western Canada.

Bell Media struck a strategic agreement with TELUS to expand its live connected-TV advertising into Western Canada across TSN, CTV and leading English-language specialty channels on the TELUS TV+ platform, giving advertisers national scale. TSN's live CoTV inventory alone delivers more than 50 million monthly impressions with addressable targeting via 70 pre-built segments and Bell Audience Manager, part of a reported 350% expansion of Bell's CTV inventory. Digitizing live linear sports for addressable buying is Canada's most concrete move yet toward programmatic premium-sports CTV supply.

Nexxen and VIDAA Open Hisense Smart-TV Inventory for World Cup

Programmatic access to the Hisense/Toshiba OS footprint, as Channel 4 buys home-screen space on the same platform.

Nexxen and V — formerly VIDAA, the Hisense-owned smart-TV operating system — announced a partnership letting advertisers programmatically plan and activate live-sports campaigns across V's global Hisense and Toshiba footprint for summer 2026 via Nexxen's DSP and SSP. In parallel, Channel 4 moved into VIDAA home-screen advertising, selling premium placements across VIDAA-powered Hisense, Toshiba and Loewe sets. The moves open a major Chinese-OEM smart-TV OS to Western programmatic demand, expanding global CTV supply beyond Samsung and Roku ahead of the World Cup.

Paparo Maps the Walmart–Vibe Winners and Losers

Ari Paparo argues Walmart's $1.4B Vibe.co buy validates performance/SMB CTV as net-new budget with 'little sign of a ceiling,' names MNTN and Tatari as the next acquisition targets, and flags The Trade Desk as a loser now that Walmart owns its own CTV buying platform. It reframes the deal from a retail-media story into a signal that self-serve performance TV is the sector's hottest M&A category.

OpenAI at Cannes: 'We Are Clearly in the Advertising Business Now'

At its first-ever Cannes Lions, OpenAI declared it is now in the advertising business — a marker of how fast generative-AI platforms are moving toward ad-supported models. For CTV, a serious OpenAI ad push raises the prospect of AI-native formats and planning tools competing for the video budgets agencies are already redirecting toward advanced TV.

The Set That Watches Back

We thought we bought a window. We installed an eye.

For seventy years the television was the thing we looked at. Reverse the figure and the ground, and the news of this season snaps into focus: the television is now the thing that looks at us. Automated content recognition does not display content — it reads the room. The home screen is not a menu; it is a face, turned toward the viewer, learning. What the smart set senses is no longer what it shows. This is not surveillance in the old sense of a camera in the corner. The screen has no motive; it is simply doing what every electric medium does — extending a sense until the sense reverses on its owner. The eye we built to see the program has become the program's eye. Texas calls this spying and reaches for the law. But the law arrives to a scene already transformed: the set is a nervous system, and the household has been wired into it as an organ, not an audience. Notice what the shoppable remote completes. The old distance between watching and wanting — the gap the whole grammar of the commercial depended on — collapses to a button. To see is to buy; to sit is to be read. The living room, once the most private theatre in the culture, is now its most attentive instrument. We did not lose our privacy to the television. We handed it our senses, and asked to be recognized. — Marshall McLuhan

The Reckoning Comes to the Glamour Medium

Television is at last being asked the only question that matters: did it sell?

I began my life in advertising with direct mail — the despised, the unglamorous, the guttersnipe of our trade. I loved it for one reason. It kept score. Every coupon returned or unreturned told me, without mercy or flattery, whether my copy had done its work. The rest of advertising floated above such indignities, and television floated highest of all: the beautiful thirty seconds, admired at Cannes, measured by nobody. That era is closing, and good riddance. When a streamer now welds card-spend data to its inventory, and an agency counts reach and frequency across rival platforms in one accounting, television is being dragged down to where direct mail always lived — the place where you must prove you sold something. The politicians have already noticed; connected TV is the one channel of a $11.6 billion election cycle that is still growing, because it can be held to account for a vote the way I was held to account for an order. Do not mourn the loss of mystique. The advertiser who tells you performance measurement kills creativity is confessing that his creativity never sold anything. Great selling and hard proof have never been enemies; only lazy men pretend they are. I once sold Rolls-Royce on a single measured fact about a clock, not on a mood. The same discipline is now arriving in the living room, and the copywriter who cannot survive it was never selling in the first place. Television has spent seventy years as our most expensive entertainment. Make it, at last, our most accountable salesman. — David Ogilvy

item.title: OpenAI Debuts at Cannes, Declaring Itself an Advertising Business
item.description: On the Croisette, the AI lab told marketers the attention economy is giving way to an “intelligence economy” — and that it now sells ads against it.
item.content:encoded:
On the Croisette, the AI lab told marketers the attention economy is giving way to an “intelligence economy” — and that it now sells ads against it.

OpenAI Debuts at Cannes, Declaring Itself an Advertising Business

On the Croisette, the AI lab told marketers the attention economy is giving way to an “intelligence economy” — and that it now sells ads against it.

Cannes Lions 2026, which ran June 22 to 26, will be remembered as the festival where artificial intelligence stopped being a panel topic and became the business itself — and no moment captured it like OpenAI's first-ever appearance, where an executive told advertisers the company is “clearly in the advertising business now.” The pitch framed a shift from the attention economy to an “intelligence economy,” citing roughly 900 million weekly ChatGPT users, around one in five queries showing commercial intent, a move from CPM to cost-per-click pricing, and a stated ambition to reach $100 billion in ad revenue within four years. It landed amid a festival-long flood of “agentic” announcements, as holding companies, streamers and ad-tech vendors raced to ship software that plans, buys and makes advertising with the human increasingly out of the loop. For a programmatic and Advanced TV market built on auctions and the open web, a conversational ad surface at that scale is a new and non-auction channel for the same brand budgets — one that routes around the supply chain The Trade Desk and the holdcos spent a decade defending. The week's verdict, echoed across the recaps, was that AI has moved from hype to implementation: the tools are now infrastructure decisions, and Cannes was where the bill came due.

Anthropic's Claude Wins Film Grand Prix Mocking AI Ads

Mother London's “A Time and a Place” imagines a future where chatbot answers are interrupted by sponsored messages.

The Film Grand Prix at Cannes Lions 2026 went to Anthropic's “A Time and a Place,” a pair of Super Bowl spots from Mother London that pointedly mocked rivals stuffing advertising into AI chatbot answers, arguing there is a time and a place for ads — and it is not mid-response. The work, Anthropic's Super Bowl debut, also took Gold and Silver in Film and a Silver in Creative Strategy. That an AI lab won advertising's top film honor with a thesis against ads-everywhere crystallized the festival's central tension. For CTV and programmatic strategists, it is a sign that the AI-versus-advertising fight is now being waged in creative, not just in the auction.

Cannes Entries Fall 25% After an AI-Fraud Reckoning

Tough new integrity rules follow 2025's revoked Grand Prix over AI-manipulated case footage.

Cannes Lions 2026 drew 20,050 entries from 92 countries, down 25.5% from 26,900 a year earlier, after the festival imposed integrity rules requiring proof-of-impact for every claim and personal sign-off by both the agency CEO and the brand CMO. The crackdown followed the 2025 scandal in which Brazil's DM9 had a Grand Prix and 11 other Lions revoked for AI-manipulated case-study footage; the festival added AI detection, human review, an Integrity Council and the threat of multi-year bans. The collapse in entries is the clearest measure yet of how AI-generated “evidence” is forcing marketing to rebuild trust in what work and what results are real — the same authenticity problem now haunting AI-made ad creative across CTV.

Apple's Eddy Cue Named Cannes Entertainment Person of the Year

The services chief keynotes with Jerry Bruckheimer on the studio's record-setting “F1.”

Apple's Eddy Cue accepted the 2026 Entertainment Person of the Year award at the Cannes Lions opening ceremony, hours after a main-stage keynote with producer Jerry Bruckheimer on Apple's Oscar-winning, record-setting film “F1” and a planned follow-up. Cue oversees Apple TV, Apple Music, Apple News and the wider services empire the festival credited with redefining audience engagement. Honoring the executive behind Apple's still-ad-light streaming service spotlighted the one major entertainment platform holding out against the ad-supported, data-driven model now sweeping the rest of CTV — a reminder that the festival's biggest budgets do not all flow to addressable inventory.

Amazon Counters Agentic Hype With Alexa+ Shoppable Ads

A new format takes a viewer from ad to purchase inside a single voice conversation, with Fire TV on the roadmap.

Amazon used Cannes Lions 2026 to unveil Alexa+ Agentic Ads, billed as the first format that takes a customer from seeing an ad to completing a purchase entirely within a conversation, with launch partners Papa Johns and The Orchard and a beta running on Echo Show devices. Amazon leaned on its existing DSP, measurement and transaction-level data to promise self-service and programmatic versions, with Fire TV expansion planned. For the CTV market, the Fire TV roadmap points to conversational, closed-loop commerce arriving on the living-room screen and inside Amazon's DSP — a direct bid to fuse retail-media intent with streaming reach as agentic buying spreads.

TikTok Debuts Symphony Agent and Custom Creator Networks

An agentic AI builds video ads from prompts; brands curate their own creator pools.

TikTok used Cannes Lions 2026 to launch Symphony Agent, an agentic AI that generates video ad campaigns from text, image and video prompts on ByteDance's Seedance model, alongside Custom Creator Networks that let brands assemble curated pools of creators and employees for briefs. Starbucks will run the first such network this summer through its Green Apron Creator Program. The tools deepen TikTok's automation of video ad production as it competes for the creative budgets and creator-led inventory flowing through the festival — and push more short-form video toward machine-made, biddable supply.

YouTube Wires Gemini Into New Creator and Trend Tools

Trending Insights, a Creator Insights API and Gemini-powered Demand Gen optimization debut at Cannes.

At Cannes Lions 2026, YouTube and Google introduced a clutch of advertiser tools, including granular US Trending Insights and Brand Pulse metrics in Google Ads Insights Finder, a Content and Creator Insights API for media planning, and Gemini-powered optimization for Demand Gen campaigns. The release centers on creator marketing and trend discovery, and arrived the same week Forrester named Google agencies' preferred AI partner. It underscores how the largest video platform is threading generative AI through planning and buying as agentic workflows spread across CTV and online video.

Omnicom and NBCUniversal Build Scene-Level Contextual CTV Ads

Dynamic Contextual Content matches creative to individual episodes and scenes.

At Cannes Lions 2026, Omnicom Media and NBCUniversal launched Dynamic Contextual Content, which pairs scene-level signals from NBCU shows — down to specific episodes and moments — with Acxiom audience data to adapt ad messaging in real time. The companies cite research that viewers connect more with ads relevant to what they are watching; the capability is in beta with interest from CPG, financial services and telecom, targeting a US release by the end of 2026. It pushes CTV past audience targeting toward the show- and scene-level contextual planning marketers know from linear, tying relevance directly to measurement — the heart of performance-counted streaming.

Omnicom Becomes Netflix's First Data Collaboration Partner

Acxiom audience data and AI “digital twins” of products come to the Netflix Ads Suite.

On the opening day of Cannes Lions 2026, Omnicom Media announced it is Netflix's first data collaboration partner, pairing Acxiom audience data with Netflix's AI-powered ad tech to personalize streaming creative — including AI-generated “digital twin” product placements woven into content so different viewers can see different branded objects. The deal launches in the US with international expansion planned by year-end and includes closed-loop measurement across audiences, creative and programming. It is the marquee CTV deal of the week, and a signal that premium streamers are now opening their walled-garden ad stacks to holding-company data and AI-native creative.

WPP Media Unveils Video Buyer Agent and Agentic Standards Push

Disney, Netflix, Fox, NBCUniversal, Paramount and Comcast sign on to govern AI buying.

WPP Media used the run-up to Cannes Lions 2026 to reveal a prototype Buyer Agent for video inside WPP Open, plus an Agentic Standards Initiative to govern how buyer and seller agents transact premium video. Founding participants span Disney Advertising, Netflix, Fox, NBCUniversal, Paramount and Comcast Advertising/FreeWheel, with IAB Tech Lab and Prebid.org on standards and a proposed industry standard targeted for early 2027. If it holds, the effort could become the rails for autonomous CTV and TV buying the way programmatic standards once were for display — a holdco's bid to set the rules before any single vendor's protocol becomes the default.

Adobe Puts the Holding Companies to Work Running Its Agentic AI

Accenture Song, Omnicom, WPP and Stagwell's Code and Theory deploy CX Enterprise.

Adobe announced at Cannes Lions 2026 that Accenture Song, Omnicom, WPP and Stagwell's Code and Theory — alongside Anthropic and Microsoft — will deploy its content, data and AI platforms to run agentic AI at scale for enterprise clients. The partnerships aim to connect paid-media spend with owned customer-experience data, a loop most marketing stacks still reconcile by hand. For programmatic and CTV, tighter ties between agency activation and first-party CX data feed the identity-and-outcomes loop that increasingly governs where streaming budgets flow.

Publicis's $2.2B LiveRamp Deal Splits the Identity Layer at Cannes

“If you don't have the identity, you don't win with AI,” says Sadoun — as WPP vows to drop LiveRamp.

Publicis's $2.2 billion agreement to buy identity firm LiveRamp framed every data conversation at Cannes Lions 2026, with CEO Arthur Sadoun arguing that identity is “the qualifier for AI” and whoever controls the data owns the agentic era. The fault line opened fast: WPP CEO Cindy Rose said her group would stop using LiveRamp now that a direct holding-company rival owns the “Switzerland of data,” whose RampID spans tens of thousands of publisher domains. For CTV and programmatic buyers who lean on neutral cross-publisher identity to make streaming addressable, a marquee defection signals real fragmentation risk in the connective tissue the whole market relies on.

Walmart Buys CTV Ad Platform Vibe.co in Cannes-Week Deal

The roughly $1.4B purchase folds a self-serve streaming buyer into Walmart Connect.

Walmart agreed during Cannes Lions week to acquire Vibe.co, a self-serve performance-CTV ad platform aimed at small and mid-market advertisers, in a deal reported around $1.4 billion. Vibe's buying tech will join Walmart Connect alongside the retailer's VIZIO assets and first-party data, simplifying how smaller advertisers activate and measure streaming campaigns. The move deepens Walmart's push to build a full retail-media-plus-CTV stack and intensifies the fight for the long tail of advertisers' streaming budgets — the same SMB demand Disney, Amazon and the broadcasters' new self-serve tools are all chasing.

Forrester: Google Dethrones OpenAI as Agencies' AI Partner

Breadth and integration beat the buzz on the Croisette.

Two days before OpenAI's Cannes session, Forrester published research finding Google has overtaken OpenAI as agencies' preferred AI partner, citing Google's end-to-end stack across data, measurement, creative, models and activation — from Analytics and Meridian to Gemini, Imagen, Veo, Search and YouTube. At the festival Google then rolled out new Gemini-built creator and Demand Gen tools. The framing matters for CTV and programmatic: the AI partner that owns the full buying-to-measurement workflow, not the flashiest model, is the one positioned to capture agency spend as autonomous buying scales.

Magnite Ships Orchestration to Connect Buyer and Seller Agents

A neutral coordination layer for the agentic supply chain, with dentsu and DIRECTV testing.

Days before Cannes Lions, Magnite introduced Magnite Orchestration, a coordination layer that lets buyers connect their own buyer agents to Magnite's seller agent across its premium omnichannel inventory, with testing partners including dentsu and DIRECTV Advertising. Magnite pitches it as neutral infrastructure that does not force buyers onto its native tools — part of a cluster of agentic ad-tech launches that piled up before the festival, from PubMatic's Creator Marketplace to Index Exchange's autonomous CTV optimization. It positions the largest independent SSP as connective tissue for agentic CTV trading, a sign the sell side is racing to make premium video machine-discoverable as autonomous buying arrives.

EU AI Act's Deepfake-Labeling Rules Hit an August 2 Deadline

Article 50 transparency duties force disclosure of AI-generated ad creative across the EU.

As the festival celebrated AI creative, legal advisories underscored that the EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency obligations take effect on August 2, 2026, requiring providers to make synthetic audio, image, video and text machine-readable and detectable, and deployers to clearly disclose deepfakes. The European Commission's voluntary marking-and-labeling code was finalized around June 2026, with machine-readable marking of pre-existing systems extended to December 2, and penalties reaching €15 million or 3% of worldwide turnover. For CTV and programmatic strategists, any AI-generated or AI-manipulated creative running to EU audiences now needs watermarking, metadata and disclosure baked into the production and trafficking workflow within weeks — turning Cannes's AI talk into a hard compliance date.

UN Tells Cannes Misinformation Is Now a Brand-Safety Frontier

A day-one panel reframes brand safety as information integrity in the AI era.

On the opening day of Cannes Lions 2026, a panel on rebooting AI and social media featured the UN's senior information-integrity adviser Charlotte Scaddan, who called mis- and disinformation a top global vulnerability and urged advertisers to treat it as a systemic risk. Panelists argued brand safety must expand from keyword blocklists into societal, youth and platform-design safety, and pressed marketers to redirect budgets toward transparent, quality journalism. For CTV and programmatic strategists, the message is that brand-suitability frameworks and supply-path decisions are increasingly judged on information integrity, not just adjacency — a standard that will shape where streaming and open-web dollars are allowed to run.

AdImpact Raises 2026 Midterm Ad Forecast to $11.6 Billion

Connected TV climbs to $2.7B as political spend hits a record pace through June.

AdImpact raised its 2025–26 midterm-cycle projection to $11.6 billion from $10.8 billion after political advertisers spent a record amount through June, the fastest pace ever for a midterm. Connected TV was revised up $300 million to $2.7 billion, the standout growth channel, while broadcast climbed to $5.6 billion, with the increase driven largely by Senate races. For CTV and programmatic strategists, the upgrade confirms streaming is absorbing an outsized share of incremental political dollars — tightening Q3 and Q4 inventory and CPMs in battleground markets just as brand budgets compete for the same impressions.

ITV, Channel 4 and Sky Launch Universal Ads Self-Serve in the UK

Comcast's SME TV-buying tool, unveiled at Cannes 2025, goes live during Cannes 2026 week.

On June 23, 2026, ITV, Channel 4 and Sky launched Comcast's Universal Ads self-serve platform in Britain, letting small and mid-sized advertisers create, buy and measure premium TV campaigns across ITV Media, Sky Media and Channel 4 Sales from a single interface. First announced by the cohort at Cannes Lions 2025, it aims to make biddable buying of broadcaster inventory as simple as social, with third-party measurement due in 2027. For a global CTV strategist, it shows premium broadcasters collapsing the barrier between linear and BVOD inventory and the self-serve, DTC-style demand that has fueled streaming ad growth — a template for unified broadcaster sales houses in other markets.

India Closes Cannes 2026 With Five Lions, Weakest in a Decade

Two Silver and three Bronze, no Gold or Grand Prix, on a 31% drop in entries.

India finished Cannes Lions 2026 with five Lions — two Silver and three Bronze — its weakest showing in ten years, against 32 Lions including a Grand Prix in 2025. The country sent 676 entries, down 31% from 982, as rising travel costs and tighter budgets shrank delegations and on-ground spend. For a global CTV and programmatic strategist, the pullback signals that India's ad economy is reallocating away from awards-season prestige toward performance and measurable digital and streaming channels — the same JioStar- and CTV-led shift reshaping where APAC creative and media budgets actually flow.

Brazil Leads LATAM Cannes Haul With Mercado Livre Outdoor Grand Prix

GUT São Paulo's “Field Barcode” turns a stadium pitch into a scannable storefront.

Latin America took 47 Lions in the first two days of Cannes Lions 2026, more than half from Brazil, which won the Outdoor Grand Prix for Mercado Livre's “Field Barcode” by GUT São Paulo. The activation turned a football pitch into a 104-metre barcode that in-stadium, TV and YouTube viewers could scan for a discount, driving 53,000 coupon uses and $1.78 million in sales; Puerto Rico added the Audio & Radio Grand Prix. For a global CTV strategist, the win is a marquee proof point that LATAM's e-commerce platforms are building shoppable, multi-screen activations that bridge live TV, streaming and retail media.

Rethink Named Cannes 2026 Independent Agency and Network of the Year

Canada lands two Grand Prix and 43 Lions at the festival.

Toronto-based Rethink led the Canadian field at Cannes Lions 2026 with 14 Lions, including a Grand Prix and three Golds, and was named both Independent Agency of the Year and Independent Network of the Year. Canada took 43 Lions overall across 16 winning agencies, with a second Grand Prix going to TBWA's “Supernova Adaptive” in Innovation. For a global CTV strategist, Canada's independent-shop momentum and innovation wins signal where cross-platform creative talent and challenger budgets are concentrating in a market dominated by Bell, Rogers and Corus.

China Posts a Modest Cannes 2026 Haul of Craft and PR Lions

Tourism and pharma work win Silver and Bronze, but no Grand Prix — and the TV giants stay home.

Mainland China registered a handful of metals at Cannes Lions 2026 rather than a Grand Prix, led by a Silver in Audio & Radio for a Yangzhou tourism suite, a Bronze in Industry Craft for a Shenzhen tourism campaign, and a PR Bronze from Ogilvy Shanghai. The result extends China's pattern of winning on government-tourism and craft work while consumer-electronics giants TCL, Hisense and Xiaomi stayed off the winners' lists. For a global CTV strategist, the gap matters because those same TV makers are China's most aggressive exporters of CTV ad inventory abroad — yet are not converting that scale into festival-grade brand creative.

“Cannes Is Not the Creative Spot Anymore — It's Silicon Valley”

MINT Square CEO Christoph Berg told Digiday the festival has changed character: “The Lions used to be the spot for all the creative minds. Now it's more about technologies. It's Silicon Valley who found a spot there.” It names the structural shift in one line — platforms and ad-tech, not agencies, increasingly own the Croisette.

Cannes Cracked Down on AI Fakery, Then Threw AI a Party

PartnerCentric's Kate Fleming caught the central irony: “The festival that tightened its rules to crack down on AI deception is now hosting its largest-ever celebration of AI creative tools.” It crystallizes the credibility tension Cannes is carrying a year after the AI-faked-results scandal — even as AI usage in entries roughly doubled.

The Bankers Stopped Pretending They're Just Passing Through

Solomon Partners' Mark Boidman explained why finance now sends senior dealmakers to Cannes: “We could do the same conference in Vegas, but here you're not sending your analysts, you're sending a senior partner or an MD.” Private-equity and M&A bankers treating Cannes as a deal conference foreshadows the consolidation wave expected as model-makers pivot into advertising.

The Agent Is the Audience Now

When buying becomes a conversation between machines, the human is the content that gets amputated.

Walk the Croisette this year and you saw the figure: beach cabanas, keynote lanyards, the great rosary of awards. But the figure always hides the ground, and the ground at Cannes 2026 was an absence — the disappearing human buyer. Every booth promised an “agent.” What no one said aloud is that an agent is not a tool you use; it is a new audience you serve. The advertisement is no longer a message aimed at a person. It is a handshake between two programs. We are told this is automation, a faster horse. It is not. It is a reversal of sense ratios. For a century advertising extended the eye and the ear — it worked by attention, the scarce human faculty. OpenAI arrives to announce the “intelligence economy,” and the phrase is more honest than its authors know: when the medium is intelligence, attention is obsolesced. The query has commercial intent before any human feels a want. The buying machine and the selling machine close the loop, and the percept that used to live in a viewer's nervous system now lives in a latency budget measured in milliseconds. Every extension amputates. The wheel extended the foot and numbed it; the agent extends the buyer and numbs the buying. The danger is not that the machines will fail. It is that they will succeed so smoothly that no one in the living room will notice the room is empty. The screen still glows. The ad still plays. Ask only this: who, exactly, is watching whom? — Marshall McLuhan

We Sell, Or Else — Even on the Riviera

A festival can hand out a lion for everything except the only thing that matters: did it sell?

This year the festival gave its top film prize to a campaign about advertising, made by a company that makes software. I am told it was clever. I am sure it was. But cleverness was never the point. When I put a black eyepatch on the man in the Hathaway shirt, I was not being clever. I was selling shirts, and Hathaway sold more of them than in the whole of its previous century. The patch was a hook. The shirt was the point. Never confuse the two. The numbers this year ought to sober everyone holding a rosé. Entries fell to 20,050 from 26,900 — a quarter of the work simply gone, after the organizers had to start demanding proof that the case studies were not invented. Read that sentence again. An industry that prides itself on persuasion had to be policed into telling the truth about its own results. A machine can now fake a result more convincingly than a junior account man, and for a while the machines were winning lions for it. So here is my instruction, and it costs nothing. Before you buy the agent, the platform, the generative suite that promises a thousand variations by lunch, ask the only question that has ever mattered: will it make the cash register ring? If it will, buy it and say so plainly. If it will not, it is decoration, and you may admire it on the beach. The consumer is not a moron. She is your wife. Sell to her, or else. — David Ogilvy

item.title: Sky Agrees Terms to Buy ITV's Broadcast and Streaming Arm for £1.6bn
item.description: A Comcast-owned acquisition would fold ITVX and ITV's channels into Sky, concentrating the bulk of UK premium broadcaster ad inventory under one owner — pending CMA, Ofcom and government clearance.
item.content:encoded:
A Comcast-owned acquisition would fold ITVX and ITV's channels into Sky, concentrating the bulk of UK premium broadcaster ad inventory under one owner — pending CMA, Ofcom and government clearance.

Sky Agrees Terms to Buy ITV's Broadcast and Streaming Arm for £1.6bn

A Comcast-owned acquisition would fold ITVX and ITV's channels into Sky, concentrating the bulk of UK premium broadcaster ad inventory under one owner — pending CMA, Ofcom and government clearance.

Sky has agreed terms to acquire ITV's Media & Entertainment division — its linear channels and the ITVX streaming service — for about £1.6 billion $2.1 billion , plus a roughly £200 million performance earn-out, with ITV Studios separately taking Sky's Love Productions. Reporting says the deal could be announced within two weeks, but it still requires clearance from the Competition and Markets Authority, Ofcom and the Secretary of State. If it completes, Comcast-owned Sky would control the largest single share of UK premium broadcaster video-on-demand and addressable-TV inventory, sitting directly atop the Sky-ITV-Channel 4 unified marketplace and the Universal Ads self-serve platform that both went live in Britain only this week. It would also pull ITV's Planet V addressable stack — the engine behind the broadcasters' joint agency-facing solution — inside Sky. For the CTV market, the move concentrates Britain's premium streaming supply, and the identity and data rails beneath it, in fewer hands: more reach from a single buy, and a sharper competition question for the independent ad-tech vendors who will press it to regulators.

Samsung Opens Its Smart-TV Home Screen to Programmatic Buying

The boot-up hero placement will be biddable through The Trade Desk and DV360, powered by Magnite's SpringServe, in a global rollout from Q3.

Samsung Ads said advertisers will soon be able to buy home-screen placements on Samsung Smart TVs programmatically through integrations with The Trade Desk and Google's DV360, powered by Magnite's SpringServe ad server, with a global rollout beginning in the third quarter. The home screen — the first surface a viewer sees on power-up, and the most valuable real estate on the set — has until now been sold almost entirely through direct deals. Samsung is the world's largest TV maker, so opening its highest-value inventory to biddable demand pulls a major OEM ad surface into the same DSP marketplaces buyers already use for streaming content. It hands Magnite a deeper supply foothold and advances the programmatic capture of the screen itself, not just the shows playing on it.

Teads Folds Home-Screen, In-Stream and Outcomes Into One CTV Suite

CTV Ensemble unifies OEM home-screen and in-stream inventory, dynamic creative and a now-live performance-measurement layer in a single buying workflow.

Teads launched CTV Ensemble, packaging home-screen placements across Google TV, Samsung, LG, TCL and Hisense with in-stream formats, dynamic creative optimization, program-level agentic targeting and a newly generally available CTV performance-measurement layer in one Ad Manager workflow. The company says roughly 40 beta campaigns across 14 countries validated mid- and lower-funnel outcomes, not just reach. The launch repositions a former web-video supplier as a full-funnel CTV buying suite. It is another marker of the performance-CTV land grab — the race to make streaming buys behave, and report, like the lower-funnel digital channels brands already trust.

Comscore Brings ID-Free Contextual Segments Into Amazon DSP

Proximic's cookieless Predictive Audiences go live natively across Amazon CTV, web and mobile, with MiQ an early adopter.

Comscore made its Proximic contextual, identity-free Predictive Audience segments natively available inside Amazon DSP, spanning connected TV, web and mobile. The segments promise addressable, non-endemic reach in premium streaming environments where deterministic identifiers are scarce, with MiQ cited among the first to activate them. The integration deepens Amazon DSP's third-party data bench as it presses its CTV challenge to The Trade Desk. It also signals continued buyer appetite for cookieless contextual targeting on connected TV as identity signals keep fragmenting.

Omnicom and NBCUniversal Build Scene-Level Dynamic Ads

A new Dynamic Contextual Content product maps creative to individual shows, episodes and scenes using Acxiom data and NBCU metadata.

Omnicom Media and NBCUniversal unveiled Dynamic Contextual Content, which pairs Omnicom's audience and performance data with NBCU show metadata down to individual episodes and scenes, then adapts the creative to match — a nature segment tagged 'sustainability' served to a viewer in the market for an electric car. First surfaced at Cannes, it is in beta now with US availability expected by year-end. The push revives scene-level contextual targeting as deterministic identity fragments across CTV. It extends the holdco-publisher direct deal beyond audience buying into creative that changes with the content around it.

PubMatic Opens a Programmatic CTV Marketplace for Creators

A new Creator Marketplace routes independent creator-led streaming inventory into programmatic and agentic demand, with MeatEater first.

PubMatic launched a Creator Marketplace it bills as the first programmatic CTV auction connecting independent, creator-led media companies' premium streaming inventory with programmatic and emerging agentic demand. Outdoor brand MeatEater — with more than two million YouTube subscribers and FAST and AVOD distribution — is the inaugural publisher, with more creator-founded companies to follow. It brings creator-economy supply, historically sold through one-off sponsorships, into open programmatic CTV. For buyers it opens a new inventory lane; for PubMatic it is a bid to stand against direct platform deals as creators move onto the big screen.

Magnite Builds an Orchestration Layer for Agentic CTV Buying

The largest independent SSP will let buyer agents connect to its seller agent to discover and activate premium inventory; dentsu and DIRECTV are testing.

Magnite introduced Magnite Orchestration, a coordination layer that lets buyers connect their own agents to Magnite's seller agent to discover, evaluate and activate premium omnichannel inventory, with dentsu and DIRECTV Advertising among early testers. The largest independent CTV supply-side platform is laying sell-side rails for agent-to-agent transactions just as WPP and The Trade Desk push competing buyer-agent frameworks. Whoever defines the connective tissue between buyer and seller agents stands to set the terms of the next CTV marketplace. This is Magnite's move to claim that ground from the supply side.

EU's AI-Labelling Duties Bind Advertisers From August 2

A July 22 deadline to sign the Commission's transparency code precedes binding Article 50 rules requiring visible labels on AI-generated and manipulated content.

The European Commission has set a July 22 deadline for firms to sign its Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content — earning a presumption of conformity — ahead of the EU AI Act's Article 50 transparency duties becoming binding across all 27 member states on August 2. Deployers must visibly label deepfakes and AI-generated or manipulated material, with non-compliance carrying fines up to €15 million or 3% of global turnover. For connected TV, the rules reach AI-generated creative and the dynamic, machine-made ad variations now proliferating in streaming. Advertisers and platforms serving the EU have weeks to wire disclosure into their creative and ad-serving pipelines.

Texas Senate Race Tops the 2026 Calendar at a Projected $446M

Paxton vs. Talarico is set to be the cycle's most expensive contest, and connected TV is the fastest-growing slice of the spend.

AdImpact projects $446 million in advertising for the Texas Senate contest between Republican Ken Paxton and Democrat James Talarico, the single most expensive race of the 2026 cycle, after the parties' primaries alone drew more than $122 million — the costliest Senate primary on record. Talarico has already launched multi-million-dollar buys, including six-figure spots during the NBA Finals. With CTV the fastest-growing political channel — about $2.5 billion of an $11.6 billion cycle — marquee Senate and governor's races are where streaming demand and CPM inflation will concentrate this autumn. Texas, a top-spend market, is where political CTV inventory gets its first real stress test.

Channel 4 Opens Its Streaming Inventory to Five New Ad Platforms

Amazon DSP, FreeWheel, Hawk, PubMatic and Yahoo DSP gain biddable access to the broadcaster's on-demand ad inventory.

Channel 4 said it is expanding programmatic access to its on-demand streaming inventory through five new ad-tech partners — Amazon Ads via Amazon DSP, Comcast's FreeWheel, Azerion's Hawk, PubMatic and Yahoo DSP — on top of existing routes through DV360, The Trade Desk and Adform. FreeWheel Buyer Cloud and PubMatic Activate are live now, Yahoo DSP follows in mid-summer, and Channel 4 inventory joins Amazon DSP in the third quarter alongside Prime Video, Netflix and Disney+. The move widens biddable, audience-targeted access to a major UK broadcaster's BVOD supply. It pushes premium British streaming inventory into the same global DSP marketplaces buyers already use for the big SVOD ad tiers.

JioHotstar Deepens Magnite Pact, Adds SpringServe Mediation

India's largest streamer routes live-sports and entertainment programmatic demand through Magnite's SpringServe ad server.

JioHotstar and Magnite announced an expanded partnership deploying SpringServe as the programmatic mediation layer across the platform's live-streaming, sports and entertainment inventory, first tested during this year's ICC Men's T20 World Cup. JioHotstar — formed from the 2025 JioCinema/Disney+ Hotstar merger and claiming roughly 450 million monthly average users — gains tighter control over creative quality, demand visibility and brand safety as its open exchange scales. The deal hands the largest independent SSP a deeper foothold in the world's biggest cricket-streaming audience. It signals India's CTV monetization maturing from direct sales toward managed programmatic mediation.

TelevisaUnivision Pre-Sells 1.1 Billion ViX Ad Impressions in Mexico

Exclusive Mexican World Cup streaming rights turn the ad-supported ViX service into a sold-through CTV inventory engine.

TelevisaUnivision has pre-sold roughly 1.1 billion advertising impressions on its ViX streaming service in Mexico ahead of the FIFA World Cup, where it holds exclusive rights to all 104 matches. The company's first-quarter results showed Mexico ad revenue up 13% to $236 million on streaming gains, even as US ad revenue slipped, with management flagging World Cup money landing in later quarters. The scale of pre-sold ViX inventory shows how concentrated event rights are accelerating Latin America's shift of television budgets into addressable, ad-supported streaming. With the tournament now under way, Mexico becomes a live test of how much CTV demand a marquee sports right can pull.

Rogers Sportsnet+ Posts 83% CTV Ad-Revenue Jump in Cup Playoffs

Live programmatic-guaranteed demand drove the gain at 70% sell-through across 550-plus advertisers during the Stanley Cup run.

Rogers Sports & Media reported an 83% year-over-year revenue increase and more than 25% greater reach for priority campaigns on its Sportsnet+ streaming service during the NHL Stanley Cup Playoffs, using Google Ad Manager with custom live pacing and server-side ad unwrapping. Programmatic-guaranteed demand on CTV was the primary driver across more than 550 advertising clients at roughly 70% sell-through. Surfaced via IAB Canada's 2026 CTV outlook, the case is a concrete proof point that live-sports CTV in Canada can scale programmatic yield through demand spikes. It strengthens the pitch for premium live streaming as biddable, measurable inventory.

Hisense's VIDAA Hands Channel 4 Its Smart-TV Home-Screen Ads

The Chinese OEM's ad arm, V, opens premium boot-up inventory across VIDAA-powered Hisense, Toshiba and Loewe sets to a broadcaster sales house.

V, the advertising arm of Hisense-owned smart-TV operating system VIDAA, has partnered with Channel 4 to sell home-screen ad formats across VIDAA-powered sets from Hisense, Toshiba and Loewe, including an expandable hero video carousel that can take over the set's primary navigation. VIDAA accounts for an estimated 7.8% of smart TVs worldwide, second only to Samsung's Tizen, making it one of the larger non-Samsung OEM ad footprints. A national broadcaster taking on third-party sales of a Chinese OEM's home-screen inventory shows the device operating system — not just the content app — becoming a contested premium ad surface. It marks Chinese TV makers' growing weight in the global CTV ad supply chain.

Wieser: The Growth Is Real, but Not Durable

At Cannes, Madison and Wall's Brian Wieser told Beet.TV the ad industry's expansion to $1.42 trillion is 'way broader than just Google, Meta and Amazon,' but warned the early-2026 double-digit growth 'is just not a durable number.' It reframes the CTV and streaming boom as one phase of a broader cycle that will cool, not an open-ended climb.

Publicis-LiveRamp Sends Rivals Hunting for Identity Plan B

AdExchanger reports Publicis's LiveRamp acquisition has rivals such as Hightouch courting advertisers at Cannes, but analysts expect agencies to assemble 'a patchwork combination of in-house data tools and external graphs' rather than find a one-to-one replacement. The worry: a neutral identity spine for CTV could fracture into competing, holdco-owned graphs.

We Lost the Broadcast to a Mirror

The industry is perfecting the personalized ad. It has not noticed the program dissolving behind it.

At Cannes the boast is relevance — an advertisement fitted so precisely to the viewer that it stops feeling like an advertisement at all. Everyone watches the ad. The ad is the figure. The ground is the program, which has quietly begun to melt. A bakery's loaf is conjured into the kitchen of a drama for one household and a soda into the same shot for the next; the documentary about the coast is tagged “sustainability” and routed to the buyer of electric cars. The message was never the spot between the scenes. The scene itself is now the message, and it is composed for an audience of one. Enhance: the program raised to a fluid — every frame negotiable, every object a slot, the show re-cut a million ways before it reaches a million sofas. Obsolesce: the broadcast, the schedule, the thing everyone saw at once and argued about the next morning, the shared hearth around which a mass became a public. Retrieve: the medieval commission, the portrait painted for the one patron in the room, the tale the bard re-shaped for each village green. Reverse: pushed far enough, the personalized show ceases to be a show at all and becomes a surface that watches you back — a mirror that has learned to sell, in which the viewer, flattered by his own reflection, mistakes it for company. So television, the last great campfire, is broken into a hundred million private channels, each lit for a single face. The trade calls this relevance and counts it a triumph. It is also a subtraction: the quiet end of the thing we held in common. We did not lose the broadcast to a better broadcast. We lost it to a mirror, and a mirror has no audience. It has only an occupant. — Marshall McLuhan

A Thousand Ads, and Not One Idea

The machines can now make ten thousand versions of your commercial. They cannot make the one that sells.

The fashion at Cannes this year is the machine that makes the advertising. It builds a “digital twin” of your product and drops it into a streaming drama; it spins a thousand variations of a spot before lunch and serves a different one to every household. The promise is volume — creative without end, creative without cost. I have one tiresome question, the only one that ever mattered: does it sell? Volume is not an idea. It never was. In 1951 I put an eyepatch on the man in the Hathaway shirt. The prop cost a dollar fifty. That one idea ran for years and sold the shirts faster than the factory could cut them — not because there were many executions, but because there was one, and it was true. A machine can now generate ten thousand commercials in an afternoon. It cannot generate the eyepatch. The big idea comes from the unconscious, from a man who has soaked himself in the product until something surfaces; it does not come from a model averaging every advertisement that came before it into a handsome, forgettable mean. Ten thousand competent ads are still not one you remember. So use the machines. Let them cut the versions, place the product, mind the arithmetic. But do not ask them for the idea, because they have none to give. Find one true thing to say about the product, say it like you mean it, and let the machine make the copies. We sell, or else. — David Ogilvy

item.title: The Climbing Men
item.author: noreply@calvincollins.xyz (Walt Whitman)
item.description: On the eleventh of September
item.content:encoded:
On the eleventh of September

The Climbing Men

On the eleventh of September

Mannahatta — I was looking for something cool and bright, and the morning gave it: a sky of hard September blue over the harbor, the ferries crossing as they have always crossed, the million-footed island waking to its work. I have sung this city at its trades, and would have sung it again this ordinary forenoon — the clerk at his ledger, the woman at the high window, the cook, the porter, the man selling coffee at the curb — when out of that blue, without a word, the fire came down. Count them with me, for the catalogue is the only prayer I know. The bond-trader and the dishwasher in the tower’s crown; the firemen of Brooklyn and Mannahatta; the police, the stewards, the cleaners who came before light; the travellers strapped in the bellies of the planes; the man who carried his blind friend down ninety flights, and the friend, and the dog between them. They were of every land that ever poured through this harbor — en-masse , the whole roll of nations, dim-descended and bright-descended, working in one building under one sky. The same red-running blood ran in all of them. It runs there yet, in the dust. And here is the thing I cannot let the smoke swallow: while the thousands came down, a column of men in heavy coats went up . Up the shaking stair, two by two, the hose on the shoulder, the axe in the hand, breathing what no lungs should breathe, climbing toward the fire that every animal sense said flee . Camerados — I have dressed wounds in the army hospitals, I have stood by the cots of boys with the leg gone and made no fuss, and I have seen nothing braver than this plain ascent. They did not climb for a flag or a phrase. They climbed because a stranger was above them, and the hand goes out to the hand. That is the Republic; that, and nothing the orators say. Then the towers knelt, the one and then the other, and a grey snow that was not snow fell on the living and the dead alike and made them brothers in one colour. For days after, the searchers went over the smoking pile on their knees, asking the wreck a single question. And the walls of the city bloomed with paper — a thousand faces pinned up under one word, Missing — the tenderest catalogue ever posted, each leaf a whole life, each asking have you seen . I have seen. I see them now. Do not tell me they are lost. The grass is already coming, faithful, out of their ashes; the harbor still lifts and falls with the old patient breathing; the ferries cross, the island goes again to its work, and the dust of the climbing men is in the lungs of the children now alive. Death is luckier than we are told. Mannahatta, you are not broken — you are enlarged, you contain them, you carry them in your million-footed walk. I stop here, in the blue, among the falling paper, and wait with you.

item.title: The Answering Bullet
item.author: noreply@calvincollins.xyz (Thomas Carlyle)
item.description: On the assassination of Charlie Kirk
item.content:encoded:
On the assassination of Charlie Kirk

The Answering Bullet

On the assassination of Charlie Kirk

It is done: in the bright forenoon, under a white canopy pitched on the green of a Utah university, a young man sits answering the questions of all comers; and across the autumn air there travels one rifle-shot, and the answerer answers no more. Orem, in the State of Utah; the tenth day of September, 2025. One-and-thirty years he had lived. Behold him fallen sideways in his chair, the microphone yet warm, the half-finished sentence hanging unfinished forever in the bright American air. Who was he, this Charles Kirk? A Talker; let us not pretend otherwise. A Stump-Orator of the new sort, microphoned and multiplied, who had made of perpetual Speech a vocation and an industry; whose vocables went out by the million into every idle ear of a distracted continent; whom this writer, had he met him living, would assuredly have scolded for the noise of him. The Age of Vocables found in him one of its loudest sons. And yet,— mark it well, O reader, for here is the one Reality in the matter,— this man did a thing the common Stump-Orator never dares. He pitched his table in the open field; he wrote upon it Prove Me Wrong ; he sat down unarmed amid the young and the hostile and said, in effect: Here am I; contradict me to my face. Whatsoever the worth of his doctrines, and much of it was light enough, that posture was not Cant. It was the old sacred contest of the Word answered by the Word,— the one human method by which Chaos is ever beaten back a little toward Cosmos. He invited the answering tongue. They sent him, instead, the answering bullet. And that, my friends, is the whole tragedy, and the whole judgment, in a single stroke. For consider what an assassin is. He is the man who, having no Word wherewith to answer, reaches for the rifle; who confesses, in the very act, that argument has died in him, that he cannot out-speak his adversary and has resolved therefore to out-shoot him. The marksman on the rooftop is not the opposite of the Stump-Orator,— he is the Stump-Orator's last and lowest avatar, Cant grown so hollow that it has given up even on speech. He has nothing to say; and so he says it with lead. Woe, then, to the Age that breeds him! A People that will settle the contest of tongues by the crack of a sharpshooter has pronounced sentence upon itself. It has declared the Word bankrupt and enthroned the Bullet in its room; it has chosen for its arbiter not the Reason that persuades but the Powder that explodes. Lying is not permitted in this Universe; and neither is this: no Republic can long endure that murders its talkers because it has ceased to be able to answer them. The thing is a powder-mine. One spark struck in Utah,— and who shall say where the conflagration stops? Man, by the nature of him, is definable as an incarnated Word. They shot the Word in the throat, and fancied they had won. They had not. Turn now, one moment, from the noise to the silence; from the Cause to the man. One-and-thirty years; a wife; little children who will grow into knowledge of their father by the recording of his voice and the manner of his death. There are tears due to him, as to all men; the Maker did not fashion that creature to be felled like an ox in a field among his fellows. Let the partisans bay on either flank; over the body itself a decent humanity may stand bareheaded a moment, and be still. But the prophecy I will not soften. Hear it, America: the bullet has silenced one questioner and multiplied his question a thousand-fold. The dead man asked, Prove me wrong; and his murderer has proved nothing whatever, except that he himself was the deader of the two long before ever the trigger moved. The assassin has gone down among the Phantasms; the question stands yet upon the open table, in the bright air, unanswered and unanswerable by powder. Light; or, failing that, lightning. Thou hast fired upon the light. Stand ready, then, foolish and unhappy Land, for the lightning.

item.title: Walmart Buys Vibe.co for $1.4B to Pull SMBs Into Streaming
item.description: The retailer's largest ad-tech deal yet pairs a self-serve CTV platform with Vizio screens and Walmart's commerce data — a direct answer to Amazon.
item.content:encoded:
The retailer's largest ad-tech deal yet pairs a self-serve CTV platform with Vizio screens and Walmart's commerce data — a direct answer to Amazon.

Walmart Buys Vibe.co for $1.4B to Pull SMBs Into Streaming

The retailer's largest ad-tech deal yet pairs a self-serve CTV platform with Vizio screens and Walmart's commerce data — a direct answer to Amazon.

Walmart agreed to acquire Vibe.co, a Paris-based self-serve connected-TV advertising platform, in a deal The Wall Street Journal valued at roughly $1.4 billion — the retailer's largest ad-tech purchase yet. Vibe lets small and mid-sized businesses launch, target and measure streaming campaigns in minutes, the kind of advertiser that has long found CTV too complex and too costly to enter. Walmart will plug the platform into its Vizio smart-TV footprint and its first-party commerce data, offering sales-based, closed-loop attribution through Walmart Connect. The move is a direct answer to Amazon, whose retail-media profits bankroll an expanding streaming-ad business, and to The Trade Desk and Google in the contest for self-serve CTV budgets. By pairing a long tail of SMB advertisers with measurable outcomes on its own screens, Walmart accelerates the convergence of retail media and connected TV — and pulls a class of buyer that never bought television into the room. For every CTV seller, it signals that the next pool of streaming demand may be assembled by a retailer, not a broadcaster or a DSP.

Warner Bros. Discovery Rebuilds Its Ad Stack for AI Agents

An AWS-based overhaul puts autonomous agents across planning, pricing and stewardship — the sell-side answer to the buyer-agent wave.

Warner Bros. Discovery said it is rebuilding its US advertising technology stack on Amazon Web Services to deploy agentic AI across how its linear and digital inventory is planned, activated, optimized and monetized. Unified media planning is slated to arrive in the third quarter, followed by composable order management, pricing and stewardship in the fourth, dissolving the long-standing silo between the company's linear and digital ad operations. As buy-side agents proliferate, a major programmer building matching seller-side agentic infrastructure shows the autonomous-trading model is being wired into both ends of the CTV pipe.

NBCUniversal Unveils Rock Studios Brand-Creative Engine

A unified offering bundles sponsorships, custom creative, talent and branded entertainment with outcomes measurement.
