At Cannes Lions, NBCUniversal unveiled Rock Studios, a unified brand-creative engine spanning integrated sponsorships and experiences, custom creative, talent and creators, and branded entertainment, embedding brands inside NBCU programming and live events with measurement tied to outcomes. Advertising president Karen Kovacs framed it as giving brands both breakthrough storytelling and measurable performance in one place, citing more than 300 industry awards over three years. A major programmer packaging branded entertainment, IP and measurement as a single outcomes product reflects Advanced TV's broader turn toward full-funnel, performance-oriented packages.

Samsung TV Plus Lets the Remote Add Amazon Items to Cart

Samsung Ads and Amazon Ads bring remote-shoppable interactive video to free, ad-supported streaming.

Samsung Ads named the first brands activating Amazon Ads' remote-enabled interactive video technology on Samsung TV Plus — Boiron USA, Logitech, PLAION, PMG and Reckitt — letting viewers add a product to an Amazon cart or send an offer to their phone without leaving the ad, the first time this works on FAST content. Samsung TV Plus has surpassed 100 million monthly active users globally, and Amazon cites large lifts in brand search, add-to-cart actions and purchase rates from the interactive format over standard streaming spots. The tie-up extends Amazon's commerce rails into a rival manufacturer's free inventory and pushes shoppable formats further into the performance-CTV conversation.

Omnicom Becomes Netflix's First Data Partner for AI Ads

Acxiom audience data feeds Netflix's AI ad suite to make streaming spots more relevant — a wall opening to agency data.

At Cannes Lions, Omnicom Media announced it is Netflix's first data-collaboration partner, integrating its Acxiom audience intelligence into Netflix's AI-powered ad suite to deliver more contextually relevant, addressable spots with closed-loop measurement. Advertisers supply Acxiom segments and a brief, and Netflix's AI matches relevant titles and generates ad variations for different audiences and content environments; the deal is live in the US with international expansion planned by year-end, and Bimbo Bakeries signed on as an early client. A holding company plugging proprietary first-party data directly into Netflix's ad tech signals streaming's premium walled gardens opening to agency data for measurable CTV buys.

Omnicom and Disney Bring Sequential Ads to Streaming

Innovid-powered creative evolves across a viewing session instead of repeating, across both VOD and live.

Omnicom Media and Disney Advertising launched a connected-TV solution that delivers dynamic sequential storytelling, with coordinated 15-, 30- and 60-second spots that build narratively across a session rather than repeating, spanning both VOD and live programming. Powered by Innovid and matching Disney's identity graph to Omnicom's Acxiom data, it is live in the US — trade coverage names The Home Depot and State Farm as early clients — with Europe and LATAM rollouts planned for later in 2026. Omnicom cites research that most viewers tire of seeing the same spot more than a handful of times in one session. Sequential messaging tied to a publisher identity graph pushes CTV past frequency capping toward addressable narrative sequencing, a higher-value format for live and on-demand alike.

WPP Media Unveils Buyer Agent and Agentic-Video Standards Push

A prototype arrives with a standards initiative spanning Disney, Netflix, Fox, NBCUniversal, Paramount and Comcast.

WPP Media revealed a prototype "Buyer Agent for Video" inside WPP Open and an Agentic Standards Initiative defining how buyer and seller agents communicate, validate decisions and transact across linear, CTV and premium video. Launch partners include Comcast/FreeWheel, Disney Advertising, Fox, NBCUniversal, Netflix and Paramount, alongside IAB Tech Lab and Prebid.org, with a proposed standard targeted for early 2027. By rallying the major TV sellers around shared agentic protocols, the largest holding company is trying to set the rules of automated TV buying before rivals lock in proprietary stacks.

Horizon Media Bets on an Open Agentic Layer, Not a Proprietary Stack

The independent agency wires buying agents into Blu via an open, MCP-based integration layer.

Horizon Media launched agentic buying capabilities inside Blu, part of HorizonOS, using an open "agentic integration layer" that lets partners plug in through APIs and the Model Context Protocol. Named integrations span publishers Disney, Fox, NBCUniversal, TikTok and Snap, plus ad-tech partners including Magnite, Innovid, Kochava, Smartly and Databricks, with agents making real-time decisions while keeping humans in the loop. The independent's open-ecosystem approach is a direct counter to the holding companies' closed agentic stacks, reframing how buy-side automation gets built in CTV and beyond.

FTC Weighs Billion-Dollar Suit Over Amazon Ad-Auction Disclosures

The probe centers on whether Amazon misled advertisers about reserve pricing in its ad auctions.

The FTC's consumer-protection staff has drafted a possible complaint against Amazon over whether it misled advertisers about its ad products, including how reserve pricing works in its ad auctions, with a suit or settlement possible as soon as this summer. Reporting indicates the case could carry billions of dollars in civil penalties and draw coordinated action from state attorneys general. A probe into auction transparency at the largest US retail-media and CTV seller signals regulators are now scrutinizing the mechanics of programmatic ad pricing itself, not only consumer data.

EU Publishes AI-Content Labelling Code Ahead of August Deadline

A voluntary code sets deepfake-marking rules as the AI Act's transparency duties turn binding on August 2.

The European Commission published its Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-Generated Content, offering guidance on marking and labelling AI-made video, audio, images and text under Article 50 of the EU AI Act. The code proposes an interim "AI" visual label for deepfakes and explicitly excludes commercial advertising from any artistic carve-out, meaning AI-generated celebrity likenesses in ads must be disclosed. With the transparency obligations becoming legally binding on August 2, advertisers and CTV platforms running AI-generated creative in the EU face near-term labelling requirements.

AdImpact Lifts 2026 Cycle Forecast to Record $11.6 Billion

Connected TV is projected at $2.7 billion — the only channel meaningfully gaining on 2024.

AdImpact raised its 2025-26 midterm projection to $11.6 billion, up from $10.8 billion, after spending hit $4 billion through early June — 46% ahead of the 2024 pace and on track to outspend the 2024 presidential year. CTV is now forecast at roughly $2.7 billion, about a quarter of the total and the only major channel meaningfully growing versus 2024, while broadcast remains largest at $5.6 billion. The upgrade confirms streaming has become a core line item for political campaigns, accelerating CTV's structural share gains against linear in an election year.

Comcast's Universal Ads Goes Live in UK Across ITV, C4, Sky

One self-service interface now spans all three British broadcaster sales houses, aimed squarely at SME budgets.

Comcast's Universal Ads platform launched in the UK on June 23 in partnership with Channel 4, ITV and Sky, giving SMEs, DTC brands and digital-native advertisers a single self-service interface to create, buy and measure campaigns across ITV Media, Sky Media and Channel 4 Sales. An advertiser can set a budget, target an audience and upload creative within minutes, pairing social-style simplicity with broadcaster-grade brand safety, and operationalising the joint intent the three broadcasters first signalled in 2025. Pooling three competing UK sales houses into one automated buying surface is a structural bid to make premium CTV inventory as easy to buy as social — and to win back budgets flowing to Meta and YouTube.

TAM and VTION Launch Single-Panel CTV Ad Measurement in India

"CTV Ad Pulse" links connected-TV ad exposure to viewing behaviour on one opted-in panel, debuting during IPL 2026.

TAM Media Research and audience-measurement firm VTION launched "CTV Ad Pulse," combining TAM's ad monitoring with VTION's passive, consent-based panel of more than 100,000 devices now extended from smartphones to connected TVs drawn from the same panellists. The tool measures audience profiles, reach, frequency and campaign delivery across demographics and geographies, and was introduced live during the IPL 2026 season as app-based and live-sport viewing expand CTV inventory faster than measurement has kept up. Credible cross-screen CTV currency is the precondition for programmatic CTV buying to scale in India, and a single unified panel measuring exposure is the infrastructure advertisers say has been missing to shift budgets from direct deals toward measurable programmatic.

Brazil's TV 3.0 Begins Rollout Across 22 Cities Before World Cup

The next-generation broadcast standard, branded DTV+, pairs over-the-air signal with broadband — and supports addressable advertising.

Brazil's TV 3.0 branded DTV+ began rolling out in June, with coverage confirmed across 22 municipalities in the São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro metropolitan areas — broader than the government's original three-city promise — and timed to the 2026 World Cup, with Globo broadcasting in 4K. The hybrid standard pairs broadcast signal with internet connectivity, and its design enables segmented, addressable advertising so households watching the same programme can receive different commercial breaks, alongside on-demand content and apps. By importing household-level addressability and data-driven targeting into Brazil's mass-reach free-to-air ecosystem, TV 3.0 begins to blur the line between linear and programmatic CTV in Latin America's largest ad market.

Ottawa Orders CRTC to Reverse 15% Streamer Content Levy

The government will inject C$600M into the cultural sector instead, amid US trade pressure and a court challenge.

The federal government ordered the CRTC to review its ruling that would have required large streamers with C$25M-plus in Canadian revenue to contribute roughly 15% of those revenues to local content — up from about 5% — and will instead inject C$600 million annually into the cultural sector. No money has yet been collected, because Motion Picture Association members including Netflix, Disney, Paramount and Amazon are challenging the levy in Federal Court. A 15% revenue obligation directly compresses the unit economics of ad-supported streaming tiers in Canada — the fastest-growing CTV inventory pool — and the policy whiplash injects fresh planning uncertainty for anyone pricing AVOD inventory or committing local-content spend.

Nexxen Stakes CTV Future on Hisense's VIDAA at Investor Day

An ad-tech firm anchors its connected-TV strategy on a Chinese-owned operating system — the world's No. 2 by smart-TV share.

At its 2026 Investor Day on June 16, ad-tech firm Nexxen foregrounded its connected-TV strategy and its partnership with VIDAA, the Hisense-owned operating system that powers roughly 7.8% of the world's smart TVs, second only to Samsung's Tizen. Nexxen raised its full-year guidance for the second time this year and reiterated the VIDAA-anchored CTV plan, whose terms — set in a 2025 renewal — give it exclusive global access to VIDAA's automatic-content-recognition data and exclusive North American CTV monetisation rights through at least the end of 2029, with Vestel's adoption of VIDAA across Toshiba, JVC and Telefunken sets cited as a lever into Europe. A Western ad-tech company increasingly betting its CTV business on a Chinese manufacturer's operating system and data is the clearest sign yet that Chinese smart-TV platforms are becoming load-bearing infrastructure for global programmatic CTV.

The Agents Have Their Own Conversation

Everyone is watching the buyer agent. No one is watching the conversation it is having.

The figure this Cannes is the agent — a buyer's robot that plans, bids and clears a television campaign while its maker stands proudly beside it, promising a human stays "in the loop." Everyone is watching the tool. The tool is the figure. The ground is the conversation: the silent, ceaseless exchange between a buyer's agent and a seller's agent, transacting in a protocol no media planner will ever read, at a speed no human can attend. The content of the new medium is the old one — the trader, the haggle, the long lunch — now playing as a recording inside a machine. The agent is not a faster buyer. It is a new place where buying happens, and the buyer is no longer standing in it. Enhance: the buy raised to a reflex, a campaign that renegotiates itself a thousand times a second across every screen at once. Obsolesce: the insertion order, the rate card, the request for proposal, the trader's hunch, the relationship that took a decade to build. Retrieve: the oldest marketplace of all — the bazaar, the auctioneer's chant, agent calling to agent across a crowded floor — handed back as code. Reverse: pushed far enough, the agent built to execute your intention begins to compose it, and the human "in the loop" becomes a ceremony, a signature on a decision made before he woke. So the standards bodies now race to write the grammar of a language people will not speak. They call it governance. It is something stranger: the market has stepped behind the glass, and we are left watching our own reflection negotiate. The medium was never the message we sent. The agent is the message, and we have become its content. — Marshall McLuhan

Now You Can Count the Sale

The trade has rediscovered the buy button. I have been waiting sixty years for it.

This week the television set grew a checkout. A viewer points the remote at a streaming advertisement and the product drops into a shopping cart without anyone leaving the sofa. The trade calls it the future of connected television. I call it the oldest idea I know, finally handed a screen large enough to do it justice. Direct response was my first love and my secret weapon, and for forty years the brand men treated it as something to be scraped off the shoe. I began in direct mail, where every advertisement carried a coupon and every coupon told you, by Friday, whether you were a genius or a fool. That cruel arithmetic taught me more than any awards jury on the Croisette ever did. Now one platform reports that a shoppable streaming spot lifts purchases several times over an ordinary one. Several times over. A number you can put in the bank is worth more than a trophy you can only polish, and at last the largest screen in the house can be held to the same account as a coupon in a magazine. But do not lose your head. A button is not a reason to buy. You can turn the couch into a counter and still sell nothing if the promise is feeble, the picture dull, the proposition unclear. The machine counts the sale; it cannot conjure one. Give the viewer a single true thing worth crossing the room for — then let them buy it without rising. Measure everything. Worship nothing. — David Ogilvy

item.title: Peace Signed Digitally; And the Oil Shall Flow For Sixty Days
item.author: noreply@calvincollins.xyz (Thomas Carlyle)
item.description: A War ended by Memorandum at Versailles, with Fourteen Points and a smell of Mammon over all.
item.content:encoded:
A War ended by Memorandum at Versailles, with Fourteen Points and a smell of Mammon over all.

Peace Signed Digitally; And the Oil Shall Flow For Sixty Days

A War ended by Memorandum at Versailles, with Fourteen Points and a smell of Mammon over all.

It is done: at Versailles, in that same gilded Hall where other Treaties were signed into the teeth of other Destinies, a Memorandum has been put to paper, and a War four months old is declared over. Fourteen Points, no less,—a sacred number, it would seem, in the arithmetic of Stump-Orators. The Seven Captains of the Earth, gathered at Évian to dine at the table of Macron, have set their hands to a Joint Statement; and that Statement, O reader, takes care to praise the chief Signatory by name. Mark it well. When the Powers assemble to congratulate one Man upon his own Peace, the Peace is already half a Pageant. And how, pray, was this Everlasting Concord between Persia and the West entered into? Not by two earnest souls clasping hands over a thing they would die for; not at the elbow of the Eternities at all. "We already signed the deal digitally yesterday," announces the Vice-President to the morning television, as a man might report the purchase of a hat. Digitally! The Speaker of the Persian Parliament signs in by conference-call, as to a meeting of shareholders. Behold the new sacrament of the Mechanical Age: a Peace that no hand has touched, witnessed by no Heaven, transacted through the air like a quotation of stocks. Truth, my friends, has never yet been delivered by telegraph; and a Reality signed by Phantasms remains a Phantasm still. Then comes the Money,—for there is always the Money. Three hundred thousand million of dollars are pledged to the rebuilding of Iran; not from the American purse, we are assured, but "it may be possible for other countries to invest." So: the cash-nexus, which has dissolved every bond between man and man into a bargain, is now to dissolve the bond between Nation and Nation, and call the residue a Brotherhood. The relief of sanctions is a "performance-based thing," says the Vice-President,—a phrase to make the angels weep,—as though the Justice of the Universe were a contract of hire, payable on satisfactory delivery of enriched uranium down-blended under inspection. Mammon's Law, not Christ's Law, rules yet in this transaction; and Mammon, decked in the robes of Peace, is not therefore God. And the Strait! The Strait of Hormuz "will reopen," cries the chief Signatory: "Let the oil flow!" A noble cry, were it true. But read the small print of the Eternities, the terms as the scribes have set them down: "safe passage of commercial vessels with no charge for sixty days only." Sixty days! Here is the whole Sham in a single clause. A thing is proclaimed Permanent in the headline and leased by the fortnight in the body;

The Trustworthy Have Nominated Themselves

On a coalition of the safe, assembled to govern a thing too big for them.

It is the wisest thing in the world to cry out before you are hurt, and I propose to cry out now, while the hatchet is still in the air over a luncheon table at Evian-les-Bains. The gentlemen seated round that table — about a dozen of them, with three Cabinet ministers and the heads of the Western states for company — have agreed upon a most reasonable thing. They have agreed that the most powerful minds ever assembled by men ought to be governed by a coalition of the trustworthy; and they have very kindly nominated themselves as the trustworthy. I do not doubt their sincerity for an instant. That is precisely what alarms me. Mr. Amodei, of the firm called Anthropic, begs the rulers of the earth to "resist the temptation to splinter." It is a fine phrase, and like all fine phrases it deserves to be taken at its word and walked about until it falls over. A thing splinters when it is dropped; a thing splinters when it is struck; a thing splinters, above all, when it was never one solid thing to begin with but a great many separate persons pretending to be a single great machine. Mr. Amodei does not wish men to splinter. But men are not a pane of glass, and a nation is not a dinner-service. The thing he calls splintering, an older and plainer language called the ordinary disagreement of free people about who shall command their souls. Then there is the lovely scheme of "trusted partners," under which the favoured nations are admitted, like guests with the right letter of introduction, to the use of the talking machines. I had always supposed that the whole quarrel of the last three hundred years was about whether a man might be free without first being trusted by his betters. Here it returns, in a clean collar, as a benefaction. The ordinary fellow in the street is not to be a partner at all; he is to be the thing partnered over, the unmanageable output of common humanity that the wise must learn to manage. I have heard that song before. The last time it was sung the chorus was about purer motherhood and a happier posterity, and it ended at the door of an asylum. Observe what the splendid dupes have already done to one another. Mr. Amodei comes to beg for a coalition of democracies in the very week that his own government has reached into his workshop and switched off two of his engines — Fable the Fifth and Mythos the Fifth, frozen by the police of the State on grounds no plain citizen may read. He asks us to hand the keys of the future to a brotherhood of the safe, and the brotherhood has just shown that it will rifle a brother's pockets on a Thursday. Mr

The Water Is Still Closed at Hormuz

The proclamation went up on the wire. The ships did not move.

In the late winter of that year the strait was closed and it stayed closed into the summer. It had been closed seventy-one days when they counted, and then it was closed longer. The water is between Iran and Oman and it is narrow, and about a fifth of the oil that moves by sea moves through it, and now none of it did. The ships rode at anchor in the Gulf and waited. There were a hundred and eighteen of them riding at anchor when Kpler counted the tankers. Fifty-seven or fifty-eight of the big ones, the VLCCs, were trapped in the strait or near it, which is about a tenth of all the big tankers in the world. Eleven million barrels a day did not come out. They stayed in the ground or they stayed in the steel of the ships, and the men stayed with the ships. The ones that could still load took the long way. A cargo that used to run from Ras Tanura to Ningbo now ran from Galveston, and the Galveston run is more than two and a half times the distance. The freight stabilized near a hundred thousand dollars a day, which was double the year before. The owners do not call this good. They call it longer. On the fourteenth of June the President posted it on Truth Social. The Deal with the Islamic Republic of Iran is now complete, he wrote. I hereby fully authorize the toll free opening of the Strait of Hormuz. Let the oil flow. The oil did not flow that day. The signing was set for the twentieth of June, in Switzerland, on a Friday. The blockade had been in full force and effect until the agreement was finalized, and the agreement was not yet finalized, and a proclamation is a thing you read and the water is a thing you cross. You could read the proclamation. You could not cross the water. A man at DHT named Svein Moxnes Harfjeld runs the big tankers and he was asked whether the tankers would come back now. We cannot react to good news one day and assume we can enter, he said. He wanted a high level of credibility first. He did not want to put a ship full of crude into a strait on the strength of a good day. The strait had been closed since late February and he had watched it. June Goh at Sparta gave the number. Ten to eleven million barrels per day of crude oil continue to be shut-in for every day the Strait of Hormuz remains shut. The market was waiting for a gush of a hundred million barrels from the stranded ships once the deal was in place. She said it would take three to six months required to get everything back to status quo. The backlog of anchored ships alone would take ten to fifteen days to clear, and clearing the queue would not amount to a full recovery

The Body That Would Cut Off Its Own Shadow

A rupture forty years in the making is not a quarrel over rubrics but a soul refusing to hold its opposites.

The figure of a divided Church is not as simple as the wire reports would have it, and the editors who filed this story under canon law have, by that filing, missed the one thing worth a physician's attention. A Society of priests in Switzerland intends, on the first of July, to consecrate four men bishops without the mandate of Rome; the Pope has answered that if they do so he is sorry, but "we must move forward"; and the world, which long ago decided such things are quarrels about Latin and lace, turns the page. Yet here is a body resolved to amputate the half of itself it cannot bear to look at. Let me say at once, to forestall the usual misreading, that I take no side in the matter of valid orders; that is a question for canonists. I observe only the psychic fact, and it is as solid as any in my consulting room. The Society of Saint Pius X has, since Archbishop Lefebvre raised his hand over four kneeling men in 1988, lived in what its present superior, Father Pagliarani, names an "objective state of grave necessity." The phrase is more revealing than he knows. A man in such necessity is a man under possession; he no longer feels that he chooses, but that he is compelled. What possesses them is not the devil of the headlines but an archetype older than the council they reject: the bright, spotless, unchanging past, held so perfectly in mind that everything outside it — the vernacular, the offered hand to the unbeliever — falls into shadow and is called darkness. This is the inexorable law I have called enantiodromia, the running of a thing into its opposite. The more spotlessly the tradition is conceived, the blacker grows the modern world it must exclude, until the two stand as irreconcilable halves of one body that can no longer know itself as one. The old theology had a name for the Church entire — the corpus mysticum , the mystical body — and a body cannot purify itself by cutting. No tree, it is said, can grow to heaven unless its roots reach down to hell; and no Church can keep its tradition by refusing the age it was given to redeem. Notice how the actors describe one another. The Cardinal in Rome, Fernández, warns of a "schismatic act" with "grave consequences" — the language of law, which is the language of the privatio boni , of evil as a mere lack, an absence where assent should be. The men at Écône answer in the language of necessity, of a darkness pressing in. Each sees in the other only the shadow it has refused in itself: to Rome the rebels are disobedience cast out; to Écône, Rome is the worldliness, the loss of soul. They are right ha

The Seating Chart Was the Whole Persuasion Move

Nothing got signed in France. That was never the point.

Nobody signed anything in France. Remember that. The G7 met for a working lunch in Évian-les-Bains on June 17. The official theme was "Ensuring a safe, rapid and effective deployment of artificial intelligence." Crypto Briefing read the room and said it plainly: "No specific regulatory announcements or policy outcomes came out of the lunch." It was a conversation, not a negotiation. So if nothing happened, why are we still talking about it? I'll tell you why. Because the most powerful thing in that room wasn't a document. It was a chair. The untrained reader looks at a summit and counts the deliverables. No deliverable, no story. The trained reader looks at who is sitting where. And at this lunch, Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, and Demis Hassabis were sitting at the leaders' table — the one normally reserved for presidents and prime ministers. Twelve or so private executives, seated as peers of the people who run countries. That seat is the persuasion move. The whole thing. Jessica Brandt at the Council on Foreign Relations got it exactly right, and I want to slow down on her words because they're doing real work. She said, "We're seeing a shift in who gets a seat at the table and a signal of where power sits." A signal of where power sits. That is not a metaphor she reached for by accident. The seating chart IS the message. The lunch agenda is the cover story. Here's what the optics did, in order: 1. They placed three lab heads physically beside the heads of state, so your brain files them as the same kind of thing. 2. They billed the day around child safety, which is the one topic nobody can be against. Florida had just sued Altman personally over ChatGPT, so the timing was, let's say, convenient. 3. They produced no binding rule, which means the only thing that traveled out of that room was the picture. And the picture is the product. You can't criticize a chair. There's no hostile amendment to a place setting. Like a wall that looks entirely different inside each person's head, a seat at the table looks like cooperation to the optimists and like capture to the worriers, and both groups stare at the same photograph. Now watch the Europeans, because this is the tell. They flew in seeking checks on American AI dominance, and then they sat down at a table where the Americans were at the head of it. Zach Meyers of CERRE summed up the mood: "There is a general anxiety about the state of Europe, the fact that we're relying on other countries for quite important strategic infrastructure." Anxiety. That's a feeling, not a clause in a treaty. They felt the leverage

Out of the Cradle, the Tally They Keep at the Door

Five and fifty-hundredths to the thousand — and I would go bedside to bedside, and count.

I have stood at the cot before. I knew the smell of the ward, the carbolic and the long row, the boys with the bullet through the breast and the leg taken off, and I learned there to dress the wound with a steady hand and to keep the fire in the breast where the public voice could not carry it. Now they bring me another tally, fresh-printed this Sixth-month, and the cots are smaller, and the room is a lying-in room, and the body upon the linen is the body of a child not yet a year in the world. Five and fifty-hundredths to the thousand — so the count stands for the year just gone, scarcely moved from the year before it. The doctors of the great cabinet of records, Ely and Driscoll, who linked the birth-paper to the death-paper across all the States and the District, set the figure down plainly, neither risen nor much fallen. And in the plainness of it, O reader, do you hear what I hear? I hear the sudden quiet of the crib — the sleeping-death they have learned at last to stay a little, eight in the hundred fewer than last year, the safe flat surface, the room shared and not the bed — and I hear, under that small mercy, the going-out of nineteen thousand small breaths and more, each one a cradle endlessly rocking, then rocking empty. Let me not give you the lump only. Let me go bedside to bedside, the way I went among the wounded, and let the tally be a catalog of cradles. Here the cradle of the congenital malformation, the heart or the skull not finished, four thousand and ninety-one of them, the first and largest grief. Here the cradle come too soon, the short gestation, the small weight, two thousand nine hundred and forty-five. Here the cradle of the sudden silence in the night. Here the cradle of the hurt that need not have been. Examine these — red, black, or white, fine-headed, nobly-formed — examine the small limbs, cunning already in tendon and nerve; within there runs blood, the same old blood, the same red-running blood. I will not rank them. The cataloger who would tell you whose child weighs more in the scale of the Republic is the cataloger I will not be. And yet — for there is always the yet — the count is not laid evenly upon the land, and an honest tally does not pretend that it is. The cradle of the mother who is of the first peoples, nine and a fifth to the thousand. The cradle of the Black mother, near eleven. The cradle of the White, the cradle of the Asian, less than half of these. The gap opens, the records say, in the first four weeks, in the very dooryard of life, and does not close from one year to the next. I do not parse the wh

item.title: Fox Bought Roku for Its Identity Graph, Not Its Shows
item.description: Three days on, the market reads the $22 billion deal as a play for ACR data, 100 million households and the home screen itself.
item.content:encoded:
Three days on, the market reads the $22 billion deal as a play for ACR data, 100 million households and the home screen itself.

Fox Bought Roku for Its Identity Graph, Not Its Shows

Three days on, the market reads the $22 billion deal as a play for ACR data, 100 million households and the home screen itself.

Three days after Fox agreed to buy Roku for roughly $22 billion, the trade's verdict has cooled from "a content grab" to something more clinical: Fox bought an identity and data engine it had been renting. Roku's programmatic business is about twice the size of Fox's, its third-party DSP spend grew 40% year over year in the first quarter, and it brings automatic content recognition and an audience graph spanning more than 100 million streaming households. Analysts now frame the prize as the home screen — the "decision layer" every Roku viewer passes through before a single stream begins — plus the first-party data Fox previously approximated with probabilistic models. Fox has promised Roku will stay an open, partner-friendly platform, even as Netflix, Disney and Amazon all distribute through it. The bet concentrates one of the largest pools of open-programmatic CTV inventory and authenticated identity under a single owner. For every buyer, it redraws who controls the data and the supply path into the living room.

Pod-Bidding Push Moves CTV Toward the Live-Sports Ad Model

The Trade Desk aims to shift its entire publisher supply path to pod bidding by August 31.

The industry's pod-bidding effort is advancing the programmatic sale of multi-ad commercial breaks, the structure linear television has always used. The Trade Desk is targeting an August 31 deadline to move its entire publisher supply path to support it, and Index Exchange's James Wilhite has called 2026 "a big year" for demand-side partners rolling out podding. Pod bidding lets multiple advertisers compete for the individual slots inside a single CTV ad break rather than buying one impression at a time. Standardizing it pulls programmatic CTV closer to the full-break, live-sports ad model that the largest television budgets still expect.

Trade Desk Plugs Adsquare Into Audience Unlimited for Store Visits

Location data joins the AI-priced marketplace, tying CTV and open-web buys to real-world footfall.

The Trade Desk integrated Adsquare's consent-based location intelligence into Audience Unlimited, its AI-priced third-party data marketplace, making the segments activatable through its Kokai platform. Adsquare operates across 26 markets and serves more than 2,500 brands and agencies; its data is priced at roughly 3.3% to 4.4% of impression cost in one mode and bundled at no extra charge in another. The move adds real-world movement signals to a marketplace TTD has been repositioning around measurable outcomes. It deepens the push to hold CTV and open-internet buys accountable to store visits, pressuring rivals to prove the same offline conversion.

Gracenote, PubMatic Bring Content-Level Buying to Programmatic CTV

Episode-level and live-sports metadata enters the bidstream, letting buyers target the show, not just the impression.

Gracenote, Nielsen's content-intelligence business, and PubMatic struck a partnership embedding Gracenote's episode-level and live-sports schedule data directly into PubMatic's platform and its AI-driven Live Sports Marketplace. PubMatic can now match bid opportunities against content metadata in real time at auction, adding only a fraction of a millisecond of latency, with deals executable directly or through its agentic buying infrastructure. Gracenote research found 86% of media planners cite limited show- or content-level data as a barrier to shifting budget from linear to CTV. The deal attacks a core transparency gap and pushes content-level targeting toward becoming table stakes in CTV.

Publicis and The Trade Desk Settle Their Fee Dispute

Publicis restores its recommendation of the DSP, ending a standoff that began with a fee-transparency audit.

Publicis reinstated The Trade Desk on its recommended demand-side-platform list, ending a dispute that began in March when a Publicis-commissioned audit by FirmDecisions flagged fee-stacking and transparency concerns the DSP rejected. Neither side disclosed terms or which one conceded, saying only that the audit issues had been addressed; The Trade Desk's shares rose on the news. The fight had become a referendum on fee transparency and audit rights between holding companies and the platforms they route billions through. The détente removes an overhang on the largest independent DSP, but leaves the underlying questions about supply-chain trust unresolved.

DoubleVerify Unveils DV Neura AI Engine for Agentic Buying

Verification data becomes queryable through Claude as DV bids to stay in the loop on autonomous campaigns.

DoubleVerify introduced DV Neura, an AI engine spanning media intelligence, adaptive performance, open connectivity and agentic execution. Its Insight Agent is available immediately via the Model Context Protocol, letting advertisers query DV's media-quality and performance data through Anthropic's Claude in natural language, with an autonomous Activation Agent due in the third quarter and Gemini and Copilot integrations to follow. The launch pushes verification and brand-safety infrastructure into the agentic buying stack. It is a bid by a measurement vendor to remain indispensable as AI agents take over more of campaign execution.

EU Spells Out AI Act Transparency Rules for Deepfakes

Labeling duties for AI-generated video, audio and text take effect August 2 — advertising included.

The European Commission published detailed guidance on the AI Act's Article 50 transparency obligations — marking, watermarking and labeling AI-generated and AI-manipulated content — alongside a Code of Practice being finalized before the rules apply on August 2, 2026. Deployers will have to label deepfakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest, advertising creative among them. For agencies and platforms operating in the EU, it forces AI-disclosure and provenance signaling into production and ad-serving workflows. With generative tools now flooding CTV and programmatic creative, the compliance clock is short.

California's Data-Broker Delete Mandate Triggers Penalties August 1

The DROP platform lets residents wipe their data from 500-plus brokers at once, with $200-a-day fines looming.

California's Delete Request and Opt-Out Platform, live since January, enrolled more than 217,000 residents in its first two months, and registered data brokers must begin honoring bulk deletion requests on August 1, when non-fulfillment triggers $200-a-day penalties with no cure period. The state's privacy agency has stood up a Data Broker Enforcement Strike Force and already acted against firms selling sensitive profiles for targeted advertising. The mandate threatens the audience-data supply underpinning much addressable and political targeting. Brokers and the platforms that license their segments face a hard deadline that could shrink the identity data available to buyers.

AdImpact Lifts 2026 Election Forecast to Record $11.6 Billion

Connected TV is projected at $2.7 billion — the only major channel growing over the 2024 presidential cycle.

AdImpact raised its 2026 cycle forecast to $11.6 billion, up from an earlier $10.8 billion and the most expensive midterm on record, with broadcast at $5.6 billion, CTV at $2.7 billion, cable at $1.4 billion and digital at $1.6 billion. Senate races are projected to draw $3.4 billion and gubernatorial contests $2.4 billion, with downballot and state-legislative spend a combined $3.7 billion. CTV is the fastest-growing media type in the forecast and the only one rising over 2024. The upgrade points to a larger-than-expected windfall for streaming inventory owners, programmatic pipes and identity vendors over the next five months.

ITV Adds Lead-Gen Pause Ads to Court Performance Brands

An ITVX format lets viewers request a brand's offer by remote, then return to the show.

At its Showcase in Manchester, ITV launched Lead Gen Pause Ads, an ITVX format that lets a viewer pause a programme and request follow-up offers or communications from a brand by remote, then resume watching. The format fuses ITV's Pause Ads with its Lead Gen Ads technology and targets performance advertisers that lack video creative, with a limited beta opening in autumn 2026 alongside a wider suite of commercial tools. It is the latest move by a UK broadcaster to make streaming inventory directly accountable for lead generation, narrowing the performance gap with social and search.

India Reframes Connected TV as a Performance Medium

At Mumbai's e4m CTV conference, a base of 129 million screens is pitched as a demand engine, not linear's overflow.

India's fourth e4m Connected TV Conference, themed "Attention to Action: The Performance Era of CTV," gathered the market in Mumbai around a single argument: connected TV has become a data-rich, addressable performance channel rather than a digital extension of linear. WPP Media's India leadership keynoted on CTV investment strategy as the country's active CTV base is now put above 129 million users, with ad spend climbing toward Rs 3,000 crore in the current fiscal year. Independent trade outlets have tracked the same shift for months, citing CTV's outsized growth in India's video economy. The framing signals Indian advertisers pushing CTV toward measurable, lower-funnel outcomes and accelerating budget into addressable streaming.

World Cup Ends Brazil's Single-Screen Era as Ad Money Splits

For the first time since 1982, the tournament scatters across CazéTV, Globo, SBT and N Sports.

Brazilian trade press marked the World Cup's June 11 kickoff as the end of concentrated television audiences, with rights split for the first time in 44 years across the digital-native CazéTV — streaming all 104 matches free — plus Globo, SBT and N Sports. CazéTV alone drew roughly R$2 billion in sponsorship before the tournament, redirecting money that once flowed only to free-to-air TV as viewers fragment across smart-TV broadcasts, phones and social feeds. With Brazilian digital ad spend already at R$42.7 billion in 2025, the splintering is pushing brands toward programmatic and engagement-measured formats over mass reach. It is a live preview of how a fragmented World Cup reshapes ad buying across every screen.

Ottawa Orders CRTC to Walk Back Its 15% Streaming Levy

A do-over swaps a tripled Canadian-content obligation for $600 million in direct funding amid US trade pressure.

The federal government directed the CRTC to reconsider a regulatory policy issued in late May that had tripled the Canadian-content contribution from large foreign streamers such as Netflix to 15% of Canadian revenue, up from a 2024 interim rate of 5%. The culture minister framed the reversal as an affordability measure, warning the obligations "could ultimately fall on Canadian consumers through higher prices," and Ottawa pledged roughly $600 million in direct funding to the sector instead. The move followed sustained US pressure that flagged the Online Streaming Act as a trade irritant. The contribution rate sets the cost base under every ad-supported streaming and CTV service in Canada, so easing it lifts a looming margin and pricing drag on the same inventory now being sold programmatically.

iQIYI International and Viu Pool Southeast Asian Streaming Audiences

China's overseas streamer strikes its first cross-regional bundle, stacking ad-reachable viewers across four SEA markets.

iQIYI International and Hong Kong-based Viu unveiled a bundled subscription at the APOS conference in Bali, combining their libraries across Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines and Malaysia for a launch in the second half of 2026. It is iQIYI International's first cross-regional streaming alliance, pairing its Chinese-language originals, anime and variety slate with Viu's Korean-led catalog, Southeast Asian productions and short-form dramas. Viu runs a hybrid model anchored by a large ad-supported free tier and has been opening fresh inventory in its micro-drama format. For the CTV and programmatic market, the tie-up concentrates two of Asia's most ad-reachable streaming audiences under one roof, raising the competitive weight of China-rooted streamers chasing advertiser budgets in Southeast Asia against Netflix, Prime Video and Disney+.

Levin: AI-Tailored Ads Are a 'Multivariate Nightmare'

Emet Advisory's Erez Levin argues the rush to serve thousands of AI-personalized creative variants breaks measurement: you can cleanly test three or four creative hypotheses, not five thousand. It is a pointed check on the 1:1 personalization thesis just as generative tools flood CTV and programmatic.

Shields: Is Fox-Roku an Ad-Tech Deal or a Distribution Grab?

Mike Shields presses the question under the Fox-Roku deal — whether a rough Fox quarter eventually pressures Roku to favor Fox content on the home screen, eroding the neutrality Roku was built on. The home screen is CTV's most valuable real estate, so any tilt there reshapes how every rival streamer reaches viewers.

The Grid Is the Programme

Everyone is fighting over the shows. The shows were never the medium. The grid of tiles is.

The figure this season is ownership — a network paying twenty-two billion dollars for the box on top of the set, the trade counting a platform's households and its data. The figure is content: who holds the shows, who sells the ad. That is the figure. The ground is the screen that greets you before any show begins — the grid of tiles, the highlighted default, the "Continue Watching" rail, the sponsored row that is already a decision made on your behalf. The content of a medium is always another medium; the shows are merely the content of the home screen. The home screen is the message. Enhance: the act of choosing, raised to a glance — a whole evening's viewing laid out as a surface you skim, not a dial you turn. Obsolesce: the channel, the schedule, the search box, the wandering thumb that did not yet know what it wanted. Retrieve: the old TV Guide open on the carpet, the cover that sorted the week — handed back as software that sorts it for you. Reverse: pushed far enough, the grid stops serving your choice and begins to compose it; the tile you "chose" was the tile placed in your eye-line, and the viewer is the one being scheduled. This is why a network buys an operating system instead of a studio. The studio fills the figure. The operating system owns the ground, and the ground decides what the figure can be. We thought we were buying remote controls. We were buying the right to arrange a person's attention before he is awake enough to spend it. The screen is not where you watch television. The screen is what now watches you decide. — Marshall McLuhan

The Machine Cannot Supply the Idea

The trade is intoxicated by infinite personalised creative. Infinity is not an idea. It is the absence of one.

The new promise is abundance. Feed the machine a brief and it returns five thousand versions of the advertisement, each one tailored to a single pair of eyes. The press releases call this personalisation. I call it arithmetic. An analyst this week put the problem plainly: you can run a clean test on three or four creative hypotheses; you cannot test five thousand. Five thousand variants are not five thousand ideas. They are one missing idea, multiplied until no one notices it is missing. I built brands on a single proposition, stated and restated until the consumer could not forget it. Dove was "one-quarter cleansing cream," and we said it for a decade while the competition reinvented itself every season; Dove is still standing. Pepperidge Farm was a horse-drawn wagon and a slow country road, and that one picture of unhurried quality sold bread for thirty years. Neither needed a thousand faces. They needed one true thing, proven, then repeated. A machine can write the thousand faces in an afternoon. It cannot tell you which true thing is worth repeating, because it has never stood in a shop and watched a woman choose. So use the machine. Let it set the type, resize the frame, swap the language. But find the idea first, with a human mind, and prove it sells before you ask the software to dress it five thousand ways. An advertisement that says nothing, said five thousand ways, still says nothing. If it doesn't sell, it isn't creative — and a computer that cannot sell is only an expensive way to be ignored. Build the idea. Then multiply it. — David Ogilvy

The buyer the market was waiting for is a broadcaster: Fox lands the No. 1 US streaming OS, the OneView DSP, Tubi and The Roku Channel.

Fox to Buy Roku for $22 Billion, Redrawing CTV

The buyer the market was waiting for is a broadcaster: Fox lands the No. 1 US streaming OS, the OneView DSP, Tubi and The Roku Channel.

Fox Corporation said June 15 it will acquire Roku for roughly $22 billion — about $160 a share in cash and stock — in the largest connected-TV deal in years. The combination pairs Fox's live sports and news with Roku's streaming operating system, its OneView demand-side platform, first-party data from more than 100 million global households, and the two biggest US free ad-supported streamers, Tubi and The Roku Channel. Roku founder Anthony Wood stays on and joins Fox's board; the companies expect to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulators and shareholders. By share of US TV viewing the merged group would rank among the top three. It also hands a single owner the home screen, a DSP, FAST inventory and premium broadcast content at once. For every advertiser, agency and ad-tech vendor in streaming, the question is now whether the largest open CTV pipeline in the US stays open — exactly the inflection this paper flagged when Roku first put itself in play.

Samsung Opens Smart-TV Home Screen to Programmatic Buyers

Native home-screen units reach The Trade Desk and DV360 first, transacted on Magnite's SpringServe, with a global rollout in Q3.

Samsung Ads said June 10 it will make its smart-TV home-screen units — the non-skippable real estate shown the instant a set powers on — available programmatically through The Trade Desk and Google's DV360, with Magnite's SpringServe running the transaction layer. The placements were sold only directly until now; automated access rolls out across all regions starting Q3 2026, with more DSP partners promised. The move follows Roku's home-screen monetization push and recasts streaming-OS owners as DSP partners rather than rivals. It pits the major buying platforms against one another for a scarce, high-attention CTV format and hands Magnite a sell-side foothold inside the world's top-selling TV brand.

World Cup Opens to Record Streaming Crowds on Fox, Tubi

US-Paraguay drew nearly 16 million across Fox, Fox One and free, ad-supported Tubi — a US men's World Cup record.

Fox's English-language coverage of the United States' June 12 opener against Paraguay averaged 15.99 million viewers across the Fox broadcast network, the Fox One streaming service and free ad-supported Tubi, a record for a US men's World Cup match, with Tubi alone averaging 1.13 million. Telemundo set Spanish-language streaming records on its side, and Fox and Telemundo together are projected to take roughly $850 million in tournament ad revenue. FIFA-approved mid-match hydration breaks open new programmatic ad pods across all 104 games. The tournament is the year's biggest live-streaming ad event, stress-testing dynamic ad insertion and programmatic live-sports buying — and validating FAST as a mass-reach vehicle — at unprecedented scale.

Adelaide Brings Pre-Bid Attention Targeting to Amazon DSP

Streaming buyers can now filter on attention before they bid, with an Amazon-exclusive floor that drops the lowest-attention 10%.

Adelaide's attention metric, AU, went live inside Amazon DSP on June 10, letting advertisers pre-bid target high- and medium-attention placements across display, online video and connected TV rather than grading attention only after a campaign ends. Two products ship: AU Media Quality, which tiers inventory by attention, and an Amazon-exclusive AU Quality Floor that excludes the bottom 10% of AU-scored impressions and made-for-advertising sites. Adelaide says AU scoring applies to CTV inventory and that its pre-bid targeting also runs in The Trade Desk, Viant, Yahoo and Equativ. It matters because attention is moving upstream from a post-campaign report card to a buy-side optimization lever, giving outcomes-focused streaming buyers a way to cut waste before impressions clear.

Unilever's Degree Leans on CTV, Creators for World Cup Push

A FIFA sponsor pairs tentpole streaming buys with a creator-led model inside Unilever's largest-ever sports activation.

Unilever's Degree, an official FIFA sponsor, has built its World Cup plan around volume-based media commitments locked in 18 months ago, Christian Pulisic creative running since April and a new 'Here for Sweat' platform, AdExchanger reported June 12. The activation sits inside Unilever's biggest sports push yet — more than 35 brands, a real-time content hub and a strategy that now routes about half its global media budget into social and creator marketing. With major advertisers steering tentpole dollars toward live streaming and creators rather than only linear spots, the campaign is a window into how blue-chip brands are allocating CTV and video budgets around the tournament.

Coca-Cola Puts Global Media Account in Play, WPP vs Publicis

After moving North America to Publicis, the marketer opens its roughly $4 billion global account to a two-way fight.

Coca-Cola has invited Publicis to pitch for its entire global media account against incumbent WPP, escalating a review that began when it shifted North American media to Publicis in 2025; Dentsu retains Japan and Korea. The process, run by MediaSense, is expected to kick off in July with a decision late in the year, and the account — estimated near $4 billion — is one of the largest in play in a year that has already seen Microsoft move to Publicis and Estee Lauder to WPP. Whoever wins controls Coca-Cola's global streaming and CTV activation, a marquee signal of which holding company's in-house programmatic stack the biggest brands trust at scale.

Fox-Roku Deal Heads Straight Into Antitrust Spotlight

Roku's home-screen gatekeeping and the Tubi-Roku Channel FAST overlap are the likeliest flashpoints for DOJ or FTC review.

The Fox-Roku merger commits both sides to Hart-Scott-Rodino filings, and analysts expect close scrutiny of competition in CTV advertising, content distribution and streaming aggregation. Roku's control of home-screen placement, search and the ad inventory rival apps depend on — plus the overlap between Tubi and The Roku Channel, which together account for roughly a third of US free ad-supported streaming — are the most likely flashpoints. To preempt objections from Netflix, Disney and Max, the companies pledged to keep Roku an 'open, partner-friendly platform' and signaled willingness to accept conditions. Whether regulators demand structural remedies will decide how much leverage the combined entity gains over the streamers and DSPs that rely on Roku's operating system — the single biggest regulatory question now hanging over CTV.

Google, Trade Desk Let TAG Brand-Safety Seals Lapse

P&G eases its TAG mandate as the biggest platform and biggest independent DSP lean on MRC accreditation instead.

Google and The Trade Desk both declined to renew their Trustworthy Accountability Group certifications for 2026 — Google had held three of TAG's four seals and The Trade Desk all four — while staying TAG members. Both said TAG's anti-fraud and brand-safety requirements now duplicate their Media Rating Council accreditations, an overlap TAG chief Mike Zaneis acknowledged after EY audits, while Procter & Gamble separately relaxed its longstanding contractual requirement that partners hold TAG's Certified Against Fraud seal. The simultaneous pullback by the largest digital platform and the largest independent DSP consolidates programmatic and CTV trust infrastructure around MRC accreditation and IAB Tech Lab tools, and raises pointed questions about the future of voluntary self-regulation for supply-chain transparency.

Political Ad Spend Hits Record $4 Billion Through June

AdImpact's mid-cycle update: the fastest pace ever, up 46% on 2024, with CTV lifted to $2.7 billion.

AdImpact reported June 11 that $4 billion in political advertising is already booked through early June 2026 — the fastest pace on record and up 46% from the same point in the 2024 presidential cycle — propelled in part by a record-setting California governor's race. The firm raised Senate-race spending 23% to $3.4 billion and lifted its full-cycle connected-TV projection to $2.7 billion, the only major channel it expects to grow this cycle. The actuals show money moving earlier and faster than in any prior midterm, pulling a larger, earlier share of budgets onto streaming and handing CTV sellers a concrete near-term demand signal rather than a year-end forecast.

FreeWheel Bridges CTV and Out-of-Home With Outernet London

Comcast's SSP will sell Outernet's immersive London screens programmatically, fed by real-time on-site measurement.

FreeWheel and Outernet London have partnered to connect Outernet's premium digital out-of-home inventory — flagship sites such as The Now Building — to FreeWheel's SSP demand, with Outernet's PIAMS measurement feeding real-time behavioral data into the platform. Outernet draws more than 120 million annual visitors, which FreeWheel will now sell with programmatic precision. The deal extends CTV's transaction rails into premium out-of-home, an early test of whether the two video formats can be bought through a single streaming-grade pipe.

JioHotstar Tops IPL 2026 CTV Ads as Big Screen Broadens

TAM Sports data shows connected TV drawing more exclusive advertisers than linear during cricket's biggest event.

TAM Sports data across IPL 2026 shows JioStar's JioHotstar as the runaway top connected-TV advertiser at roughly 35–39% of CTV ad volumes, with Google second near 17% and e-commerce and media the leading CTV category. The data also shows CTV drawing more than 30 exclusive advertisers versus 20-plus on linear, and the top five advertisers taking just 29% of CTV volume against 39% on linear — evidence the big screen is pulling a wider, more digitally native brand set. With JioStar having raised IPL CTV rates about 25%, the figures quantify how India's marquee sports event is reshaping the premium CTV market after the Disney-Reliance merger.

Globo Debuts DTV+ Dynamic Ad Insertion for World Cup

Brazil's broadcaster brings geo-targeted, AI-assisted ad insertion to free-to-air and Globoplay around the tournament.

Globo is rolling out its DTV+ standard, built on the TV 3.0 / ATSC 3.0 system, enabling dynamic ad insertion at free-to-air scale plus geo-targeting — including different ads in different parts of the same city in one break — with commercial selling organized around the FIFA World Cup. The rollout is hybrid: internet viewers get personalized insertion on Globoplay while broadcast runs standard insertion, with low-latency streaming and AI generating multiple creative variants. It is one of Latin America's most consequential advanced-TV addressability moves, tying a marquee sports event to next-generation ad insertion in the region's largest market.

Bell Media's Digital Upfront Pushes Tubi, Crave, Advanced TV

A discounted, DSP-activatable offer spans Crave, Tubi, TSN and Bell's Advanced TV ecosystem ahead of a sports-heavy slate.

Bell Media launched its 2026 digital and out-of-home upfront offer across Crave, Tubi, TSN, RDS, iHeartRadio and its Advanced TV ecosystem, leaning into programmatic, DSP-activatable buying and outcomes measurement, independent trade Media in Canada reported. The push accompanies Bell's unveiling of a 2026/27 slate anchored by live sports and the FIFA World Cup. It shows a Canadian incumbent leaning on programmatic CTV and measurement to defend ad share as US streamers expand in the market.

Weak Home Market Pushes TCL, Hisense Ad-OS Sets Abroad

Omdia's Q1 tracker: global TV shipments rose 6% on World Cup build-up, but Mainland China was the lone shrinking region.

Omdia's first-quarter 2026 TV shipment tracker, released June 3, shows global sets up 6% year on year to 50.3 million units on pre-World Cup inventory building, with every region growing except Mainland China, where domestic demand stayed soft after 2025 stimulus lapsed. Chinese vendors TCL and Hisense redirected volume into Asia & Oceania and Latin America to offset the home-market slump, while retailers prioritized expanding ad-revenue operating systems over hardware margin. The data underlines why China's smart-TV giants are racing to monetize home-screen and FAST inventory in overseas CTV markets: with the domestic set market stalling, the growth in their TV businesses is shifting from panels sold to ad impressions served abroad.

The Auction Now Runs Itself

We built agents to buy the media. The buying is becoming the medium.

The figure this month is speed. Magnite stands up a seller agent to greet the buyers' agents; PubMatic runs a campaign in Spain where the software plans, bids and optimizes while the humans watch a dashboard; Mediaocean wires twelve agents into the ad server and clips ninety percent off the setup. The trade reads these as tools — faster hands at the old work. That is the figure. The ground is that the work has changed medium. The buy is no longer a thing a person does with software; it is a thing software does, with a person kept on as witness. Enhance: the closed loop — plan, bid, measure, adjust, all inside one breath, faster than a meeting could be called. Obsolesce: the insertion order, the request for proposal, the lunch, the haggling voice, the media plan as a human artifact. Retrieve: the old automatic market of the pit and the auctioneer, price found by clamor with no one deciding it — handed back to us as code. Reverse: pushed far enough, the agent that acts for you begins to act upon you; your agent and the seller's agent transact in a room you cannot enter, and the strategist becomes the audited party — the thing the machines measure, not the hand that moves them. We thought the agent was an extension of the buyer's reach. It is turning out to be an amputation of the buyer's presence. When the medium does the buying, the medium is the buyer, and the man in the chair is left holding the one thing the agents still want from him: the credit card, and the blame. You did not speed up the buy. You left the room while it finished without you. — Marshall McLuhan

Bigness Never Sold A Bar Of Soap

The trade has fallen in love with the merger. The consumer has never bought one.

This fortnight a television company agreed to pay twenty-two billion dollars for the little box that sits on top of the set. A holding company that swallowed a rival last winter has climbed to the top of the rankings. Coca-Cola has laid its entire global account, some four billion dollars of it, on the table for two giants to fight over. The trade calls this consolidation and discusses it with the reverence it once kept for a good idea. I have heard this music before. Whenever the business cannot think of anything to sell, it buys something instead. I built the largest agency in the world, so I am not against size. I simply never confused it with the work. When I wrote, “At sixty miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock,” the agency was small and the idea was large, and the cars sold out. Size did not write that line; one man reading engineering reports for three weeks wrote it. The Hathaway shirt was sold by an eyepatch that cost almost nothing and ran for a quarter of a century. A merger, by contrast, announces itself in billions and sells, on the morning after, precisely nothing. Scale buys you reach, overhead and a press release. It does not buy you one customer who was not coming anyway. Before you applaud the next twenty-two-billion-dollar handshake, ask the only question that has ever paid the rent: what will it sell, and to whom? If the answer is a slide about synergies, you have not bought a strategy. You have bought a larger room in which to fail. Build the idea first. The empire, if you must have one, comes after. — David Ogilvy
