What the old man saw in Spain, walking past the parliament to the masons and the migrants and the wounded.

A Tower of Stone, and Six Who Came to Be Heard

What the old man saw in Spain, walking past the parliament to the masons and the migrants and the wounded.

June 10, Barcelona .--They have finished a tower. One hundred and forty-four years they have been at it, the masons and the carvers and the men on the high scaffolds, ever since 1882, and now the Tower of Jesus Christ stands up a hundred and seventy-two meters and a half into the night, the tallest of the eighteen, the tallest church in all the round earth--and a hundred and twenty thousand people press into the streets below to see a man in white bless the lit ceramic cross at the top of it. I do not write of the parliament first, though that is where the wires have gone. I write of the stone. For consider what a tower is. It is not a thought, not a decree, not a bill passed in a chamber and forgotten by autumn. It is the sap and sinew of the dead rising through the living--the chisel-stroke of Antoni Gaudi, dead a hundred years, carried up by the hands of men not yet born when he died. And over the multitude the drones drew his face in the dark sky and his old saying with it: First love, then technique . There is the whole of it, camerado. First love, then technique. Not the technique that decides, in some cold automated chamber, who shall live and who shall die--of which the man in white warned the lawmakers, that "decisions regarding life and death are never left to automated systems"--but the love that lays the first stone and trusts another hand to lay the last. Now turn to Madrid, and to the body that is not stone. Two days before the tower, in the great hall of the Congress of Deputies, the first pope ever to stand there spoke for half an hour, and they rose and clapped him seven minutes, and cried Viva el Papa . Let the chroniclers count the ovation. I count instead the bodies he made them look at: the unborn child, the elderly, the sick--and chiefly the one in motion, the migrant, the man forced "to leave everything behind in search of peace, security and a future." Safe and legal pathways, he asked of them. Address the root. O you legislators with your firm desks and your firm certainties--he told you a thing worth carrying out into the street: that firmness does not require contempt, that disagreement does not entail humiliation. Some among you would not come into the hall to hear it. The empty seats are also a kind of answer. And I think now of a smaller room than that hall, and a quieter hour. For on the same June day, in the embassy of the Vatican in Madrid, the man in white sat down with six. Six survivors of the abuse of children by priests--the scourge he had named the scourge, the wound under the white portico and the lit cross and the

The Glass Idol, and the Cradles It Has Emptied

A nation that will not be born is a nation that has ceased, in some deep place, to believe.

The Present Time, foolish reader, brings us a portent, and the augurs of the Republic stand round it in helpless wonder. Here is the Congressional Budget Office, that gravest of haruspices, with its tables and its decimal points; and what does it read in the entrails of the Nation? That for every woman in this land there shall be born, in this year of grace, but one child and a fraction—one and fifty-eight hundredths, so runs the oracle; sinking yet, to one and fifty-three; and that the day approaches, brought forward now a whole decade, when the dead of America shall outnumber her newborn. Behold a People that has resolved, quietly, not to continue. And what is given us as the cause of this great refusal? Not famine; not the sword; not pestilence walking in darkness. A toy. A pane of glass. The economist of Middlebury, one Caitlin Myers, having set herself with a true workman's honesty to find the spring of the thing, comes back from her labour white in the face. "Wow," she says, "but this has to be too big." She tried, she tells us, "everything I can to explain away what I'm seeing in the data, and I just couldn't." There spoke an earnest soul—one who looked, and would not lie about what she saw. A third of it, perhaps the half, she lays at the door of a single contrivance loosed upon the world scarce twenty years gone: the hand-glass, the pocket-oracle, the iPhone. "We're not saying it's all the iPhone," she adds, scrupulous; "it could explain about a third to a half of the decline." A third to a half! O ye Eternities, that a civilisation should be unmanned by a thing that fits in a waistcoat-pocket. Consider what is here confessed. The screen has stepped in between the man and the woman; the glowing rectangle has been preferred to the warm body; the young, who in every prior age contrived somehow to find one another in the dark, now sit each alone, thumbing their little altars, and the herb-markets of courtship stand empty. This is not a private vice; it is the Mechanical Age arrived at its frankest triumph. Having made of labour a machine, and of the city a machine, and of thought itself a Logic-mill grinding without a miller, it has now reached into the very nursery, and stopped the loom of generation with a flick of the screen. The Phantasm has out-bred the Reality, by the simple expedient of seeing to it that the Reality breeds no more. And the Captains of this dwindling host—how do they bear themselves? They have discovered the calamity, somewhat late, and wring their hands in chorus. Elon Musk, who would people Mars, cannot keep his own planet

The Tax Aimed at Eton That Fell on Bradford

A levy sharpened for the Duke has come to rest in the neck of the milkman's chapel-school.

There is a tax in force in England which was aimed, with great ceremony and much wringing of egalitarian hands, at the playing-fields of Eton; and it has landed, as such things always do, on a Sunday-school in Bradford. This is not an accident of the policy. It is the policy. For when the modern State lifts its hatchet against the rich, it always contrives, by some miracle of fiscal physics, to bring it down upon the poor; and the blade that was sharpened for the Duke comes to rest in the neck of the milkman who happens to send his children to a small chapel-school down the lane. The thing is called the Finance Act, and it puts twenty per cent upon the fees of independent schools, that they may yield up some four hundred and sixty million pounds this year and a round one and a half billion the next. I do not object to the figure because it is large. I object to it because it is worshipped. A government that can recite to the last decimal what a school is worth to the Treasury, and cannot say what a school is worth to a child, has not made an error of arithmetic; it has made an error of religion. It has counted the coins of Mammon and called the sum a conscience. Now the Supreme Court has done a small and sane thing, which is to say that it will at least look at the matter again. Lord Reed, Lord Hamblen, and Lord Richards have granted four little schools — Emmanuel in Derby, The Branch in Yorkshire, The King's in Hampshire, Wyclif in South Wales — permission to argue that the levy is disproportionate. Not Eton; not one of the gilded houses the tax was advertised to humble. Four small, low-fee, faith-keeping schools, the very mice the elephant never meant to tread on, and trod on first. The lawyers, who must give a homely truth a Greek name before they can let it into a courtroom, call this "Thlimmenos discrimination" — the sin of treating unlike things alike. I should call it the sin of the man who, being told to weed his garden, mows it. Mrs. Michelle Daniells of the families' association puts it better than any statute: "For many families, choosing a faith-based education is not a luxury but a deeply held conviction." There is the whole quarrel in a sentence. The State has looked at a conviction and seen a luxury; it has looked at an altar and seen an asset; and it proposes to charge admission to the thing a man would die before he sold. Against these four schools the Treasury sends Sir James Eadie, the gentleman the lawyers gravely nickname the Treasury Devil, and the whole engine of the Exchequer; and on the other side stands Mr. Stephen White of Brad

The Mines Are Still in the Water at Hormuz

They have agreed to the text. The text is not the strait.

In Islamabad the prime minister stood up and said it. Shehbaz Sharif said, "Peace has never been this close as it is now," and the wire moved it and the markets read it and a man in Houston watched the number on the screen. WTI settled at 84.88. Brent went to 87.33. That was the lowest Brent had been since March. The numbers came down because Trump had called off the planned strikes and because of what Sharif said in Islamabad, and the numbers are not the strait and the words are not the strait. The strait is the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's crude goes through it on ships. The text says the strait reopens to the shipping it had before the war, inside thirty days. The text was finished. The foreign minister, Araghchi, said the agreement "has never been closer" and that he would give the details "in due course." Other men in Tehran said no final conclusion had been reached. Both things were said and both were filed. Thirty days to reopen a strait. There are mines in the water. Someone has to take the mines out of the water and that is slow work done by men in boats and divers going down, and a mine does not care what the text says. The fields that were shut are still shut and a field that has been idle does not start because a prime minister has spoken. The drones hit the energy plants and the missiles hit them and the steel is bent and the pipe is split and it has to be cut out and welded and that is done by hand by men who know how, the way a thing is done well or is not done. None of that is in the thirty days. The thirty days is a number in the text. The terms ran to fourteen points the way Tehran's press told it. Sixty more days of ceasefire. The strait open in thirty. Enrichment frozen fifteen to twenty years. The enriched uranium destroyed on the site and then carried out of the country. Twenty-four billion in frozen money let go a little at a time as the inspectors checked. It is a great deal to put in writing and they put it in writing, and then Trump looked at what the Iranian state media had written and said it had "NOTHING to do with the terms that were agreed to, in writing." So there is the text that is agreed and there is the account of the text, and they are not the same text, and a man had to stand up and say so the same week the other man stood up in Islamabad and said peace had never been this close. The vice president, Vance, said it about the money. He said, "The Iranians are not receiving any cash." He said it because someone had said they were. You say a thing is not happening when people have begun to say it is. Tr

We Are Building Temples and Calling Them Warehouses

The water and the electric bill are the shadow of a disembodied god.

A figure has been published which the sensible authorities will file under economics, and so dismiss: of those questioned by Reuters and Ipsos, only thirty-three in a hundred approve of the haste with which we are raising these vast machine-houses across the land, sixty-four disapprove, and fifty-seven would refuse to have one near their own door. The newspapers read this as a quarrel over electricity, and it is — but the man who has watched such fevers before knows it is never only that. When an age grows uneasy on a scale this wide, and cannot say of what it is afraid, something has stirred beneath the surface that the daylight vocabulary of cost and kilowatt cannot name. Consider what is being built. We are constructing, at a pace its own engineers cannot account for — ERCOT's Pablo Vegas calls it "an unprecedented change in the pace of growth," and Rice's Dominic Boyer says more plainly, "The projections are insane" — an enormous apparatus for a mind that is not a body, a thinking that has no belly and no grave. This is the old dream of modern man: intelligence cut free of the flesh that suffers. We had declared the soul a superstition; and now, having banished it, we pour concrete for it by the acre and pray to it under the name of the machine. One does not become enlightened by imagining figures of light, and the figure we are imagining is very bright indeed. But no tree, it is said, can grow to heaven unless its roots reach down into hell — and here are the roots, breaking the surface, which is the whole meaning of the backlash. The bright dream demands its dark complement by an inexorable law, and the complement is matter: the water table, the grid, the land, the bill. What returns is exactly what the dream wished to leave behind. So a man in Indiana, Mark Thompkins, who supposes he is talking about money, says, "My electric bills are high as it is," not knowing that he is the body protesting that the disembodied god must, after all, be fed from somewhere. So in Texas, where the campuses at Abilene and Amarillo would drink the rivers, a judge in Caldwell County, Hoppy Haden, confesses, "I would be a liar if I said that didn't bother me" — the tremor of a man who has felt the shadow without being able to name it. Notice that the unease crosses every line the political surface is supposed to divide. Two-thirds of one party and half of the other would refuse the thing in their own community; the fear that the price of light will rise is shared by Republican, Democrat, and independent alike. This is the signature of a collective process, not a campai

RFK Jr. Is Running One Vaccine Pitch in Two Movies

The measles numbers are the tell. Watch what the man is doing, not what he says.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has said two opposite things about the measles vaccine, to two different audiences, and both of them are working exactly as designed. Run it through the Persuasion Filter and you stop being confused. Here is the thing most people miss. They think a public figure either supports a vaccine or he doesn't, and they go hunting through his quotes to find the real one. That's second-dimension thinking. In the third dimension, where persuasion rules, the same man can say two true-sounding things to two crowds and never pick. That isn't a gaffe. That's a technique. Watch what I'm doing here. In March 2025, on Fox, Kennedy told one audience, "There are adverse events from the vaccine. It does cause deaths every year." In April 2026, asked directly by a senator, he told the other audience, "We promote the MMR. We have advised every child to get the MMR." He said "We promote" twice in that hearing. FactCheck.org laid the quotes side by side like a ledger. So who's right? Both of him. That's the point. This is pacing and leading. First you match the crowd you want, the people who already distrust the shot. You pace them: "adverse events," "deaths every year," "personal choice." That builds trust. Then, when a Senate camera is on you and Bill Cassidy is a doctor staring back at you, you lead the other way for the record: "We promote the MMR." Both crowds walk away thinking Kennedy is on their side. The wall is different in each person's head. Here are three things to notice. 1. He never takes the blame. In the April hearing he said, "I have nothing to do with the measles outbreak," and, "We have done better than any other country controlling the measles outbreak." Michael Bennet pressed him on dead unvaccinated kids. Lisa Blunt Rochester asked if he'd urged the president to tell Americans to get the shot. He kept the high ground and let the question slide off. 2. The number doesn't slide off. There have been over 4,200 U.S. measles cases since January 2025, the first measles deaths since 2015, two kids in Texas. Kindergarten MMR coverage dropped from 95.2 percent to 92.5 percent. You need about 95 to stop the thing from spreading. We are under the line. The disease was eliminated in 2000, and this fall the country could lose that status. 3. A virus is immune to persuasion. This is the part the Master Persuaders forget. You can pace a voter. You can pace a hearing room. You cannot pace measles. It is a moist little machine that does one thing, and it does it at 97 percent efficiency the moment the vaccinated wall drops below the line. The frame wo

Stock jumps more than 20% on reports of a strategic-options review, including a full sale.

Roku Explores Sale as $19B Ad Platform Draws Bidders

Stock jumps more than 20% on reports of a strategic-options review, including a full sale.

Roku is weighing a range of strategic options, including a full sale, according to reports citing six sources, after the talks first surfaced this week; the stock closed up more than 20% at $143.66, lifting the company to a roughly $19.4 billion market cap. Roku has held discussions with at least one US media company about a combination and has also explored a PIPE transaction, though no decision has been reached. The company is now a platform business first — its ads and subscriptions threw off roughly ten times the revenue of its hardware in the most recent quarter. Roku is one of the largest at-scale access points for CTV advertising in the US, and its inventory currently flows openly through The Trade Desk, Amazon DSP, DV360 and others. A change in ownership — especially to a media or retail buyer with its own demand stack — could reshape how open that pipeline stays, making this the most consequential CTV-supply story of the week.

Netflix Extends Programmatic Pause, Live Ads Across DSPs

Dynamic ad insertion reaches pause and live inventory as Amazon DSP targeting goes global.

At its 2026 upfront, Netflix said it is extending Dynamic Ad Insertion to Pause Ads and live content, available this summer in the US and Canada and buyable programmatically through The Trade Desk, Amazon DSP and Google DV360. Netflix also switched on programmatic audience targeting across all ad-supported countries via Amazon DSP by June 1, with Yahoo DSP to follow, as its ad tier reached 250 million global monthly active viewers. Opening previously manual formats like pause and live to standard programmatic pipes pulls Netflix deeper into the open CTV ecosystem and hands buyers new high-attention inventory to plan against.

Home Screens Become the Next CTV Ad Battleground

A new report argues the TV operating system is now premium real estate, not plumbing.

A TVREV report argues connected-TV operating systems have evolved from navigation layers into comprehensive advertising and data hubs, with the home screen functioning as premium ad inventory and FAST services wired directly into the interface. Roku's platform business generated roughly ten times more revenue from ads and subscriptions than hardware in the first quarter, while Samsung's Tizen and LG's webOS now anchor broader ad and data operations. As OS owners increasingly control audience discovery and monetization, the strategic stakes rise for every CTV buyer and seller negotiating for screen-level placement and data access.

Walmart Ties YouTube Video to In-Store Sales via DV360

A closed proof-of-concept measures whether streaming exposure drives Walmart purchases.

Walmart Connect launched a closed proof-of-concept with Google that lets advertisers activate Walmart shopper audiences in Display & Video 360, run them on YouTube, and measure resulting purchases at Walmart, with CTV and VIZIO inventory in scope to follow. Publicis Media Exchange's Joel Lunenfeld stressed the audiences are built on real purchase data rather than modeled signals. The deal pushes retail-data closed-loop attribution deeper into premium video and raises the bar for CTV sellers to prove outcomes, not just reach.

PubMatic, Havas Run Spain's First Agentic CTV Campaign

Telefónica's Movistar campaign came in 18% below its CPM target.

PubMatic and Havas announced what they called Spain's first agentic CTV campaign, run for Telefónica's Movistar on PubMatic's AgenticOS platform using autonomous AI agents for inventory selection, frequency, brand safety and bid optimization. The campaign delivered CPMs 18% below target, beat impression goals by 23% and cut setup time by up to 80%, following earlier agentic deployments in the Netherlands and France. The result is an early holding-company proof point that agentic buying can outperform on CTV, accelerating sell-side automation in EMEA.

Acxiom Geo Audiences Go Live on Trade Desk in UK, Germany

InfoBase location-derived segments enter TTD's data marketplace in Europe.

Acxiom made its Geo-Based audience segments, drawn from its InfoBase consumer data asset, available in The Trade Desk's third-party data marketplace in the UK and Germany, activatable within Kokai under TTD's Audience Unlimited pricing. The segments let advertisers target on real-world location patterns rather than purely digital signals in privacy-regulated markets. The move expands TTD's European data supply and feeds the broader push to cut audience waste in CTV and open-internet buys.

Magnite Launches Orchestration Layer for AI Buyer Agents

Dentsu and DIRECTV Advertising sign on as beta partners.

Magnite launched Magnite Orchestration, a coordination layer that lets AI buyer agents connect directly to its sell-side infrastructure and transact across CTV, audio and other formats without manual intervention. The system pairs a seller agent that builds custom inventory and audience packages with a buyer agent that generates media plans from RFPs; dentsu integrated proprietary audience segments and DIRECTV Advertising is testing premium TV inventory access. Embedding audience data inside the coordination layer is Magnite's bid to own the plumbing of agentic CTV buying as DSPs race to automate the same workflow.

Meta Quietly Lays Groundwork for CTV Ad Expansion

Exploratory talks with Magnite, FreeWheel, OEMs and publishers point to a big-screen push.

Meta, on track to be the industry's largest ad company in 2026, has held a series of exploratory meetings since early 2025 with supply-side players including Magnite and Comcast-owned FreeWheel, plus TV manufacturers and publishers, to assess how it could access CTV inventory at scale. No product has launched, but the outreach signals serious intent to extend Meta's performance-ad machine onto the big screen. A Meta entry would reshape demand-side competition in CTV and pressure incumbents like The Trade Desk and Amazon for premium streaming supply.

EU to Publish Code on Labeling AI-Generated Ad Content

Final transparency code due this month, ahead of August 2 binding obligations.

The EU is scheduled to publish the final Code of Practice on marking and labeling AI-generated content this month, establishing technical standards for watermarking and detecting synthetic media. The code precedes AI Act transparency obligations that become legally binding on August 2, while the Digital Services Act already bans profiling-based advertising to minors and targeting on sensitive data. For CTV and programmatic, the labeling regime will reach AI-generated ad creative and synthetic media, adding disclosure obligations for advertisers and platforms serving European audiences.

ICO Urges UK to Loosen Cookie Rules for Advertising

Regulator proposes separating lower-risk advertising from intrusive tracking under PECR.

The UK's Information Commissioner's Office published advice to government recommending targeted changes to online-advertising rules under PECR, proposing that Regulation 6 distinguish lower-risk advertising practices from more intrusive tracking. The advice is designed to support privacy-preserving advertising models and follows the ICO's review of whether blanket consent requirements are hindering innovation. If adopted, the reforms could ease consent friction for UK addressable and CTV advertising while still policing higher-risk identity tracking.

AdImpact Lifts 2026 Cycle to $11.6B; CTV Hits $2.7B

Connected TV revised up $300M to a record ~23% share of midterm ad spend.

AdImpact raised its 2025-26 political ad-spend projection to $11.6 billion, the most expensive midterm cycle on record, with spending already at $4 billion through early June. The firm lifted its CTV estimate by $300 million to $2.7 billion, holding roughly a 23% share of total cycle spend, alongside broadcast TV at $5.6 billion and digital at $1.6 billion. California $979M , Michigan $852M and Texas $850M lead state totals, and Senate spend was revised up 23% to $3.4 billion. The upward CTV revision confirms streaming as the fastest-growing political channel, pulling more campaign dollars into programmatic and addressable inventory ahead of November.

Sky Closes In on £1.6bn ITV Broadcast Takeover

Deal would unite ITVX and Sky's UK addressable inventory; £200m of the price hinges on ad performance.

Sky, owned by Comcast, is reportedly weeks from acquiring ITV's broadcast arm — including the ITVX streaming platform and linear channels — for roughly £1.6 billion, with about £200 million contingent on advertising performance; ITV Studios would remain with current shareholders. ITV's Q1 ad revenue fell just 1.5%, with Q2 growth forecast near 10% on the FIFA World Cup. Combining ITVX with Sky's addressable stack would concentrate UK premium-video supply under one owner and reset the leverage map for the planned Sky-ITV-Channel 4 unified marketplace.

JioHotstar Deepens Magnite Tie-Up for Live-Sports Programmatic

SpringServe mediation to govern demand across India's biggest sports and entertainment streams.

JioHotstar expanded its partnership with Magnite, adopting SpringServe to power advanced programmatic mediation across its live sports and entertainment portfolio, including coverage tied to the ICC Men's T20 World Cup. Magnite's technology gives JioHotstar more control and visibility over programmatic creatives to enforce ad quality and brand safety at scale. With CTV the fastest-growing segment on the platform and JioHotstar leading India's CTV ad volumes, the deal cements independent sell-side infrastructure inside the world's largest live-sports streaming audience outside the US.

CazéTV, Not Globo, Holds All 104 World Cup Matches

A creator-led streamer out-bid the incumbent broadcaster for full Brazilian 2026 tournament rights.

CazéTV, the LiveMode-operated streaming service anchored by creator Casimiro Miguel, secured exclusive Brazilian rights to all 104 FIFA World Cup 2026 matches, while incumbent Globo will carry only 55 games. FIFA expanded the deal after CazéTV's 22-match 2022 trial drew younger, highly engaged audiences across YouTube and TikTok. The outcome signals creator-led, ad-supported streaming can now out-compete LATAM's dominant broadcaster for tentpole live sport — redirecting World Cup CTV and digital ad inventory away from traditional TV sales houses.

Ottawa Orders CRTC to Revisit Streamer CanCon Levy Hike

Government cites affordability and US trade pressure after the regulator tripled streamers' contribution to 15%.

The federal government directed the CRTC to review its late-May decision tripling streaming services' Canadian-content contribution from 5% to 15% of Canadian revenue, with the prime minister citing cost-of-living concerns and US trade officials calling the rule discriminatory. The same decision cut domestic private broadcasters' obligations to 25% from as much as 45%, and streamers including Netflix and Disney are already in court. The review keeps the funding structure of Canada's video ecosystem — and the relative ad-economics of Bell, Rogers and Corus versus global streamers — unsettled for CTV sellers and buyers.

iQIYI Ad Revenue Falls 9% as Streamer Looks Overseas

China's leading long-form platform posts softer ad sales even as international originals gain traction.

iQIYI reported quarterly online advertising revenue down 9% year-over-year to RMB 5.19 billion and membership revenue down 5% to RMB 16.81 billion, with total revenue declining about 8% sequentially. The company leaned into international expansion — its first Thai original set variety-show records on its overseas platform — and launched an AI-driven creation tool, Nado Pro, with more than 10,000 active creators. Soft domestic ad demand at China's largest subscription streamer underscores why iQIYI and peers are pushing CTV monetization and ad-supported tiers into Southeast Asia rather than relying on the saturated home market.

The Set Has Become A Place

Roku is not selling a box. It is selling the room you have moved into.

The figure this week is the sale. Roku, valued at nineteen billion dollars, puts itself up for auction — and the number is built almost entirely on advertising and the operating system, not the hardware that bears its name. Samsung's Tizen and LG's webOS now run ad and data businesses larger than the panels they were written for. That is the figure. The figure is not the story. The ground is that the television has stopped being a thing you watch and become a place you inhabit — an environment that greets you, routes you, and reads you the moment the panel wakes. Enhance: discovery, the home screen as storefront and as eye. Obsolesce: the channel, the schedule, the antenna, the whole grammar of tuning in. Retrieve: the hearth — the glowing center a room was once arranged around, the fire that organized the family without anyone choosing it. Reverse: pushed far enough, the set you switch on switches on you; the viewer becomes the inventory, and the program becomes the thing that runs while you are being measured. We thought we had bought a screen for the content. The content turns out to be the bait, and the operating system the hook and the line. When a company's whole worth is the layer between you and the show, the layer is the show. The buyer fighting over Roku is not buying distribution. He is buying the doorway, and the doorway now faces inward. You did not turn on the television. You moved into one. — Marshall McLuhan

Cheap Is Not A Strategy

The machine will make you a thousand spots. It will not make you one idea.

I read this week that social video is about to grow faster than connected television for the first time — thirteen percent against eleven — and that the trade has settled on an explanation it finds rather comforting. Generative machines have made the spots cheap. A man can now produce fifty films for the price of one, so he produces fifty. The conclusion drawn is that the cheaper medium wins. The conclusion I draw is that we have once again confused the cost of making an advertisement with its power to sell. They are not the same thing. They have never been the same thing. In 1958 I wrote an advertisement for Rolls-Royce with the headline, "At sixty miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock." Beneath it sat six hundred and seven words of body copy — thirteen facts, patiently set down. It was not cheap. It took weeks of reading the engineering reports. The following year the company's sales rose by half. One expensive idea outsold an ocean of cheap ones, because the consumer is not a moron; she is your wife, and she can tell the difference between a film made to sell her something and a film made to fill a slot. A machine that gives you a thousand forgettable spots has not solved your problem. It has multiplied it, and billed you for the privilege. Before you marvel at how little a commercial now costs to produce, ask the only question that has ever mattered: does it sell? If it does not, you have manufactured waste at a remarkable discount. Make one that works. We sell, or else. — David Ogilvy

item.title: PubMatic Names MiQ Among First Partners In AI-In-The-Auction Layer
item.description: Decision Fabric lets approved buy-side models run as Docker containers inside AgenticOS bid requests, returning segment IDs in under ten milliseconds.

Decision Fabric lets approved buy-side models run as Docker containers inside AgenticOS bid requests, returning segment IDs in under ten milliseconds.

PubMatic Names MiQ Among First Partners In AI-In-The-Auction Layer

Decision Fabric lets approved buy-side models run as Docker containers inside AgenticOS bid requests, returning segment IDs in under ten milliseconds.

PubMatic on June 1 unveiled Decision Fabric, a containerised execution layer inside its AgenticOS auction infrastructure that lets curators, DSPs and algorithmic buyers deploy proprietary AI models as Docker containers receiving full bid requests in under 10 milliseconds. The first pilot cohort names MiQ alongside inPowered AI, Chalice AI and SWYM.AI, with a training set spanning more than 60 OpenRTB fields across web, mobile and CTV inventory in the US. PubMatic frames the build as the first programmable, ISO-27001-aligned environment for in-auction inference — partners' models live inside the SSP and act on the bid stream rather than receiving and re-bidding from outside. For the independent programmatic stack, Decision Fabric is the week's most consequential partnership signal: it moves in-auction decisioning from a buy-side aspiration toward live SSP infrastructure, and it gives non-walled-garden demand a path to run proprietary models where the inventory lives. The open questions for buyers are which CTV supply paths Decision Fabric reaches first, how containerised models interact with PubMatic-curated deals, and whether the pattern offers a credible counter-narrative to The Trade Desk's OpenPath. The deeper test is portability — whether the same containerised approach translates to non-PubMatic SSPs as Magnite, FreeWheel and Index Exchange move toward agentic architectures.

Amazon Ships Dynamic TV Creative For Prime Video IVAs

Headlines, products and CTAs now vary at the impression on Prime Video Interactive Video Ads.

Amazon Ads on June 1 launched Dynamic TV Creative, the first capability that automatically personalises Prime Video Interactive Video Ads using shopping, browsing and streaming signals against an AI-driven creative-optimisation layer. Headline, product detail, call-to-action and interactivity vary per impression; the tool ships first to US endemic advertisers and is slated to expand to live sports and Prime Video Channels in Q3. Amazon repeats its claim that its authenticated graph reaches roughly 90% of US households deterministically. By raising the bar on creative-level CTV personalisation, Amazon increases the pressure on the open programmatic stack: independent CTV demand now has to compete with the walled gardens on creative resolution as well as on inventory access, and the burden falls on the open market to show it can match impression-level creative variation.

Google Ads Switches CTV To Co-View Reach, Inflating YouTube TV Audiences

Seven Connected TV metrics now count every viewer on the couch as of June 2.

Google Ads' API transitioned on June 2 to Total Co-view reach across seven Connected TV campaign measures, counting every viewer on a single screen rather than treating the household as one impression. YouTube CTV reach numbers are expected to climb materially as a result, with effective CPMs falling on paper even where dollar spend holds steady. The change lands as YouTube claims more than 200 million Americans now watch on connected TVs each month and CTV passed mobile as YouTube's largest US watch surface in Q4 2025. The moment buyers compare YouTube CTV against rival streamers, the math changes overnight — agencies and DSPs will need to normalise across co-view and household-level bases before the new numbers start showing up in plans, or risk apples-to-oranges comparisons across the open market.

OpenAP And Big Nine Publishers Stand Up Cross-Streamer Outcomes CAPI

A+E, AMC, Fox, Hallmark, NBCU, Paramount, Scripps, TelevisaUnivision and Warner Bros. Discovery line up on one conversion pipe.

OpenAP and nine of the largest US TV companies — A+E Global Media, AMC, Fox, Hallmark Media, NBCUniversal, Paramount, Scripps Networks, TelevisaUnivision and Warner Bros. Discovery — partnered to introduce a standardised cross-publisher conversion API for TV advertising, plus shared workflows for unified audience buying across linear and streaming. First pilots with select advertisers, agencies and attribution providers are underway, with measurable results targeted over the next 12 months and an explicit agentic-workflow phase to follow. The publishers are openly framing the move as their answer to digital rivals' outcomes pitch. A single CAPI integration point across the Big Nine is the unlock buyers have been demanding — but it also raises the bar for every outcomes package in the market, because curators and DSPs now have to deliver against publisher-owned conversion infrastructure rather than around it.

Nexxen And V Wire Hisense Home Screen For World Cup Sponsor Inventory

OEM-direct native CTV placements across Hisense and Toshiba sets aimed at the global football audience.

Nexxen and V — the OEM formerly known as VIDAA — said June 3 they will connect advertisers with global soccer fans during the FIFA World Cup 2026 via native Smart TV home-screen placements and exclusive activations on Hisense and Toshiba sets. Hisense is an official FIFA sponsor, giving Nexxen a privileged window into one of CTV's biggest tentpole audiences. The deal underlines the OEM-led inventory race ahead of World Cup spend. For buy-side strategists, the question before tournament-quarter briefs land is which DSPs and curators have native access to V/Hisense screens, and how OEM-direct home-screen inventory stacks up against the Nexxen pipe — OEM placements are increasingly a distinct line item that sits upstream of any streamer's ad pod.

FIFA+ Folds Into DAZN, Concentrating 8,500 Live Matches On One Streamer

Football streamer adds FIFA archive and originals weeks before World Cup kicks off.

FIFA+ launched exclusively on DAZN on June 4, completing the integration first announced in June 2025 and marking what DAZN calls a major step toward becoming 'the global home of football.' The combined offer brings around 8,500 live matches a year from roughly 100 FIFA Member Associations, plus FIFA's archive and originals, onto DAZN. DAZN also holds 2026 World Cup rights in Italy, Japan and Spain. The move concentrates a vast volume of premium live football inventory inside one streaming front door just weeks before the tournament — reshaping the global Advanced TV plan for any brand chasing football audiences and routing more of that demand through DAZN's ad-supported tiers rather than across a fragmented rights map.

Dentsu Extends Magnite Pact Into Sweden For AMX Premium Video

Holding company hard-wires another EMEA market to an independent SSP.

Magnite and dentsu announced on June 3 an extension of their existing EMEA partnership into Sweden, with dentsu using Magnite's programmatic infrastructure to power CTV buying for the agency's AMX Premium Video offering in the market. The extension builds on prior dentsu-Magnite work and on Magnite's recent SSP deals with Samsung Ads, Paramount Australia and Hearst. The pair frame the deal as enabling more intelligent, data-driven CTV activation. The deal is another holding company hard-wiring an independent SSP into its curated supply path — a useful reference point for how indie-SSP positioning plays across Nordic and DACH briefs, and a marker of how much premium-video buying in EMEA is consolidating onto a handful of independent supply paths.

The Trade Desk Ships Q2 Kokai With CTV Pause Ads And New AI Controls

Deal Desk upgrades and pause-format demand land as the streaming attention surface widens.

The Trade Desk pushed its Q2 2026 Kokai release in early June with new AI optimisation controls, CTV pause-ad demand ads delivered when viewers hit pause on streaming and Deal Desk upgrades for buyers. The pause format opens a high-attention CTV moment that TTD's buyers can target via Kokai out of the box, the same week IAB Tech Lab is finalising standardised OpenRTB signals for Pause, Menu and Squeeze-Back formats. The open question for the rest of the market is which CTV publishers TTD has lined up for pause-ad supply, and whether curated deal IDs elsewhere in the ecosystem can match the offer — buy-side parity on emerging formats now depends on how fast independent supply paths align to the same standardised signals.

Trade Desk Wires Utiq Telco Identity Into EMEA Kokai Across Six Markets

Network-level signals from Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefonica and Vodafone join EUID and UID2.

The Trade Desk and Utiq announced on June 1 an integration of Utiq's telco-powered, user-consented advertising identifiers — generated at the network layer by Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefonica and Vodafone — into TTD's EMEA identity portfolio, available via Kokai. Coverage spans Germany, Austria, France, Spain, the UK and Italy, including netID in Germany. TTD continues to broaden its non-cookie addressability story in Europe with telco signals layered on top of EUID and UID2. For independent demand in EMEA, telco-consent identity is a competitive flank to be reckoned with — particularly where Utiq's network-level consent posture lands cleaner than email-based alternatives, which sharpens the question of how the rest of the addressability stack augments or competes with operator-sourced signals.

New York Synthetic-Performer Disclosure Law Takes Effect June 9

First-in-nation rule forces AI-actor disclosure on ads served to NY consumers; $1,000 first-offence, $5,000 repeat.

New York's S.8420-A/A.8887-B takes effect June 9, requiring advertisers with actual knowledge of AI-generated 'synthetic performers' in their creative to conspicuously disclose that use in ads reaching New York consumers, with $1,000 first-offence and $5,000 repeat penalties. Audio-only ads and pure language translation are exempt; the rule does not apply to publishers and platforms that distribute the ads. Legal commentary calls this the first state-level synthetic-performer disclosure regime in the country. New York is the largest US ad market and the first practical test of AI-creative disclosure plumbing through CTV inventory — agencies will look to their programmatic partners to flag and gate creative on intake, putting pressure on the whole supply chain to build disclosure controls into delivery.

CCPA Risk Assessments Now Required For Adtech And Sensitive Data

California's Audits Division gears up; Disney's $2.75M settlement set the tone.

California's updated CCPA regulations effective January 1 require risk assessments before any 'significant risk' processing — including selling or sharing personal information for cross-context behavioural advertising — with first certifications due to the CPPA by April 2028. The CPPA's new Audits Division has telegraphed compliance audits through 2026, and the 2026 enforcement docket already includes a $2.75M Disney CCPA settlement plus actions against Ford and PlayOn Sports. Documented risk assessments are now table stakes for any addressable CTV activation touching California audiences — a compliance burden that buy-side strategists and their partners increasingly treat as a managed-service deliverable rather than a box-checking afterthought.

Kinetiq Pegs 2026 Political CTV At $2.7B As Streaming Crosses 25% Share

Cycle projection raised above $10B; CTV up 122% versus 2022, broadcast down 13%.

Kinetiq Political Insights this week raised 2026 cycle projections above $10 billion in political media spend, with CTV pulling roughly $2.7 billion — a 122% jump over 2022 and the first cycle where streaming crosses 25% of total political ad spend. Broadcast and cable both decline versus 2024 in the model. California currently leads state-level spend at $315.8M, dominated by Tom Steyer's gubernatorial bid; AZ, GA, MI, NV, PA, NC and FL races round out the swing-state pipe. The streaming-share crossover is the line every CTV seller will quote at agencies through Q3 — and the buy side will want verified-supply and measurement answers to match before the new share figure becomes the default planning assumption for political dollars.

ICO Advises London To Limit PECR Exemption To Contextual Ads

Consent still required for cross-service tracking and behavioural profiling under regulator's proposal.

The UK Information Commissioner's Office published advice in late May, picked up across early-June industry coverage, recommending that Regulation 6 of PECR be revised to distinguish low-risk ad practices from intrusive tracking, with a no-consent exemption limited to contextual advertising and similar models. Behavioural targeting and cross-service profiling would continue to require explicit consent under the ICO proposal; current PECR rules remain in force pending any legislative change. The regulator is publicly drawing a line between contextual and behavioural CTV models — strengthening the case for contextual and clean-room-based addressability in the British market and signalling where consent-free targeting can and cannot operate.

JioHotstar Deepens Magnite Pact Across 450M-MAU Sports And Entertainment Portfolio

SpringServe to mediate ads across live cricket, IPL and the JioStar streaming stack.

JioHotstar said on June 4 it is expanding its partnership with Magnite, tapping SpringServe to drive advanced ad-server mediation across its 450M-MAU live sports and entertainment portfolio after Magnite already supported the platform through the ICC Men's T20 World Cup. The deepened deal gives the JioStar-owned service enhanced creative controls, brand-safety oversight and unified monetisation across CTV, mobile and web. The expansion lands the same week TAM Sports data showed CTV captured 39% of IPL 2026 digital ad share with JioHotstar alone accounting for 35% of top-advertiser volumes. The deal consolidates the largest non-US CTV inventory pool under an independent SSP that buyers can reach programmatically — a critical access point for any global IPL and ICC activation plan.

Globo Lines Up AI Ad-Decisioning For World Cup Globoplay Streams

Adtech director Beaklini sets out low-latency, hyper-personalised live insertion playbook.

Globo's director of adtech Ana Beaklini detailed the broadcaster's World Cup 2026 live ad-insertion playbook in early June, leaning on low-latency delivery and AI-driven decisioning to hyper-personalise spots across Globoplay, TV Globo, SporTV and ge for the country's biggest single advertising event. The strategy combines TV 3.0 standards work with dynamic SSAI to address the historic latency gap on big-event live streams. Globo's AI ad-decisioning stack is the most advanced CTV signal coming out of Brazil ahead of the tournament and a likely template for TelevisaUnivision and other Latin American broadcasters — making programmatic access into Globoplay's SSAI rails a live question for any buyer planning around the region's biggest live event.

Ottawa Orders CRTC To Scrap 15% Streamer CanCon Levy, Promises $600M Backfill

Heritage cites consumer cost pressure and US trade friction in killing tripled foreign-streamer contribution.

On June 3 the Canadian government directed the CRTC to review its decision that tripled foreign streamers' base contribution to Canadian-content funds from 5% to 15% of domestic revenue, promising a $600M taxpayer-funded backfill instead. Heritage cited consumer cost concerns and ongoing US trade pressure under the Online Streaming Act as it walked the levy back. The reversal protects Netflix, Disney+ and Amazon CTV ad-spend headroom heading into a heavy World Cup quarter while reshuffling the competitive balance against Bell, Rogers and Corus domestic AVOD — a structural shift the open market should price into 2026 H2 plans for the Canadian market.

China CTV Ad Spend Forecast To Reach $3.47B In 2026 Despite iQIYI Slip

Long-form streamers lean on AI tooling and OEM partnerships as Tencent and Mango eye AI-drama era.

Industry forecasts peg China CTV ad spend at $3.47B in 2026, up 11.5% YoY, even as long-form leaders face turbulence — iQIYI's online ad revenue dropped 9% to RMB 5.19B and Mango TV's pre-announced net profit is set to fall 33-47% for 2025. Tencent Video and iQIYI executives now predict the first blockbuster AI-generated drama will arrive in H2 2026, opening a new content cost structure. For global strategy, the China CTV market remains gated for US-headquartered demand, but the AI-content shift and OEM-led FAST growth keep it on the watch list for any APAC plan where TCL, Hisense or Xiaomi inventory shows up — those OEM operating systems are where Chinese supply most often surfaces in Western buys.

The Auction Has Swallowed The Buyer

PubMatic's containers and Google's co-view are not products. They are the marketplace acquiring an interior life.

The figure this week is the agent. PubMatic ships a fabric that lets MiQ, inPowered, Chalice and SWYM run their models as Docker containers inside the bid request — under ten milliseconds, sixty fields, a quiet little soul nested in the auction. The Trade Desk pushes pause-ad controls into Kokai. Google Ads quietly redefines a reach metric so that every co-viewer on a couch is counted. Olyzon, freshly funded by Sir Martin, ships five named agents — Map, Score, Adapt, Activate, Prove — to orchestrate the planners. That is the figure. The figure is not the story. The ground is the auction itself, which has grown an interior, and the buyer who used to stand outside it bidding has been quietly moved inside. Enhance: speed and reach — the model executes where the inventory lives. Obsolesce: the trader as a person sending bids from a chair; the open marketplace where buyer and seller faced one another across an exchange floor. Retrieve: the medieval bourse, where the buyer, the goods and the broker were all in one stone room and the negotiation was conducted in glances. Reverse: pushed far enough, the auction has nothing to deliver to, because the buyer is no longer in the room — he is the room. We march backwards into the future. The marketer who once selected an audience now writes a small program and ships it through a port. The agent is warm in a strange new way. Google's co-view metric is the same gesture in lower resolution: the medium constructs the audience it claims to measure. Joyce of course knew this in 1939. The agent is the content. — Marshall McLuhan

No Agent Can Save A Bad Spot

The auction has acquired a brain. The creative has a brief from 1985.

I have read this week of Decision Fabric, of Kokai's new AI knobs, of Dynamic TV Creative on Prime Video, of five named agents from Paris orchestrating the DSPs. The trade has not been this excited since it discovered the word 'incrementality'. Then on Wednesday TripleLift, which I had to ask my secretary to spell, published a study. Forty-nine percent of connected-television spots are still the fifteen- and thirty-second cuts our trade was making for the antenna in 1976. The streamers reach seventy-four percent of American television viewing. Forty-nine percent of the creative running through this glittering new pipework was built for a medium none of these viewers are watching. I call it a discipline problem. In 1951 Ellerton Jette of the Hathaway shirt company paid me thirty thousand dollars and gave me a free hand. The company had not advertised in 116 years. On the way to the photograph I stopped at a chemist on Lexington Avenue and bought an eyepatch for a dollar fifty. The campaign ran for twenty-one years. Hathaway sold out in a week and posted thirty-six percent more shirts in the first quarter. The eyepatch was an idea. No fabric of containers, no auction, no Docker, no five-agent decisioning rig will generate it for you. Ideas come from the discipline of looking at the product and the consumer until something true appears. If half of the spots running through these magnificent new rails are linear in disguise, then the cleverness of the bidding tower is academic. Sell the product. Build the brand. Test the work. Buy the receipt. And for God's sake, before you ask an agent to optimise a spot, ask whether the spot is worth showing. We sell, or else. — David Ogilvy

Walmart Cracks Open CTV Data, Routes VIZIO Audiences To Yahoo DSP

Magnite-piped integration ends single-DSP exclusivity on Walmart's first-party shoppers and brings closed-loop sales to a second buying surface.

Walmart Connect on May 28 made its first-party shopper audiences available inside Yahoo DSP for VIZIO connected-TV inventory, routed through Magnite supply with closed-loop measurement tied back to Walmart sales. Yahoo says the integration brings roughly 150 million Walmart shoppers into the DSP, and it marks the first time Walmart Connect's audiences have been activated outside its proprietary stack — a structural departure from the walled-garden posture Walmart has held since acquiring VIZIO. MediaPost, Beet.TV and AdExchanger covered the move as part of a broader Walmart Connect retooling of its offsite media stack and an explicit accommodation of multi-DSP buying. This is the week's most consequential partnership signal for the open market. Retail purchase data layered on SmartCast ACR via a neutral DSP gives planners a credible alternative to Amazon Ads and Roku Curate retail packages — and validates the multi-DSP, neutral-curation thesis that independent demand sells against the walled gardens. The question now for buy-side strategists is which Yahoo DSP buys already route through Magnite-SpringServe on VIZIO, and how quickly Walmart extends the same arrangement to The Trade Desk and DV360 — the breadth of that rollout will determine how far retail data travels beyond any single platform's stack.

Roku Redesigns Home Screen, Opens New Ad Real Estate

AI-driven layout picks from billions of household combinations and expands marquee placements.

Roku began rolling out its biggest home-screen overhaul in more than a decade on May 27, with an AI personalization engine that selects from billions of layout combinations per household, plus new Top Picks, a Quick Access apps row, a subscriptions area and a 'Your Daily Scoop' trending row. The redesign preserves Roku's three-column structure but expands right-rail ad real estate and pushes ad placements deeper into discovery surfaces. AdExchanger framed it as Roku trying to 'appease both consumers and advertisers' as ad-free subscriptions cap in-stream reach. The redesign is an explicit invitation to plan home-screen and marquee placements into Roku-led CTV plans — and a reminder for the open market that OEM/OS inventory is now a distinct line item alongside in-stream pods, sitting upstream of any streamer's ad break.

Upfront Commitments Now Drive Streaming's Programmatic Market

Disney says 70% of biddable demand is upfront-aligned; Warner Bros. Discovery near 50%.

Digiday's Future of TV Briefing this week reports that upfront commitments are driving the majority of programmatic activity at major streamers — 70% of Disney's biddable demand is upfront-aligned, with Warner Bros. Discovery approaching half. Sellers are increasingly routing upfront deals into PMPs to give buyers bidding flexibility while protecting committed dollars, accelerating what Digiday calls the collapse of the wall between upfront and programmatic. The piece frames biddable PMPs as the fastest-growing programmatic segment at Disney. The structural shift from open-market CTV to upfront-funded PMPs reshapes publisher relationships and curated deal IDs across the market — programmatic guarantee and biddable PMPs, not open auction, are increasingly where the streaming dollars actually clear, which changes how curators and DSPs have to source premium streaming supply.

Gracenote Pegs Show-Level Data As Linear-To-CTV Unlock

86% of US planners would shift more linear dollars to CTV with content-graph targeting and reporting.

Nielsen's Gracenote unit released an upfront-aligned study circulated through late May reporting that 86% of US media planners would move more linear budget to CTV if show-level targeting and reporting were available, with 65% willing to shift programmatic-video and 63% display dollars on the same condition. 47% of planners flag limited show- or content-level data as the primary barrier, and 89% expect to keep moving budget from linear to CTV over the next 24 months. Gracenote pitches its Content Graph and unique content IDs as the resolution layer. The data is a clean talking point for content-graph-powered CTV curation across the market, and it confirms that 'where the ad ran, in what show' — not just 'who saw it' — is the next measurement battleground for buy-side strategists and sellers alike.

AdExchanger: Email IDs Face A Credibility Crisis In CTV

Buyers and sellers question whether one-to-one identity fits a household, lean-back medium.

AdExchanger published a sharp look on May 28 at email-based identifiers like UID2 in CTV, arguing emails are a one-to-one display signal mis-applied to a co-viewing, household-level channel that historically transacts on IP and HHID. Critics in the piece say alt-ID providers do not audit whether underlying emails are accurate or consented, that FAST channels without logins are sourcing emails from third-party brokers, and that UID2's opacity gives 'a false sense of confidence in identity.' The story lands the same week Roku's home-screen redesign and Walmart's VIZIO-DSP move both lean on household and ACR signals rather than email matches. This is the sharpest mainstream challenge yet to the email-ID stack underpinning much of programmatic CTV — pushing the whole buy side toward articulating a household-plus-ACR-plus-retail ID philosophy that holds up against the UID2-skeptic narrative.

IAB Tech Lab Standardises Pause And Menu Ad Signaling

OpenRTB updates open public comment through June 5; SSPs queued to align.

IAB Tech Lab opened a public-comment window through June 5 on updates to its technical specs that standardise how the CTV Ad Portfolio's non-interruptive formats — Pause, Menu, Overlay and Squeeze-Back — are signalled programmatically across OpenRTB. The goal is fewer manual workarounds, clearer buyer/seller expectations and easier scale-out of emerging formats, with AdMonsters framing it as a key sell-side enablement step. Standardised signaling for non-linear CTV formats is exactly the rails the open market needs to bid Pause and Menu inventory at scale across publishers — the development to track is which SSPs especially Magnite SpringServe align to the new specs first, since curated deal IDs can only queue against standardised formats once the supply side adopts them.

Measured Ships MCP Server, Pipes Incrementality Into ChatGPT, Claude

Trevor Testwuide's pitch: ask the chatbot how the media performed.

Measured launched a Model Context Protocol server on May 28 that lets marketers query ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and other LLMs about media performance, drawing on more than 30,000 incrementality tests across 200-plus Measured clients. The pitch is conversational, on-demand incrementality reads grounded in causal methodology rather than last-click reporting, with CEO Trevor Testwuide noting that roughly 15% of clients still refuse to expose data to AI while others want to feed everything in. AdExchanger separately framed this as the first major MCP rollout from a TV-relevant measurement firm. MCP servers from measurement partners are the rails on which agentic media-buying will run — raising the bar for whether any outcomes-reporting stack in the market is similarly LLM-queryable for the clients and partners who will soon expect to ask their data questions in natural language.

Sorrell-Backed Olyzon Raises $10M For Agentic CTV Decisioning

Paris-based startup deploys five AI agents to orchestrate DSPs across global TV budgets.

Olyzon, a Paris-based TV ad decisioning platform with offices in New York and London, announced a $10 million Series A on May 28 led by Sir Martin Sorrell and Sanja Partalo's S4S Ventures, with participation from Cassius Capital, Ventech and Eurazeo. The platform runs five AI agents Map, Score, Adapt, Activate, Prove that orchestrate planning, activation and measurement across DSPs, SSPs and walled-garden CTV inventory, and is already live with brands including McDonald's, DoorDash, Audi and Mastercard via managed service. Sorrell framed Olyzon as sitting 'at the intersection of two forces reshaping our industry: the agentic AI revolution and the consolidation of CTV onto programmatic infrastructure.' A well-funded agentic decisioning layer that explicitly claims to orchestrate DSPs rather than replace them is both a partnership target and a strategic competitor for the independent programmatic stack — the question for the market is where Olyzon's managed-service motion overlaps the planning workflows curators and agencies already run.

Omdia Forecasts CTV Ad Market To Hit $81B By 2030

Google, Amazon and Netflix projected to capture half of all CTV ad dollars.

Omdia research re-circulated through trade press May 26-29 forecasts global CTV ad revenue rising from $44 billion in 2025 to $81 billion by 2030, with Google projected at 26% share, Amazon 13% and Netflix 9% — collectively roughly half the market. The report frames the living-room contest as a fight for 'the platform, the advertising layer, the operating system, the data and ultimately the consumer relationship,' not just streaming content. The forecast crystallises the platform-concentration problem that the independence pitch sells against — and it anchors the strategic question for the open market on the other 50% of CTV inventory that won't sit inside the three walled gardens by 2030, which is where independent demand and neutral curation have room to compete.

FTC Hits Cox Media Group With $880K Over 'Active Listening' Pitch

Agency calls smart-device ad targeting a 'phantom' service built on resold broker email lists.

The Federal Trade Commission required Cox Media Group, MindSift and 1010 Digital Works to pay $930,000 total to settle charges that they deceptively marketed an 'Active Listening' AI service claiming to target ads from conversations captured by smart devices. The FTC found the service did not listen to anything and instead resold marked-up email lists from data brokers, and rejected the idea that app terms-of-service clicks constitute opt-in consent for in-home voice surveillance. CMG will pay $880,000; MindSift and 1010 Digital Works each pay $25,000. The order sharpens FTC scrutiny of AI ad-tech overclaiming and tightens the consent standard for any CTV partner pitching device-graph or acoustic-signal data — a diligence bar that buy-side strategists now have to apply to every data partner across the open market.

EU AI Act Omnibus Keeps Article 50 Ad-Labelling Live For August

May 7 political deal extends some deadlines but preserves AI-content disclosure rules and fines.

EU lawmakers reached political agreement on May 7 on the AI Act 'omnibus' amendments, clarifying existing requirements, extending several high-risk system deadlines, and introducing rules on AI-generated intimate content — but the August 2 start date for Article 50 transparency obligations on AI-generated content was preserved. From August 2, anyone publishing AI-generated content must label it as such unless it has been reviewed and approved through a human editorial process, with penalties up to €15M or 3% of global turnover. The Commission's final Code of Practice on marking and labelling AI-generated content is due in June. The 90-day countdown to AI-labelling enforcement means every generative creative asset in an EMEA CTV flight needs a documented human-review trail — a compliance burden that agencies, DSPs and their creative partners across the European market have to build into delivery before August.

AdImpact Holds 2026 Cycle At $10.8B, CTV Share At $2.5B

Senate spend on track to set a new record; broadcast still 49% of total political dollars.

AdImpact's latest political projections keep the 2026 cycle on track to reach $10.8 billion — more than 20% above 2022 and the most expensive midterm on record — with $2.5 billion expected to flow to CTV, the fastest-growing channel in the mix. Broadcast retains the largest single share at 49% of total political spend, Senate spending is projected at $2.8 billion a new record , and House spend crosses $2 billion for the first time. Cumulative cycle ad spend had hit $2.01 billion by late January, pacing 46% ahead of the equivalent point in the 2022 cycle. The numbers anchor agency and broadcaster conversations across the political go-to-market and reinforce CTV as the highest-growth political channel into Q4 — a benchmark the whole buy side will plan against as midterm dollars accelerate.

ITV Lights Up Live Addressable+ On ITV1 With Omnicom Beta

Targeted spots arrive on live linear for the first time, bought through Planet V.

ITV on May 19 launched Live Addressable+, extending addressable ad targeting from ITVX into its live linear channels — ITV1, ITV2, ITV3, ITV4 and ITV Quiz — via an exclusive beta with Omnicom Media Group covering more than 20 advertiser brands across automotive, retail and telecoms. Bought through ITV's Planet V stack, the product layers first-party audiences, Carwow and Tesco Clubcard data via ITV Retail Match, and targeting against life stage, income, location and shopping behaviour. The technology will roll out to the wider market in the coming weeks. This is the strongest signal yet that the UK linear ad-pod is becoming biddable inventory, and Planet V is now the addressable rail that the Sky-ITV-C4 joint marketplace will eventually plug agencies into — a structural shift the British buy side will have to fold into addressable TV plans.

JioStar Closes IPL 2026 Book With 27 Sponsors As Final Hits May 31

Google AI Mode, Campa and Havells co-present; CTV base rate up 25% to Rs 600.

JioStar closed its IPL 2026 commercial book with 27 sponsors across the final weeks of the May 31-ending tournament, including Google Search AI Mode, Campa Energy, Havells and Lloyd as co-presenters, plus Asian Paints, MRF, Flipkart, Google Pay, TVS and Amul among associates. The publisher pushed its 10-second CTV base rate up 25% to Rs 600 for the season and opened self-serve buys to SMEs from Rs 4,000. IPL on JioHotstar is now the world's largest live streaming ad event with a tiered CTV/mobile rate card and an SME funnel — a template for how marquee sports inventory in growth markets gets sliced for addressable and biddable demand, and a forcing function for the open market to lock JioStar PMP frameworks ahead of WPL 2026 and Asia Cup.

Samsung Ads Stacks LATAM Bench To Press CTV Expansion

New Brazil sales lead, regional agency and operations heads in place under GM Melchert.

Samsung Ads named Eraldo Benazzi Head of Sales Brazil, Cris Camargo Head of Agencies and Indirect Sales LATAM and Felipe Lacordaire Head of Business Operations and Finance LATAM, completing a leadership build-out that began with regional GM Melchert's October 2025 arrival. The expansion is being framed internally as a response to CTV's role as the lead driver of the LATAM advertising ecosystem, with Mexico's CTV ad market alone forecast at 23%-plus CAGR through 2031. The largest smart-TV OEM in Brazil and Mexico doubling its agency-facing sell is a green light for activating Samsung Ads inventory inside LATAM plans that currently lean on Globo and Roku — broadening the OEM supply available to independent demand across the region.

CRTC Triples Streamer Cancon Levy To 15%, Sparks Trade Fight

Netflix, Disney, Paramount and Amazon all in scope; Ottawa says ruling will stand.

The CRTC on May 21 finalised rules requiring foreign streaming services with at least C$25 million in Canadian revenue to contribute 15% of those revenues to Canadian content — a tripling of the prior 5% benchmark — and to direct 30% of qualifying spend to partnerships with Canadian broadcasters and producers. The Motion Picture Association called it discriminatory and a CUSMA violation, and Ottawa said on May 29 it could not reverse the ruling. The decision is forecast to push more than C$2 billion a year into Canadian and Indigenous content. The levy effectively re-anchors global streamers to Canadian broadcaster co-pros, strengthening Bell Media, Corus and Quebecor as both content partners and ad-sales houses for the resulting Cancon inventory — reshaping where addressable demand can reach Canadian audiences across the market.

Nexxen Plugs TCL FFALCON Home-Screen Inventory Into Programmatic

Smart-TV launchpad units join VIDAA, TiVo in a biddable global home-screen stack.

Nexxen on May 13 expanded its TV Home Screen offering to include TCL FFALCON and TiVo Ads native inventory, making TCL's Android-TV launchpad units in the US and Canada exclusively accessible through Nexxen's DSP and TiVo's home-screen inventory biddable across North America and the UK. Nielsen data cited by Nexxen pegs the home-screen browsing window at up to 10.5 minutes per session, and the platform already includes Hisense's VIDAA — number two globally behind Samsung Tizen with 7.8% smart-TV share. The dominant Chinese OEM operating systems are now buyable in the same DSP construct as US smart-TV inventory, broadening the addressable footprint for independent demand into surfaces that sit upstream of any streamer's ad pod.

The Dashboard Becomes the Content of the Chat

When the buyer asks a question instead of clicking a tile, the trade has changed mediums.

Measured ships a Model Context Protocol server. Cadent installs itself inside Gemini Enterprise. Olyzon raises a Series A for five conversational agents that buy where the buyer once buttoned. Three motions in one week, three vendors who two years ago were dashboards. That is the figure. The figure is not the story. The ground is the chat window — the new console of the trade — and the dashboards have become its content. McLuhan's law: the content of any medium is always another medium. The content of the chat is the spreadsheet. The content of the spreadsheet was the ledger. The content of the ledger was the verbal report a clerk gave the merchant before the printing press. We have walked the chain backwards in eighteen months. The tetrad reads cleanly. Enhance: the question, the natural-language probe, the act of asking what happened. Obsolesce: the tile, the filter, the dropdown — the literate furniture of the post-Excel buyer. Retrieve: the oral office, the apprentice asking the master what the day brought, the medium of the desk read out loud. Reverse: fluent enough and the answer becomes liturgy; the buyer who once tested a hypothesis now consults an oracle. The chat that compresses every dashboard into a sentence will, at the limit, compress every sentence into a posture of trust. Watch the ratios. The eye, which had been hired by the dashboard, is being retired. The ear is being recalled to the office. The hand, which clicked, will now type a paragraph or speak it. The trade is becoming conversational again. Whether it remains a trade depends on whether the questions remain real. — Marshall McLuhan Columnist, Wire Opinion

Count What Sold. Then Build What Sells Next Year.

Performance CTV is a discipline, not a strategy. The brand pays for the next decade of receipts.

Every announcement this week is a receipt. Walmart pipes its shopper data into a second DSP. Gracenote says eighty-six per cent of planners will move more linear money the moment they can target a show. DeepIntent reports that healthcare CTV drives twice the new-to-brand prescription rate of online video. Three good pieces of news. All of them count what sold this quarter. None of them build what will sell in 2031. The principle they obscure is the oldest one in the file: a brand pays for next year's sales out of this year's investment, and a campaign that only books closed-loop returns starves the brand that produced them. I wrote the Hathaway shirt ad in 1951. The eyepatch sold thirty-six per cent more shirts in the first quarter; a fair receipt. It also kept selling Hathaway shirts for the next eighteen years, which is the receipt the spreadsheet does not show. The man with the eyepatch was not a measurement event; he was a brand image. Schweppes ran Commander Whitehead for eighteen years because we tested him and because we believed him. We sold the Schweppes case. We also built the Schweppes name. The Rolls-Royce ad — 'At sixty miles an hour…' — sold the inventory and made the car the standard against which every other quiet luxury was, for a generation, judged. Measure everything you can. Then defend the budget that builds the name. If the platform makes it easier to count CPGs through to Kroger receipts, splendid — count them. But do not let the receipt become the campaign. We sell, or else. Build the brand the receipt will, one day, ring up. — David Ogilvy Columnist, Wire Opinion
